cards.answer: The critical periods for weed competition are 3 weeks after planting and 14 weeks after planting, when weeds can cause high yield losses. Weeds are removed manually or by chemical methods; common control methods include manual weeding, cultivation and, in some cases, chemicals.

cards.question: Which insect pests and diseases affect sugar cane in Ethiopia, and how are they controlled?
cards.answer: Major insect pests are sugar cane borers, army worms, locusts and termites. Control includes pre-planting cultivation that destroys some insects and the use of insecticides. Common diseases are the fungal disease smut and the bacterial Ratoon Stunting Disease. Recommended remedies include disease-resistant sugar cane varieties, removal of diseased plants and the use of chemicals.

cards.question: Describe sugar cane harvesting operations, including the use of fire.
cards.answer: Sugar cane matures in about 14 to 18 months from planting. Harvesting includes removal of the leaves and the top of the plant before cutting the stem. Sometimes controlled fire is used to remove dry leaves before cutting the stem, and the stem is then transported to the processing facility.

cards.question: What was the status of sugar production in Ethiopia in 2022 and 2023, and what is the aim for the sector?
cards.answer: In 2022 there were 8 state-owned sugar producing factories in Ethiopia, annually producing 400,000 metric tons of sugar. In 2023 the demand for sugar in Ethiopia exceeded production, so production must increase. The aim is to fulfill local demand as well as export sugar.

cards.question: Name the eight state-owned sugar producing factories in Ethiopia listed in 2022.
cards.answer: The eight factories were Wonji-Shewa, Matahara, Finchawa, Kessem, Tendaho, Arjo, Omo kuraz II and Omo kuraz III.

cards.text: Sugar cane ({{c1::Saccharum officinarum L.}}) is a {{c2::tropical and sub-tropical}} crop that requires a long warm season and is grown mainly for {{c3::sugar}} production.
The dark liquid produced from sugar cane juice is {{c1::molasses}}, which is used in the production of {{c2::ethanol}}.
{{c1::Bagasse}} is the fibrous residue left after juice extraction; it is used to make {{c2::papers and plastics}} and can be used as firewood.

Newly planted sugar cane matures in {{c1::14 to 18 months}}; a ratoon crop regenerates from the roots and is ready in about {{c2::12 months}}, with only {{c3::2 or 3}} ratoon harvests after first planting.
Sugar cane requires large amounts of {{c1::nitrogen}} fertilizer, but excessive application can {{c2::delay the maturity time}} of the cane.
Sugar cane stem cuttings are about {{c1::30 cm}} long with at least {{c2::2 or 3 buds}} and must be free from diseases and pests.
Sugar cane cuttings are planted in rows about {{c1::1.6 m}} apart, placed end to end in a furrow and covered with {{c2::2 to 5 cm}} of soil.
The critical periods for weed competition in sugar cane are {{c1::3 weeks}} and {{c2::14 weeks}} after planting, when weeds can cause high yield losses.
Major sugar cane insect pests in Ethiopia are {{c1::borers}}, {{c2::army worms}}, {{c3::locusts}} and {{c4::termites}}; control includes pre-planting cultivation and {{c5::insecticides}}.
Common sugar cane diseases are the fungal disease {{c1::smut}} and the bacterial {{c2::Ratoon Stunting Disease}}; remedies include resistant varieties, removal of diseased plants and chemicals.
Before cutting the sugar cane stem, the {{c1::leaves}} and the {{c2::top}} of the plant are removed; sometimes {{c3::controlled fire}} is used to remove dry leaves.
In 2022 Ethiopia had {{c1::8}} state-owned sugar producing factories, which annually produced {{c2::400,000 metric tons}} of sugar.

cards.question: What are farm animal species raised for?
cards.answer: Farm animal species are raised for human use, either for food or for work functions.

cards.question: What are domesticated animals?
cards.answer: Domesticated animals are animals that have been selectively bred to live alongside humans.

cards.question: How does a species differ from a breed?
cards.answer: A species is the largest group of animals capable of interbreeding and producing fertile offspring. A breed is a specific group within a species that are visibly similar in most characteristics, which distinguishes it from other breeds of the same species; a species is often composed of several breeds.

cards.question: What are the three categories of farm animals found in Ethiopia?
cards.answer: They are mammalian, avian and honeybee species. Mammals include cattle, sheep, goats, camels, donkeys, horses and mules; avian species include chicken, ostrich and turkey; the stinging honeybee is the important bee species.

cards.question: What is a local breed? Give the textbook example.
cards.answer: A local breed is native to a specific territory of origin and is well adapted to local conditions; for example, Horro cattle.

cards.question: What are exotic breeds and how are they used?
cards.answer: Exotic breeds are mainly foreign breeds used primarily to improve the productivity of local breeds through cross breeding, for example Holstein Friesian.

cards.question: What is a hybrid (cross breed)? Give an example.
cards.answer: A hybrid, also called a cross breed, is produced from two genetically different parent lines, for example the offspring of a Horro cow crossed with a Holstein Friesian bull.

cards.question: Define Mammalia and Avian as used in the unit.
cards.answer: Mammalia are vertebrate animals whose young are nourished with milk from special mammary glands of the mother; Avian is a characteristic of birds or flying creatures.

cards.question: What is true about the breed composition of Ethiopia's livestock population?
cards.answer: Nearly all of the livestock population of the country is local breed; some are hybrid and others are exotic breeds.

cards.text: Domestication is the conversion of {{c1::wild animals}} to {{c2::domestic use}}.
Most domesticated animals familiar today were domesticated not long after people began farming and living in permanent settlements, probably between {{c1::8000}} and {{c2::2500 BC}}.

A {{c1::species}} is the largest group of animals capable of interbreeding and producing fertile offspring, while a {{c2::breed}} is a specific group within the species with visibly similar characteristics.
In Ethiopia, cattle, sheep, goats, camels, donkeys, horses and mules are the major {{c1::mammalian}} farm animals, while chicken, ostrich and turkey belong to the {{c2::avian}} category.
Ostrich and turkey are not widely used in Ethiopia, and the {{c1::stinging honeybee}} is the most important bee species in the country.

Local breeds are native to a specific territory and well adapted to local conditions, e.g., {{c1::Horro cattle}}; exotic breeds are mainly foreign and improve productivity of local breeds through {{c2::cross breeding}}, e.g., {{c3::Holstein Friesian}}.
A hybrid (cross breed) is produced from {{c1::two genetically different parent lines}}, e.g., offspring from a Horro cow × Holstein Friesian bull.
Mammalia are vertebrates whose young are nourished with milk from special {{c1::mammary glands}} of the mother; Avian is a characteristic of birds or flying creatures.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 4::4.1.1 Farm Animals in Ethiopia and Their Description

cards.text: Cattle are hoofed animals belonging to the family {{c1::Bovidae}} and genus {{c2::Bos}}, with Bos indicus and Bos taurus the two most common species in Ethiopia.
Bos indicus are {{c1::humped}} cattle commonly found in tropical countries, while Bos taurus are usually without humps and common in {{c2::temperate zones}}.
Cattle are raised all over the world and there are over {{c1::1000}} cattle breeds in the world.
Cattle are {{c1::ruminant}} herbivores that feed primarily on {{c2::pasture}}, which in modern farming is usually supplemented with industrially manufactured feeds.
In the rumen, softened plant material called {{c1::cud}} is {{c2::regurgitated}} for the animal to chew again, helping digestion of fibrous plants.
Sheep ({{c1::Ovis aries}}) belong to family Bovidae and genus Ovis, and over {{c2::200}} breeds of sheep are recognized worldwide.
Goat ({{c1::Capra hircus}}) is a hollow-horned mammal belonging to family Bovidae and genus Capra, with over {{c2::300}} distinct breeds.
The {{c1::Angora}} breed of goat is raised for its hair, which is used to make fabric or yarn called {{c2::mohair}}.
Camels are even-toed ungulates belonging to the family {{c1::Camelidae}} and genus {{c2::Camelus}}.
The Dromedary camel ({{c1::Camelus dromedary}}) has a {{c2::single hump}}, whereas the Bactrian camel (Camelus bactrianus L.) has two separate humps.
Pseudo-ruminants have only three stomach compartments — {{c1::omasum}}, {{c2::abomasum}} and {{c3::reticulum}} — lack a rumen, and do not regurgitate food or chew the cud.
Layers are raised for {{c1::egg production}}, while broilers are kept for meat and usually slaughtered at {{c2::6–8 weeks}}.
Chickens are {{c1::omnivorous}} in feeding habit, and poultry in general are {{c2::monogastric}} animals dependent on less fibrous feeds such as ground grains and mixed rations.
Most monogastrics are generally unable to digest much {{c1::cellulose}} food material such as grasses.
A honey bee colony is composed of {{c1::worker}}, {{c2::queen}} and {{c3::drone}} bees, each with its own specific duty.
Queens are reproductive and larger than workers; drones are male with much larger {{c1::compound eyes}} and no {{c2::stingers}}.
The estimated cattle population of Ethiopia is {{c1::70,291,776}}, of which {{c2::97.40%}} are local breeds, 2.29% hybrid and 0.31% exotic (CSA 2021 / 2013 E.C.).
The estimated sheep population is {{c1::42,914,865}} with 99.52% local breeds, and the goat population is {{c2::52,463,535}} with 99.9% local breeds.
The estimated chicken population is {{c1::56,992,987}} (78.85% local, 12.03% hybrid, 9.11% exotic), while camel population is {{c2::8,145,790}} and beehives {{c3::6,986,100}}.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 4::4.1.1 Farm Animals in Ethiopia and Their Description

cards.question: How do Bos indicus and Bos taurus cattle differ?
cards.answer: Bos indicus are humped cattle commonly found in tropical countries, whereas Bos taurus do not usually have humps and are commonly found in temperate zones.

cards.question: List the purposes and by-products of cattle production.
cards.answer: Cattle breeds serve multiple purposes: they are reared for meat, milk and as draft animals; their hides are processed into leather and manure is a by-product of cattle production.

cards.question: Explain what a ruminant is and what a cud is.
cards.answer: Ruminants are herbivores such as cattle that have a rumen; in the rumen eaten plants are softened, and the softened material is called cud, which is regurgitated for the animal to chew again. This helps digestion of fibrous plants.

cards.question: Define herbivore and pasture.
cards.answer: Herbivores are animals such as cattle, sheep and goats that feed on plants. Pasture is land with vegetation used for grazing animals.

cards.question: For what are sheep raised, and what do they eat?
cards.answer: Sheep are raised for meat, wool and skin; some farmers also keep them for milk. Like cattle they are ruminant herbivores, feeding on short fine grasses and coarse brushy weeds.

cards.question: Why are goats important in tropical livestock production and what products do they provide?
cards.answer: Goats are important domestic animals in tropical livestock production systems and are raised for milk, meat and skins across much of the world.

cards.question: Describe the feeding habits of goats.
cards.answer: Goats are ruminant herbivores that browse on shoots, twigs and leaves of brush plants; they also eat hay and grain-based complete feeds.

cards.question: Compare the Dromedary and Bactrian camels.
cards.answer: The Dromedary camel (Camelus dromedary) has a single hump on its back, while the Bactrian camel (Camelus bactrianus L.) has two separate humps.

cards.question: Why are camels called ships of the desert and what do they provide?
cards.answer: Camels have peculiar characteristics that adapt them to drier parts of the world, hence the name ships of the desert; they are recognized as pack or saddle animals and provide milk, meat, wool and hides.

cards.question: Define pseudo-ruminant animals and give an example.
cards.answer: Pseudo-ruminants have only three stomach compartments, lack a rumen, and do not regurgitate food or chew the cud; the camel is an example.

cards.question: Describe the feeding habits of camels and the role of their lips.
cards.answer: Camels are herbivores that eat tree leaves, branches and thorny bushes; their thick and tough lips allow them to feed easily on thorny bushes.

cards.question: List the common types of poultry and identify the most common one.
cards.answer: Common poultry types are chicken/fowl, duck, guinea fowl, turkey and geese; chicken is the most common type of poultry in many countries.

cards.question: Distinguish layers from broilers.
cards.answer: Layers are raised for egg production; broilers are kept for meat and are usually slaughtered at 6–8 weeks.

cards.question: Define omnivorous and monogastric animals, giving examples.
cards.answer: Omnivorous animals such as chicken feed on a variety of food of both plant and animal origin. Monogastric animals have a single stomach; examples include poultry, pigs and horses, and most cannot digest much cellulose such as grasses.

cards.question: Describe the three types of bees in a honey bee colony.
cards.answer: A colony has workers, queen and drones, each with specific duties. Workers and queen are female; the queen is reproductive and larger than workers. Drones are male, have much larger compound eyes and do not have stingers.

cards.question: What do honey bees rely on for food and what are they known for?
cards.answer: Honey bees rely on pollen and nectar of flowers as sources of food and are known for pollination and honey production.

cards.question: What is fish farming and why is it important?
cards.answer: Fish have served as important food sources worldwide; in fish farming, fish are raised in enclosures and used for food. Fish farming is the fastest growing area of animal food production, and Tilapia is shown as an example.

cards.question: According to Table 4.1, which species has the largest shares of hybrid and exotic breeds?
cards.answer: Chicken, with 12.03% hybrid and 9.11% exotic breeds, compared with very small shares in cattle, sheep and goats.

cards.text: Ruminant animals have a {{c1::four-chambered}} stomach and are mainly herbivores such as cows, sheep and goats that eat large amounts of roughage or fibre.
The {{c1::esophagus}} is a long tube that carries feed from the mouth to the stomach of a ruminant.
The four chambers of the ruminant stomach are the {{c1::rumen}}, {{c2::reticulum}}, {{c3::omasum}} and {{c4::abomasum}}.
The rumen is the {{c1::first and largest}} compartment and acts as a big fermentation vat where microorganisms such as {{c2::bacteria}} digest feed and allow digestion of cellulose.
Ruminants chew their feed numerous times through a process called {{c1::regurgitation}} or {{c2::rumination}}.
The reticulum is the second compartment, also called the {{c1::honeycomb}}, involved in rumination and passage of food from the rumen to the {{c2::omasum}}.
The rumen and reticulum are connected and work in concert, so they are sometimes called the {{c1::reticulorumen}}.
The omasum is the third chamber situated between the {{c1::reticulum}} and {{c2::abomasum}}; it squeezes water from feed and is called {{c3::many plies}} because of its folds.
The {{c1::abomasum}} is the fourth compartment and the true stomach, where digestive juices are produced before feed passes to the small intestine and large intestine.
In the horse, the stomach serves as a reservoir for {{c1::short term storage}} and digestion where enzymes break down feed components for absorption into the bloodstream.
The horse cecum is an enlarged structure containing {{c1::microorganisms}} needed for fermentation and digestion of roughage.
In chickens, food taken in with the beak moves through the esophagus to the {{c1::crop}}, an expandable storage compartment at the base of the neck where it can remain up to {{c2::12 hours}}.
The chicken stomach is subdivided into the {{c1::proventriculus}} (glandular stomach producing acid and enzymes) and the {{c2::gizzard}} (muscular stomach and pacemaker of gut motility).

In chickens, residue passes through the {{c1::ceca}} where bacteria break down undigested food, then to the large intestine which absorbs water, and finally through the {{c2::cloaca}} out at the {{c3::vent}}.
The white in chicken droppings is {{c1::urine}}, which mixes with waste in the cloaca before both exit at the vent.

cards.question: Why is the ruminant digestive system more efficient than that of monogastrics?
cards.answer: The ruminant digestive system is more efficient than that of monogastric animals in breaking down food and absorbing nutrients, which suits their large intake of roughage or fibre.

cards.question: Describe the first steps of digestion in ruminants.
cards.answer: Digestion begins with ingestion of feed into the mouth, where the tongue and teeth gather feed and break it into smaller pieces; the esophagus then carries feed from the mouth to the stomach.

cards.question: What is the function of the rumen?
cards.answer: The rumen is the first and largest compartment, a big fermentation vat that allows ruminants to digest cellulose in plants; microorganisms such as bacteria inside the rumen digest the feed.

cards.question: What is the reticulum and what does it do?
cards.answer: The reticulum is the second stomach compartment, called the honeycomb because it looks like a bee honeycomb; it helps digest food, is involved in rumination and controls passage of food from the rumen to the omasum.

cards.question: Why are the rumen and reticulum sometimes called the reticulorumen?
cards.answer: Because they are connected and work in concert to digest feed and move it onward.

cards.question: What is the omasum and where is it located?
cards.answer: The omasum is the third chamber, situated between the reticulum and abomasum; it helps digest feed, squeezes water from the feed and is called many plies because of its many folds.

cards.question: What is the abomasum and what happens after it?
cards.answer: The abomasum is the fourth compartment, called the true stomach; digestive juices are produced there and help feed pass into the small intestine, then the large intestine, and finally out through the rectum or anus.

cards.question: What general features describe monogastric animals?
cards.answer: Monogastric animals have a single stomach and generally rely on feedstuffs that are easy to digest; they can have all types of food habits, and horses and poultry are agricultural examples.

cards.question: Trace the digestive tract of the horse from ingestion to excretion.
cards.answer: Feed enters the mouth where tongue and teeth break it down, moves through the esophagus to the stomach for short-term storage and enzymatic digestion, then to the small intestine for further breakdown and nutrient absorption, then to the cecum for fermentation of roughage, and is excreted through the rectum or anus.

cards.question: What role does the horse cecum play?
cards.answer: The horse cecum is an enlarged structure containing many microorganisms needed to ferment and digest the large amount of plant material and roughage the horse consumes.

cards.question: Describe how food moves through the mouth, esophagus and crop in a chicken.
cards.answer: Food is taken in with the beak; a small bit of saliva and digestive enzymes are added as it moves through the esophagus to the crop, an expandable storage compartment at the base of the neck where food can remain up to 12 hours.

cards.question: How do the proventriculus and gizzard differ?
cards.answer: The chicken stomach has two parts: the proventriculus (glandular stomach) produces acid and enzymes, while the gizzard is the muscular stomach and pacemaker of gut motility; both are pivotal for digestion and gut health.

cards.question: Describe the remaining route of feed through the chicken digestive system.
cards.answer: From the gizzard food passes to the small intestine for nutrient absorption, then through the ceca (blind sacs where bacteria break down undigested food), to the large intestine which absorbs water and dries indigestible food, then to the cloaca where urine mixes with waste, and out at the vent.

cards.question: Compare the digestive systems of ruminants, pseudo-ruminants and monogastrics.
cards.answer: Ruminants have a four-chambered stomach (rumen, reticulum, omasum, abomasum) and chew the cud; pseudo-ruminants such as camels have three compartments (reticulum, omasum, abomasum), no rumen and no cud chewing; monogastrics such as poultry, pigs and horses have a single stomach and rely on easily digested feed.

cards.text: Animal production, also called {{c1::animal husbandry}}, is the keeping of farm animals for human use.
More than {{c1::34%}} of global food protein supply comes from farm animals, which are also rich sources of fats, minerals and vitamins essential for a healthy balanced diet.
Several animals convert {{c1::high-fiber feeds}} into edible food consumed by humans.
Animal production provides the livelihood for {{c1::65%}} of the population in Ethiopia.
Since {{c1::2018}}, the livestock sector has contributed {{c2::45 to 48%}} of the Agricultural Gross Domestic Product in Ethiopia and {{c3::16 to 19%}} of total export earnings.
Bullocks and camel draw working machinery like {{c1::ploughs}}, harrow and ridge, and some animals are used in crop husbandry such as seeding with drills and in crop processing such as threshing.
Camels, donkeys and horses are used to {{c1::transport people and goods}} in many parts of the developing world.
Livestock ownership, especially ownership of {{c1::cattle}}, is an index of social wealth, usually assessed in a traditional society by the {{c2::herd size}} owned.
Funerals, {{c1::ritual slaughter}} and {{c2::bride wealth}} of families and communities are social functions fulfilled by slaughtering animals.

cards.question: Summarize the roles farm animals play in the farm ecosystem.
cards.answer: Farm animals are primarily reared for production of consumable foods, provide pulling power as draught services, supply by-products used for clothing, feed, fertilizer or medicine, and play economic, cultural and social roles in society.

cards.question: What are the two most important categories of animal work?
cards.answer: Traction and transport. Bullocks and camels draw machinery such as ploughs, harrows and ridges, are used in seeding with drills and threshing, while camels, donkeys and horses transport people and goods.

cards.question: How are animal by-products used for clothing?
cards.answer: Skin, wool and fur are used to prepare clothing, footwear, bags and drums; poultry feathers are used in the production of mattresses and pillows.

cards.question: List raw materials obtained from animals and their uses.
cards.answer: Skins and wool from goats and sheep supply cottage-industry household products; bones and hooves are used for adhesives; fats for candles and soap; chemical or liquid extractions from internal organs are used in pharmaceutical industries to manufacture hormones and other drugs.

cards.question: How do slaughter residues become livestock feed?
cards.answer: Residues from slaughtered animals are used to prepare feed for monogastric animals: bone meal, fish meal, blood meal and meat meal are good sources of protein and amino acids for optimal feeding.

cards.question: Explain the socio-cultural roles of livestock.
cards.answer: Livestock ownership, especially cattle, is an index of social wealth judged by herd size; livestock also serve savings and investment, security and insurance, stability and social functions such as rituals, funerals, ritual slaughter and bride wealth.

cards.question: Why are animal products important in the diet?
cards.answer: Animal products are rich sources of fats, minerals and vitamins and are essential for a healthy and balanced diet, alongside being a major source of food protein.

cards.question: How does animal production support income and capital accumulation?
cards.answer: Farm animals are an important source of income and a way of capital accumulation and savings; the livestock sector contributes substantially to agricultural GDP and export earnings in Ethiopia.

cards.question: What traditional household products come from skins and wool?
cards.answer: Skins and wool from goats and sheep are used as raw materials for various traditional household products in the cottage industry.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 4::4.3 Constraints in Animal Production and Their Mitigation Strategies

cards.text: The major constraint affecting animal production in Ethiopia is {{c1::inadequate feed supply}} in both quantity and quality; main feed resources are natural pastures and crop residues.
Feed shortage in quantity can be mitigated through expanding {{c1::commercial feed production}} of improved grasses, legumes and formulated feeds.
Feed quality can be enhanced with young succulent grass at the {{c1::30% flowering stage}}, mixing mature grass with legumes, and chopping matured grass with {{c2::molasses}}.
Indigenous animals are known for quality products in terms of {{c1::yolk color, milk fat and meat taste}}.
Genetic improvement can be achieved through proper feeding, {{c1::selecting those with good production}} and crossing with exotic breeds.
Examples of animal diseases in Ethiopia include Anthrax, Blackleg, {{c1::Contagious bovine pleuropneumonia}} and Newcastle disease.
Disease prevention includes proper feeding, {{c1::vaccination}}, isolation and treatment of sick animals, and proper cleaning and management of animals and housing.
In mixed farming, draft animals are the major focus; in pastoral farming, {{c1::milk}} is the main focus and meat is considered a {{c2::by-product}}.
Pastoral farmers consider livestock a means of {{c1::capital accumulation}} and sell them when need arises or when feed and water are short, due to absence of {{c2::entrepreneurial awareness}}.
Modern animal production knowledge can be enhanced through recurrent capacity building, demonstration of modern farming, availing {{c1::credit facility}} and a strong {{c2::extension system}}.
Socio-economic constraints include weak extension services, shortage of appropriate technologies and poor {{c1::infrastructure}}.
Farmers have little or no access to training on modern animal rearing and there is inadequate flow of {{c1::market information}}; taboos include not eating {{c2::goats' meat}} or fish in some areas.
The unit summary lists feed shortages, genetic factors, diseases and parasites, farmers' poor knowledge, lack of favorable infrastructure and {{c1::water shortages}} as major constraints.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 4::4.3 Constraints in Animal Production and Their Mitigation Strategies

cards.question: What are the main feed resources and their feeding value?
cards.answer: Natural pastures and crop residues supply more than 90% of the annual feed but have poor feeding value in crude protein (3 to 6%), energy value, minerals and digestibility.

cards.question: How does seasonal variation in feed affect animals?
cards.answer: Feed resources are exhausted quickly in the dry season, so animals are maintained with less feed than their usual requirement, affecting productivity and reproductive potential.

cards.question: Why is the use of agro-industrial by-products limited?
cards.answer: By-products such as wheat bran, oil seed cakes and molasses are very limitedly used because of unavailability, expensiveness and lack of awareness of their importance as animal feed.

cards.question: How can the quantity shortage of feed be mitigated?
cards.answer: By expanding commercial feed production, including improved grasses, legumes and formulated feeds.

cards.question: List the feed quality enhancement strategies mentioned.
cards.answer: Using young and succulent grass at the 30% flowering stage, mixing mature grass with legumes, and chopping matured grass and mixing it with molasses.

cards.question: What advantages do local breeds have?
cards.answer: Local breeds are well adapted to local conditions, resistant to many tropical diseases, can survive and produce on low quality feed, and are known for quality products in terms of yolk color, milk fat and meat taste.

cards.question: What genetic improvement measures are recommended?
cards.answer: Proper feeding, selecting animals with good production, and crossing with exotic breeds.

cards.question: What effects do diseases and parasites have on production?
cards.answer: Diseases affect the efficiency of animal productivity, hamper export market development, and internal and external parasites place additional burdens on the sector.

cards.question: List the disease prevention mechanisms given in the text.
cards.answer: Proper feeding, vaccination, isolation of sick animals, treating sick animals, and proper cleaning and management of animals and their housing.

cards.question: How does the traditional production system constrain animal production?
cards.answer: Many farmers have no knowledge of modern animal production; draft animals are the focus in mixed farming and milk is the focus in pastoral farming, making meat a by-product, with livestock sold only when needed or when feed and water are short because of absent entrepreneurial awareness.

cards.question: How do pastoral farmers treat their livestock?
cards.answer: Pastoral farmers consider livestock a means of capital accumulation and sell them if the need arises or when shortages of feed and water occur, reflecting absence of entrepreneurial awareness.

cards.question: What measures can enhance farmers' knowledge of modern animal production?
cards.answer: Recurrent capacity building, demonstrating the modern way of farming, availing credit facilities and a strong extension system.

cards.question: What are socio-economic constraints in livestock development?
cards.answer: They are a lack of services and facilities vital for development, such as weak extension services, shortage of appropriate technologies and poor infrastructure.

cards.question: How do electricity and transport shortages affect livestock development?
cards.answer: Electricity is needed to preserve perishable items such as meat, milk, drugs and vaccines; scarcity of transport facilities hampers the flow of livestock and their products.

cards.question: List the remaining socio-economic and social constraints.
cards.answer: Lack of credit and saving services, little or no access to training on modern rearing, inadequate market information, and taboos such as not eating goats' meat or fish in some areas and not preferring cross breed products like egg, meat and milk.

cards.text: Livestock farming systems, differentiated by the production processes that take place in them, are generally classified as {{c1::extensive}}, {{c2::semi-intensive}} and {{c3::intensive}} systems.
Extensive farming is an animal production system that uses small inputs of {{c1::labour}}, {{c2::fertilizers}} and {{c3::capital}} relative to the land area used.
Extensive livestock farming is common in areas of {{c1::low agricultural productivity}}, uses locally known breeds, and feed depends on the condition of the {{c2::climate}}.
{{c1::Pastoralism}} is an extreme example of extensive farming where herders move their animals to get pastures from occasional rainfall.
Major problems of the pastoral production system are feed and water shortage, poor market outlet, disease and {{c1::number oriented livestock production}}.
{{c1::Nomads}} have no permanent home but move from place to place with their herds and flocks in search of water and feed, usually without much long-term planning.
{{c1::Transhumance}} have a permanent home to which they return each year, with seasonal and recurring movement of livestock across regions.
Transhumance aims to use distant pasture during the {{c1::rainy season}} and what remains after harvest around farm houses, with fixed seasonal grazing areas and routes.
In the {{c1::agro-pastoral}} system, crops are produced for subsistence and market while livestock are kept for draft, sale and primary products such as milk, meat and eggs.
{{c1::Ranching}} is the practice of raising large numbers of animals on fenced land or land with fixed boundaries, with relatively little labor input compared to land and animal numbers.
In mixed farming, equines ({{c1::horse, mule and donkey}}) are used for transport and animal dung serves as manure to improve {{c2::soil fertility}}.
Natural pasture and crop residues such as {{c1::teff, barley and wheat straws}} are the major feed resources in mixed farming, which is {{c2::subsistence-oriented}}.

cards.question: Describe the general characteristics of extensive livestock farming.
cards.answer: It commonly refers to cattle, sheep and goat farming in areas with low agricultural productivity, uses locally known breeds, feed depends on climate, and there is severe pasture and fodder shortage in the dry season.

cards.question: Compare productivity and labour in extensive versus intensive farming.
cards.answer: Extensive farming tends to have much lower productivity, slower growth rate and longer time to maturity, but requires less labour per unit area than intensive farming.

cards.question: What is the role of pastoralism and what problems does it face?
cards.answer: Pastoralism allows communities to feed themselves in areas that do not support other agriculture and is a livelihood system and way of life for millions in Ethiopia; major problems are feed and water shortage, poor market outlet, disease and number-oriented production.

cards.question: Where is nomadism found and what is its production goal?
cards.answer: Nomadism is mainly found in arid and semi-arid areas, and the production system is largely based on increasing animal number.

cards.question: How does transhumance differ from nomadism?
cards.answer: Transhumant pastoralists have a permanent home to which they return each year, moving flocks and herds away for part of the year in seasonal, recurring movement across regions along fixed grazing areas and routes; nomads have no permanent home.

cards.question: What is an agro-pastoral system?
cards.answer: A system in which livestock are important components of the farming system; crops are produced for subsistence and market, and livestock are kept for draft, sale and other primary products such as milk, meat and eggs.

cards.question: Why is ranching considered a modern alternative to pastoralism?
cards.answer: Ranchers commonly raise grazing animals such as cattle and sheep for meat, dairy or wool, with the function of providing cash income and making profit, and relatively little labor input.

cards.question: What is mixed farming?
cards.answer: A system in which crops and livestock are raised on the same farm: cows for milk, goats and sheep for meat and wool, food crops and hay grown to feed animals, equines for transport, and manure to improve soil fertility; it is subsistence-oriented.

cards.question: Which extensive production system involves relatively better livestock management according to the review question?
cards.answer: Ranching.

cards.question: List the different forms of extensive production system described.
cards.answer: Pastoralism (including nomadism and transhumance), agro-pastoral system, ranching and mixed farming.

cards.text: The semi-intensive system lies between extensive and intensive systems and is characterized by {{c1::high input and high output}} relative to extensive production.
Semi-intensive systems are usually located around the periphery of {{c1::large towns}} and are commonly practiced by {{c2::small scale producers}}.

cards.question: What is the purpose and potential of the semi-intensive system?
cards.answer: Animals are reared for family consumption but surplus can be sold for income generation, and the system can easily be intensified.

cards.question: Where and by whom is semi-intensive production usually practiced?
cards.answer: Usually around the periphery of large towns and commonly by small-scale producers.

cards.text: Intensive production systems are characterized by {{c1::high inputs with high output}}, with livestock raised at high stocking density.
Intensive systems are {{c1::market-oriented}}, often located near highly populated urban centers, and use {{c2::crossbred or exotic}} animals.
Feed in intensive systems is grown forage used in a {{c1::cut and carry system}}, along with industrial by-products and balanced rations supplemented with proteins, minerals and vitamins.
Examples of intensive farming include {{c1::pig production}}, broiler production, feedlot operations and commercial dairy production.
Cut and carry system, also called {{c1::zero grazing}}, is feeding fresh grass cut daily to housed animals throughout the grazing season.
A balanced ration supplies proper amounts and proportions of nutrients for a specific purpose such as growth, maintenance, {{c1::lactation}} or gestation.
A {{c1::feedlot}} is a plot of land where livestock are fed intensively for fattening for slaughter; cattle, sheep, goats and camels are fattened for 3 to 4 months for market.

The unit summary describes the extensive system as traditional and subsistence, the intensive system as modern and market-oriented, and the semi-intensive system as {{c1::somewhere in between}} the two.

cards.question: Describe the main features of intensive livestock production.
cards.answer: It is a modern, market-oriented farming system with high inputs and operations, high stocking density, animals often crossbred or exotic, usually located near populated urban centers, and an environment that can be modified for specialized breeds and production systems.

cards.question: Give examples of intensive farming and its main products.
cards.answer: Examples are pig production, broiler production, feedlot operations and commercial dairy production; main products are meat, milk and eggs.

cards.question: Define cut and carry system.
cards.answer: Cut and carry system, also called zero grazing, is a feeding system where fresh grass is cut daily and fed to housed animals throughout the grazing season.

cards.question: What is a balanced ration?
cards.answer: The amount of feed that supplies the proper amount and proportions of nutrients needed for an animal to perform a specific purpose such as growth, maintenance, lactation or gestation.

cards.question: What is a feedlot and for how long are animals fattened?
cards.answer: A feedlot is a plot of land where livestock are kept and fed intensively for fattening for slaughter; cattle, sheep, goats and camels are usually fattened for 3 to 4 months for market.

cards.question: Compare intensive and extensive farming using Table 4.2 parameters.
cards.answer: Intensive uses high labour and capital, high animal density per land size, exotic or crossbred animals, large output per land size and is generally closer to market; extensive uses low labour and capital, low animal density, largely indigenous animals, small output per land size and is largely distant from market.

cards.question: What is animal nutrition, and why is feed the most important factor in livestock production?
cards.answer: Animal nutrition is the science of feed preparation and feeding. Feed determines animal performance and profitability; feed cost is the largest operating cost in a livestock enterprise, varying from 50% to 80% depending on the operating area.

cards.question: What are the consequences of overfeeding and underfeeding farm animals?
cards.answer: Overfeeding is wasteful and costly, while underfeeding decreases animal performance and profitability. Farmers must supply the right amount of feed; feasibility of livestock enterprises always depends on proper feeding and nutrition.

cards.text: Feed cost is the largest operating cost in livestock production, varying from {{c1::50% to 80%}} depending on the operating area.
The main livestock feed resources available in Ethiopia are natural pastures, {{c1::crop residues}}, improved forages and {{c2::agro-industrial by-products}}.

cards.question: What are natural pastures, and how much of livestock feed do they usually provide?
cards.answer: Natural pastures are naturally occurring grasses, shrubs and tree forages (edible portions of plants) that grow on their own and are fed upon by farm animals. They usually provide more than 60% of livestock feed.

cards.question: Which management practices ensure a continuous supply of grasses and legumes from pasture?
cards.answer: Grazing land management, fertilizer application (e.g., urea and DAP), oversowing legumes, and prevention of weeds, pests and diseases. The correct number of animals should graze the pasture; overgrazing does not ensure increased productivity of pasture.

cards.text: Grazing is the {{c1::least expensive}} way to deliver feed to animals; natural pasture usually provides more than {{c2::60%}} of livestock feed.
Natural pasture is of good quality in the {{c1::wet season}} but usually diminishes in the dry season; applying {{c2::urea and DAP}} ensures rapid and succulent growth.

cards.question: Define crop residues and give examples shown in the textbook.
cards.answer: Crop residues are the remaining portions of crops after harvesting the main crop for human consumption. Examples include straws, stovers, cobs, hulls and chaffs: wheat stubble, millet straw, maize stover, barley straw and teff straw.

cards.question: What are the nutritional limitations of crop residues, and how can their quality be improved?
cards.answer: They are low in crude protein, energy and micronutrients (vitamins and minerals), fibrous, and of low palatability and digestibility. Quality is improved by supplementing with improved forages (forage legumes and browse species), grains and other concentrates, by physical methods such as chopping, or chemically by treating with ordinary urea fertilizer.

cards.question: Why are crop residues generally not suitable for pig and poultry feeding?
cards.answer: Because they are fibrous, low in palatability and digestibility and low in crude protein, energy and micronutrients, crop residues generally are not suitable for pig and poultry feeding.

cards.text: Crop residues provide the majority (greater volume) of livestock feed but are low in {{c1::crude protein}}, energy and micronutrients.

Crop residue quality can be improved physically by {{c1::chopping}} or chemically by treatment with {{c2::ordinary urea fertilizer}}; residues are generally not suitable for {{c3::pig and poultry}} feeding.

cards.question: What are forage crops, and what are the two basic types?
cards.answer: Forage crops are plants cultivated for their edible vegetative portions and used fresh or preserved for feeding livestock. The two basic types are grasses and legumes.

cards.question: Compare grasses and legumes as forage crops for livestock.
cards.answer: Grasses are the best and cheapest bulk feed for ruminants, produce more yield per unit area than legumes and are higher in fiber; examples are Rhodes grass, Sudan grass and Elephant grass. Legumes contain more protein, vitamins and minerals than grasses and are a cheap supplement with crop residues and natural pastures; examples are Alfalfa, Vetch and Sesbania sesban.

cards.question: What happens to forage crop quality as the plants mature, and how can farmers use cultivated forages?
cards.answer: Nutritive value and digestibility generally decline as forage crops mature. Cultivated forage crops can be cut and fed fresh or conserved for the dry season; farmers should be encouraged to produce improved forages to increase animal productivity.

cards.question: Why is forage production an attractive business, and what products can be sold?
cards.answer: Feed shortage is a major challenge for animal farming in Ethiopia, so forage production has good year-round market demand and growth potential. Grass-legume mixtures give the best yield, nutritional quality and highest profit margins. Farmers can sell green forage, good quality hay and planting materials (seed, cutting, splits and seedlings); youth and women groups can be supported with land and regulated short-term loans.

cards.text: Grasses are the best and cheapest {{c1::bulk feed}} for ruminants, yield more per unit area and are higher in {{c2::fiber}} than legumes; examples are Rhodes grass, Sudan grass and Elephant grass.
Legumes contain more {{c1::protein, vitamins and minerals}} than grasses; examples used for feed are Alfalfa, Vetch and {{c2::Sesbania sesban}}.

cards.question: What are agro-industrial by-products, and which are commonly used as animal feed?
cards.answer: They are by-products obtained from various agro-industries, usually used to supplement crop residues such as straw. Commonly used ones are flour milling by-products, oilseed cakes, molasses and brewery by-products. They are rich either in energy or protein compared with pastures and crop residues.

cards.question: What are flour milling by-products and what is their feeding value?
cards.answer: They are very palatable and readily consumed by all classes of farm animals; examples are wheat bran, wheat middling and rice bran. Brans are pleasant-tasting and laxative, good sources of thiamine and niacin, and supply fair amounts of protein and energy. Cereal middlings and rice polish are lower in fiber and higher in energy than brans.

cards.question: What are oilseed cakes or meals, and give examples used as feed.
cards.answer: Oilseed cakes are residues obtained after the extraction of oil from oilseeds. They have high protein, carbohydrate, mineral and nitrogen contents. Examples are soybean meal, noug seed cake, cottonseed cake, peanut cake and ground nut cake.

cards.question: What is molasses, what is its nutrient value and what special roles does it play in feed?
cards.answer: Molasses is a by-product of the sugar industry. It is a good source of energy (54% TDN), low in protein (3%) and minerals. It is an appetizer and a dust settler: animals like the taste and it stops dry food from becoming dusty.

cards.question: Which brewery by-products are used as feed, and what do they contain?
cards.answer: The main brewery by-products are spent grain and spent yeast. Brewer's spent grain contains good protein, fiber and energy and is higher in fiber, protein and minerals than the initial grains. Brewer's spent yeast is a cheap source of protein, minerals and vitamin B-complexes.

cards.text: Bran consists of the outer layers ({{c1::cuticle, pericarp and seed coat}}) combined with small amounts of starchy endosperm; examples are wheat bran, maize bran and rice bran.
Cereal middlings are the product of flour milling that is not {{c1::flour}} (e.g., wheat middling and maize middling); rice polish is obtained by {{c2::brushing the grain}} to polish the kernel.
A laxative feed ferments quickly in the stomach and therefore stimulates {{c1::elimination of the bowels}}.
Oilseed cakes are residues obtained after the {{c1::extraction of oil}} from oilseeds and are high in protein, carbohydrate, minerals and nitrogen.
Molasses is a by-product of the sugar industry containing {{c1::54% TDN}} and only {{c2::3%}} protein; it acts as an appetizer and {{c3::dust settler}}.
Brewer's spent grain is higher in {{c1::fiber, protein and minerals}} than the initial grains, while brewer's spent yeast supplies protein, minerals and {{c2::vitamin B-complexes}}.

cards.question: How are feeds broadly classified in livestock feeding?
cards.answer: Feeds are broadly classified into roughages and concentrates, based on their nutritive value.

cards.text: The feeds used in livestock feeding are broadly classified as {{c1::roughages}} and {{c2::concentrates}}.

cards.question: Define roughages in terms of crude fiber and Total Digestible Nutrients (TDN).
cards.answer: Roughages are bulky feeds high in fibrous carbohydrates, with low digestible energy and low nutrient digestibility. They contain more than 18% crude fiber and less than 60% TDN; the high crude fiber makes them less digestible than concentrates.

cards.question: What does TDN stand for, and what does it measure?
cards.answer: TDN means Total Digestible Nutrients: the sum of the digestible fiber, protein, lipid (fat) and carbohydrate components of an animal feedstuff.

cards.question: What are the two main forms of roughages, and what are their dry matter contents?
cards.answer: Dry roughages include hay, straw, stover, husks and sugarcane bagasse and contain about 80 to 90% dry matter. Green or succulent roughage from growing pastures has high water content and low dry matter (10 to 30%); silage is produced from green roughage.

cards.question: Why are roughages important in livestock feeding?
cards.answer: They are the natural feed for herbivore animals and constitute over 50% of the feedstuff fed to livestock, even though their digestibility is low.

cards.text: Roughages contain more than {{c1::18%}} crude fiber and less than {{c2::60%}} Total Digestible Nutrients (TDN).
TDN is the sum of digestible {{c1::fiber}}, protein, lipid (fat) and {{c2::carbohydrate}} components of an animal feedstuff.
Dry roughages include hay, straw, stover, husks and {{c1::sugarcane bagasse}} and contain about {{c2::80 to 90%}} dry matter.
Green, growing pastures provide {{c1::green or succulent}} roughage with {{c2::10 to 30%}} dry matter, and silage is produced from green roughage.

cards.question: Define concentrates and give their crude fiber, TDN and protein ranges.
cards.answer: Concentrates are rich sources of nutrients with higher nutritive value than roughages, high energy content and high digestibility. They contain less than 18% crude fibre, more than 60% TDN, and their protein content varies from 2% to 80%.

cards.question: What are energy-rich concentrates, and give examples.
cards.answer: They are excellent sources of energy: high in carbohydrate, medium in protein (<18% CP) and low in fat, fiber and moisture. Examples are all cereal grains, roots and tubers, and agro-industrial by-products such as bran, middlings and molasses.

cards.question: What are protein-rich concentrates, and give plant and animal examples?
cards.answer: Protein-rich concentrates contain more than 18% CP and may be of plant or animal origin. Oilseed cakes and meals are the most common plant protein concentrates (soybean meal, cottonseed cake). Animal source protein concentrates include meat meal, dried blood meal and fish meal.

cards.text: Concentrates contain less than {{c1::18%}} crude fibre and more than {{c2::60%}} TDN and are highly digestible.
Concentrates are classified into {{c1::energy-rich}} and {{c2::protein-rich}} concentrates.
Energy-rich concentrates are high in {{c1::carbohydrate}}, medium in protein (<18% CP) and low in {{c2::fat}}; examples include cereal grains, roots and tubers, bran, middlings and molasses.
Protein-rich concentrates contain more than {{c1::18%}} CP; plant examples are soybean meal and cottonseed cake, while animal examples are {{c2::meat meal, dried blood meal and fish meal}}.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 5::5.3 Nutrient Requirements of Farm Animals

cards.question: Define nutrients and nutrient requirement.
cards.answer: Nutrients are elements, compounds or groups of compounds required and/or used for animal nourishment and performance. Nutrient requirement is the minimum amount of nutrients necessary to meet an animal's needs for maintenance (neither gain nor loss), growth, reproduction, lactation (milk production), work and good health.

cards.question: List the six basic animal nutrients.
cards.answer: Carbohydrates, fats, proteins, minerals, vitamins and water.

cards.question: What roles does water play in the animal body?
cards.answer: Water constitutes more than one-half of the animal body, is vital for digestion, blood circulation and waste elimination, is the medium in which all nutrients are dissolved, and regulates body temperature. Farm animals need adequate supplies of fresh and clean drinking water.

cards.question: What are carbohydrates, and what are their main sources in livestock feed?
cards.answer: Carbohydrates are energy-rich organic compounds and the main source of energy in animal feed. Main sources are grains (wheat, maize and sorghum), plus crop residues, molasses, forages and hay. Table 5.1 also lists cracked maize, cooked wheat, teff, barley, sorghum, millet, bean, grass pea, cereal bran, flour, middlings, shorts, sweet potato vine, sugar cane tops and atela.

cards.question: What are the functions and sources of fats in the animal diet?
cards.answer: Fats act as storehouses of energy and insulate the body. Normal roughages such as grazing pasture contain very little fat; oilseed cakes such as soybean meal or cottonseed cake are the main source, and concentrates such as oilseed cakes contain up to 10% fats and oils. Energy for growth and activity comes mainly from carbohydrates and fats, though proteins also supply some energy.

cards.question: Describe proteins and explain why they must be supplied every day.
cards.answer: Proteins are polymers formed through the combination of amino acid molecules; amino acids are the building blocks essential for the formation of animal tissues. Protein is essential for healthy growth, maintenance and reproduction. Plant sources are oilseed cakes/meals, pulses and legumes; animal sources include fish meal and meat scraps. There is no storage of protein in the body, so the daily requirement must be provided; excess protein is deaminated and converted into fat stored as energy.

cards.question: How are minerals classified, and what are their functions in the body?
cards.answer: Minerals are inorganic elements required in small amounts for normal body functions: good health, bones, teeth and tissues, and regulation of the body's chemical processes. Macro minerals required in larger amounts are calcium (Ca), phosphorus (P), magnesium (Mg), potassium (K) and sodium (Na); micro or trace minerals are copper (Cu), iodine (I), iron (Fe), manganese (Mn) and zink (Zn). Deficiency leads to major metabolic disorders and excess intake causes toxicity.

cards.question: What are vitamins, and how are they classified?
cards.answer: Vitamins are organic compounds required in small amounts for metabolism, growth and reproduction, red blood cell maturation, digestion, and bone and teeth formation; they help the body combat stress and prevent infection. Fat-soluble vitamins are A, D, E and K; water-soluble vitamins are B and C. Water-soluble vitamins cannot be stored in the body and must be taken daily.

cards.question: State the sources and deficiency signs of protein given in Table 5.1.
cards.answer: Sources: leguminous plants (e.g., Sesbania sesban, Lucerne), oilseed cakes (noug seed cake, cottonseed cake, linseed cake, soybean meal), poultry litter and urea. Deficiency signs: low weight gain, stunted growth and poor product quality.

cards.question: State the sources and deficiency signs of vitamins given in Table 5.1.
cards.answer: Sources: vegetables, green fodders (alfalfa, grasses, green wheat, green sorghum, green maize) and vitamin preparations. Deficiency signs: rough and loose hair coat, coughing, nasal discharge, watery eyes, diarrhea, staggering gait, scaly skin and pneumonia.

cards.question: State the sources and deficiency signs of minerals and water given in Table 5.1.
cards.answer: Mineral sources: agro-industrial residues, bone meal, limestone, common salt, bole salt and mineral lick. Mineral deficiency signs: reduced fodder intake, low weight gain, chewing and suckling of wood and metal, stiff joints, weakened bones and teeth, impaired energy utilization and drop in milk production. Water sources: water bodies and succulent feeds; deficiency signs: reduced feed intake, low weight gain and milk yield.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 5::5.3 Nutrient Requirements of Farm Animals

cards.text: Nutrient requirement is the {{c1::minimum amount}} of nutrients necessary for maintenance, growth, reproduction, lactation, work and good health.
The six basic animal nutrients are carbohydrates, fats, proteins, {{c1::minerals}}, vitamins and {{c2::water}}.
Water constitutes more than {{c1::one-half}} of the animal body, is the medium in which nutrients are dissolved, and regulates {{c2::body temperature}}.
Carbohydrates are {{c1::energy-rich}} organic compounds and the main source of energy in animal feed; grains such as wheat, maize and sorghum are the main sources.
Carbohydrate deficiency signs include reduced feed intake, low weight gain, {{c1::prolonged fattening}} and a drop in {{c2::milk yield}}.
Fats act as {{c1::storehouses of energy}} and insulate the body; oilseed cakes such as soybean meal or cottonseed cake contain up to {{c2::10%}} fats and oils.
Fat deficiency can cause poor skin and hair coat, inability to maintain a successful {{c1::pregnancy}} and potentially inadequate absorption of {{c2::fat-soluble vitamins}}.
Proteins are polymers formed through the combination of {{c1::amino acid}} molecules; amino acids are the building blocks essential for the formation of {{c2::animal tissues}}.
There is no storage of protein in the body, so protein must be provided {{c1::each day}}; excess protein is deaminated and converted into {{c2::fat}} and stored as a source of energy.

Protein deficiency signs include low weight gain, {{c1::stunted growth}} and poor product quality; protein sources include Sesbania sesban, Lucerne, noug seed cake, cottonseed cake, linseed cake, soybean meal, poultry litter and {{c2::urea}}.
Vitamin deficiency signs include rough and loose hair coat, coughing, nasal discharge, watery eyes, diarrhea, {{c1::staggering gait}}, scaly skin and {{c2::pneumonia}}.
Mineral sources include agro-industrial residues, bone meal, limestone, common salt, {{c1::bole salt}} and {{c2::mineral lick}}.
Water-soluble vitamins ({{c1::B and C}}) cannot be stored in the body and must be taken in daily; fat-soluble vitamins are {{c2::A, D, E and K}}.

cards.question: Define feed formulation and state the information needed to formulate a ration.
cards.answer: Feed formulation is the process of quantifying the amounts of feed ingredients to be combined to form a single uniform mixture for a particular animal, so that the feed meets the animal's nutrient requirements. It requires information on cost and availability of ingredients, nutrient content of the feed and nutrient requirements of the animals.

cards.text: Feed formulation requires information about the {{c1::cost and availability}} of ingredients, nutrient content of feed and {{c2::nutrient requirements}} of animals.

cards.question: What is a maintenance ration?
cards.answer: The minimum quantity of feed required to maintain an animal so that its body mass remains constant. It depends on the body mass and type of animal; roughly half of the feed an animal takes is required for maintenance.

cards.question: What is a production ration?
cards.answer: In addition to the maintenance ration, certain nutrients are needed to produce products such as milk, eggs and meat. The additional feed beyond the maintenance ration used for production is called the production ration.

cards.text: A maintenance ration is the {{c1::minimum quantity}} of feed required to maintain an animal; roughly {{c2::half}} of the feed an animal takes is required for maintenance.
The feed beyond the maintenance ration used for milk, eggs and meat is the {{c1::production ration}}.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 5::5.4.2 Characteristics of a Good Ration

cards.question: List the characteristics of a good ration.
cards.answer: It should satisfy the total dry matter requirement of the animal based on weight; provide highly digestible nutrients including enough minerals and vitamins; be palatable; be fairly bulky to satisfy hunger and expel undigested material; be digestible, which can be improved by grinding and crushing; and be fresh and free from undesirable weeds and dust.

cards.question: Define ration and balanced ration.
cards.answer: A ration is the amount of feed given to an animal to meet its needs during a twenty-four hour period. A balanced ration has all the nutrients the animal needs in the right proportion and amount.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 5::5.4.2 Characteristics of a Good Ration

cards.text: A good ration should be {{c1::palatable}} and fairly bulky to satisfy hunger and expel {{c2::undigested material}}; digestibility can be improved by grinding and crushing.

cards.question: Name the four methods of balancing a diet given in the textbook and identify the most well-known.
cards.answer: The Trial and Error method, the Pearson Square method, substitution formulation and computer-assisted formulation. The Pearson Square Method is the most well-known method of balancing animal diets.

cards.question: What is the Pearson Square method used for, and what condition must the two feeds satisfy?
cards.answer: It is used to calculate the portion of two feeds needed to meet either the protein or energy requirements of an animal. One of the feeds must be higher in Metabolisable Energy (ME) or crude protein (CP) than the desired level and the other must be below the desired level.

cards.question: State the four steps for calculating crude protein with the Pearson Square method.
cards.answer: Step 1: draw a square and insert the desired % CP in the middle. Step 2: place the first feed and its % CP in the upper left corner and the second feed and its % CP in the lower left corner. Step 3: subtract the desired % CP from each feed CP across the diagonal (top left − middle = bottom right; bottom left − middle = top right), disregarding negative or positive values, and write the results on the right. Step 4: add the two figures on the right, divide each by this total and multiply by the weight of feed required; repeat for ME as required.

cards.question: Worked example: maize (CP 9.5%) and soybean meal (CP 42%) are used to make 100 kg of feed with 16% CP. How much of each feed is needed?
cards.answer: Maize parts = 42 − 16 = 26; SBM parts = 16 − 9.5 = 6.5; total = 32.5. Maize = (26 ÷ 32.5) × 100 = 80.0 kg; SBM = (6.5 ÷ 32.5) × 100 = 20.0 kg. The farmer mixes 80 kg maize with 20 kg soybean meal.

cards.question: Exercise 5.1: Selam has maize (10.5% CP) and soybean meal (37.4% CP). How much of each is needed for 2000 kg of broiler starter ration with 23% CP?
Review exercise: maize (10% protein) and fish meal (48% protein) are used for 100 kg of laying hen feed with 16% protein. Calculate the amount of each.
cards.answer: Maize parts = 48 − 16 = 32; fish meal parts = 16 − 10 = 6; total = 38. Maize = (32 ÷ 38) × 100 ≈ 84.21 kg; fish meal = (6 ÷ 38) × 100 ≈ 15.79 kg.

cards.text: In the Pearson Square, {{c1::top left − middle = bottom right}} and {{c2::bottom left − middle = top right}}; disregard the negative or positive value of the numbers.
The Pearson Square method calculates the portion of {{c1::two feeds}} needed to meet protein or energy requirements; one feed must be above and the other {{c2::below}} the desired level.
In Step 4, the weight of each feed = (right-side figure ÷ {{c1::sum of the two right-side figures}}) × {{c2::weight of feed required}}.
For 100 kg of 16% CP feed from maize (9.5% CP) and SBM (42% CP): maize = ({{c1::26}} ÷ 32.5) × 100 = {{c2::80.0 kg}} and SBM = (6.5 ÷ 32.5) × 100 = 20.0 kg.
For Selam's 2000 kg broiler starter ration (23% CP), maize = ({{c1::14.4}} ÷ 26.9) × 2000 ≈ {{c2::1070.6 kg}} and soybean meal = (12.5 ÷ 26.9) × 2000 ≈ 929.4 kg.
For 100 kg of 16% protein layer feed from maize (10%) and fish meal (48%): maize = ({{c1::32}} ÷ 38) × 100 ≈ 84.21 kg and fish meal = (6 ÷ 38) × 100 ≈ {{c2::15.79 kg}}.

cards.question: Why is feed conservation necessary, and what are the common methods?
cards.answer: Livestock must be fed all year round, but green or succulent feed is available only at certain times and forage production decreases during dry periods. Conservation overcomes seasonal nutritional deficits and enhances animal productivity. The common methods are hay making and silage making.

cards.question: What is hay, and what is curing?
cards.answer: Hay is forage harvested during the growing period and preserved by drying. Curing is the process of reducing the moisture content of green crops from 70–90% to 15–20%, normally accomplished with energy provided by the sun and wind. It preserves grasses, legumes and fodders for later feeding.

cards.question: Describe the hay storage systems given in the textbook.
cards.answer: Hay can be stored in a bale or tripod system. Bales may be small squares, large squares, rectangular bales or round bales; baling makes compact cubical bundles that reduce space compared with loose or chopped hay, and bales may be stored in the open or in a barn. A tripod is a three-legged stand, on average 2 to 3 meters high, that helps drain rainy water.

cards.question: What are the advantages of hay as a conserved feed?
cards.answer: Hay is the oldest and still the most important way of conserving feed. It can be made with little cost other than labor and with simple equipment, is easy to transport and store, can be fed with little or no wastage, and is often marketed as a cash crop, usually baled.

cards.question: What are the shortcomings of hay?
cards.answer: Hay varies in nutrient content and palatability more than any feed, is very dependent on weather conditions, and late crop harvest affects quality by decreasing the nutrient content of the feed.

cards.question: What is silage, and what does the term ensilage mean?
cards.answer: Silage is the preserved material produced by the controlled fermentation of green crops under anaerobic conditions. The process of silage making is also known as ensilage, and its main purpose is to preserve succulent feeds for use at times of scarcity.

cards.question: From which crops is very good silage made, at what growth stages should they be harvested, and how long does the process take?
cards.answer: Very good silage can be made from grasses, grass-legume mixtures or fodders such as maize and sorghum. Grasses should be harvested at head forming stage, legumes at early blooming and fodders at dough (milky) stage. The crop is wilted, chopped and stored in a silo; the process takes 2 to 4 weeks for best production and feed intake.

cards.question: List the main steps in the Table 5.2 checklist for making and feeding good quality silage.
cards.answer: Harvesting (assess quantity, avoid bad weather, harvest at flowering stage with 35–40% DM / 60–65% moisture); optional wilting to 30% DM avoiding over-wilting and chopping to the proper size; optional additives (molasses, urea, salt, acids, limestone) while filling; proper filling of an impermeable, easily sealed silo with uniform material distribution completed on time; tight dumping and packing to encourage fermentation and discourage spoilage; tight sealing; opening only one end of the narrow side; feeding to ruminants only, starting bit by bit and gradually increasing the quantity.

cards.question: What happens during silage packing and sealing?
cards.answer: Carbohydrates (sugar) break down to organic acids; anaerobic fermentation converts organic materials to carbon dioxide and water, plus heat; the organic acids (lactic acid) reduce pH to 4 or lower; aerobic bacteria die and anaerobic bacteria multiply rapidly; fermentation takes 2–4 weeks for completion.

cards.question: What precautions are given for feeding silage to livestock?
cards.answer: Feed silage to ruminants only and not when their rumen is empty. Do not feed cows in late pregnancy, calves less than 6 months old, or sick, hungry and weak animals. Start bit by bit and gradually increase the quantity.

cards.question: Summarize the eleven-step practical procedure of silage making.
cards.answer: 1) Put on personal protective equipment and clothing. 2) Prepare materials (plastic sheet, spring balance, container, molasses, fresh forage such as alfalfa, grass, cactus leaves, maize or elephant grass, urea), cut and allow to dry for 2 days, and gather some straw. 3) Make a silo above or below ground, sized according to number of animals, feeding period and quantity of feed, or use a plastic sheet. 4) Harvest crops at 30–35% moisture content. 5) Chop the crop to make compaction easy and remove air. 6) Measure 1% molasses, 1–3 liter water and 1 kg urea for 50–70 kg silage. 7) Make a solution of molasses and urea in water. 8) Mix the solution with the chopped forage. 9) Fill the silo layer by layer, continuously, and seal it quickly to prevent air entrapment and speed fermentation. 10) Cover the silo with soil to control entrance of air. 11) After 2–3 weeks feed according to age, health condition, time of production (not to pregnant animals) and type of production.

cards.text: Curing reduces the moisture content of green crops from {{c1::70–90%}} to {{c2::15–20%}} using energy from the sun and wind.
Hay may be stored as compact bales (small squares, large squares, rectangular or {{c1::round bales}}) or on a {{c2::tripod}}, a three-legged stand 2 to 3 meters high that drains rainy water.
Hay is very dependent on {{c1::weather conditions}}, and late crop harvest decreases the {{c2::nutrient content}} of the feed.
Silage is preserved material produced by {{c1::controlled fermentation}} of green crops under {{c2::anaerobic conditions}}; the process is also called ensilage.
For silage, grasses are harvested at the {{c1::head forming stage}}, legumes at early blooming and fodders at the {{c2::dough (milky) stage}}.
At silage harvesting, the crop should be at flowering stage with {{c1::35–40% DM}} ({{c2::60–65% moisture}}), then wilted (optionally) to 30% DM and chopped to facilitate packing.
During sealing, lactic acid reduces pH to {{c1::4 or lower}}, aerobic bacteria die and {{c2::anaerobic bacteria}} multiply rapidly; fermentation takes 2–4 weeks.
For 50–70 kg of silage, measure {{c1::1% molasses}}, 1–3 liter water and {{c2::1 kg urea}}; fill the silo layer by layer and seal quickly to prevent {{c3::air entrapment}}.
Silage should be fed to {{c1::ruminants only}}, never when the rumen is empty, and not to cows in late pregnancy or calves less than {{c2::6 months}} old.
When opening a silo, never open the whole pit at one time; open only one end of the {{c1::narrow side}} because a small opening prevents {{c2::air entry and silage spoilage}}.
Additives that may be used while filling a silo pit include molasses, urea, salt, {{c1::acids}} and {{c2::limestone}}.
After {{c1::2–3 weeks}} the silage can be fed, depending on age, health condition, time of production and type of production.

cards.question: Define compound feed manufacturing.
cards.answer: Manufacturing animal feed involves blending several raw feed ingredients of different physical, chemical and nutritional composition into a homogenous mixture that meets the nutrient requirements of the target species.

cards.question: What are the main ingredients of commercial compound feeds in Ethiopia, and what else may they contain?
cards.answer: Cereals and agro-industrial by-products are the main ingredients of commercial feeds in Ethiopia. Compound feed may also contain salt, limestone and premixes.

cards.question: What is stated about the operations, equipment and quality control in compound feed manufacturing?
cards.answer: The manufacturing process involves several operations; the sequence of operations and the size and sophistication of the equipment may vary with the output of feed required. Quality control is essential at all stages of the operation.

cards.text: Compound feed manufacturing blends raw ingredients of different physical, chemical and nutritional composition into a {{c1::homogenous mixture}} that meets the nutrient requirements of the target species.
Cereals and {{c1::agro-industrial by-products}} are the main ingredients of commercial feeds in Ethiopia; compound feed may also contain salt, limestone and {{c2::premixes}}.

Premixes are complex mixtures of {{c1::vitamins, minerals, trace elements}} and other feed additives, incorporated at small levels in compound feed to provide a balanced contribution to the animal's needs.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 6::6.1 Introduction to animal genetics and breeding

cards.question: Define genetics.
cards.answer: Genetics is the study of heredity, meaning the passing of genetic information and traits from parents to offspring. It includes the study of genes and their effects on living organisms.

cards.question: What is heredity?
cards.answer: Heredity is the passing of genetic information and traits from parents to offspring; it is the subject studied in genetics.

cards.question: What does DNA stand for, and what is its role in organisms?
cards.answer: DNA stands for deoxyribonucleic acid. It is the molecule that contains the genetic code of organisms and is inherited by offspring from their parents.

cards.question: What are genes, and where are they found?
cards.answer: Genes are small sections of DNA coded for specific traits. They are found in chromosomes.

cards.question: What have animal geneticists identified within genes, and what effect can these advances have?
cards.answer: They have identified elements within genes that can enhance animal growth, health, and the ability to utilize nutrients efficiently. These genetic advances can increase production and reduce environmental impacts.

cards.question: Name the pillars of livestock development mentioned in this unit.
cards.answer: Animal genetics is one pillar, alongside animal health, animal nutrition, and husbandry issues such as animal housing.

cards.question: Define animal breeding.
cards.answer: Animal breeding is the mating of selective animals for the purpose of enhancing particular characteristics in subsequent generations. The characteristics are usually chosen to increase production and profitability.

cards.question: How does animal breeding bring about continuous improvement of farm animals?
cards.answer: Different animal traits are measured and the best animals are used as parent animals. Breeders thereby provide farmers with a better next generation, so breeding ensures continuous improvement generation after generation.

cards.question: State the three objectives of animal breeding.
cards.answer: The objectives are to increase animal yield or productivity, to improve the desirable quality of animal product, and to produce disease-resistant animals.

cards.question: In genetics, what is an allele?
cards.answer: An allele is an alternative form of a gene at a given location on a chromosome. An individual inherits one allele for each gene from each parent; alleles are the basis of dominant and recessive traits.

cards.question: Distinguish genotype from phenotype.
cards.answer: Genotype is the genetic makeup of an individual, the genes and alleles it carries. Phenotype is the individual's observable traits, such as height and color, produced by the genotype interacting with the environment.

cards.question: What is genetic variation, and why does it matter in breeding?
cards.answer: Genetic variation is the existence of differences in inherited characteristics among individuals of a population. It supplies the differences among animals that make selection and genetic improvement possible.

cards.question: Explain dominance and recessiveness between alleles.
cards.answer: A dominant allele masks the effect of a recessive allele when both are present in an individual. A recessive trait appears only when the individual carries two copies of the recessive allele, which is why recessive undesirable traits can appear in inbred offspring.

cards.question: What do homozygous and heterozygous mean?
cards.answer: Homozygous means carrying two identical alleles for a gene; heterozygous means carrying two different alleles for that gene.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 6::6.1 Introduction to animal genetics and breeding

cards.text: Genetics is the study of {{c1::heredity}}, which is the passing of genetic information and traits from {{c2::parents to offspring}}.
Genes are small sections of {{c1::deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA)}} that are coded for {{c2::specific traits}}.
Genes are found in {{c1::chromosomes}}, and DNA is {{c2::inherited by offspring from their parents}}.
Genetic advances can increase {{c1::production}} and reduce {{c2::environmental impacts}}.
Animal genetics is one of the pillars of livestock development alongside {{c1::animal health}}, {{c2::animal nutrition}} and {{c3::husbandry issues such as animal housing}}.
Animal breeding is the mating of {{c1::selective animals}} for the enhancement of particular characteristics in {{c2::subsequent generations}}.
Animal breeding helps in the accumulation of {{c1::superior genes}} and the elimination of {{c2::less desirable genes}}.
The objectives of animal breeding are to increase {{c1::animal yield or productivity}}, improve the {{c2::desirable quality of animal product}} and produce {{c3::disease-resistant animals}}.
Alternative forms of a gene are called {{c1::alleles}}; an individual inherits one allele for each gene from {{c2::each parent}}.
An individual's observable traits, such as {{c1::height and color}}, make up its {{c2::phenotype}}, whereas its genetic makeup is its {{c3::genotype}}.
Differences in inherited characteristics among individuals of a population are called {{c1::genetic variation}}, which makes {{c2::selection}} possible.
A {{c1::dominant allele}} masks the effect of a {{c2::recessive allele}} when both are present in an individual.
An animal with two identical alleles for a gene is {{c1::homozygous}}, while one with two different alleles is {{c2::heterozygous}}.

cards.question: What are the three methods of genetic improvement applied in farm animals?
cards.answer: The three methods are breed introduction, selection, and breeding.

cards.question: What is the principle on which genetic improvement is based?
cards.answer: Genetic improvement is based on the principle that the products of animals, such as milk, meat and wool, and their services, such as transport, draught power and cultural services, are functions of their genes and their living environment.

cards.question: Which examples of productivity per animal are given, and how else can productivity be increased?
cards.answer: Examples are growth rate, milk yield and egg number. Productivity can also be increased by better feeding, better health care and better management of existing animals, in addition to genetic improvement.

cards.text: The three methods of genetic improvement applied in farm animals are {{c1::breed introduction}}, {{c2::selection}} and {{c3::breeding}}.
Animal products and services are functions of their {{c1::genes}} and their {{c2::living environment}}.
Productivity per animal, for example {{c1::growth rate}}, {{c2::milk yield}} and {{c3::egg number}}, needs to be increased to make livestock production profitable.

cards.question: Define breed introduction.
cards.answer: Breed introduction is bringing high-quality breeds of livestock into a farm or a country. High-quality breeds have a high productive capacity and other desirable characteristics.
