cards.question: From where can high-quality breeds be introduced, and what should be checked before introduction?
cards.answer: They can be introduced from another farm or another country. Before introduction, it is important to be sure that the breeds possess higher quality characteristics than the local ones.

cards.question: Name the different categories of farm animal breeds found around the world.
cards.answer: The categories are local breeds, exotic breeds, and cross breeds.

cards.question: Describe local breeds in Ethiopia, including their strengths and weaknesses.
cards.answer: Local breeds in Ethiopia are usually small animals that mature slowly and are poor producers. However, they are adapted to the local environment and are resistant to diseases.

cards.question: Describe exotic breeds and the problems they may face in Ethiopia.
cards.answer: Exotic breeds are not native to Ethiopia. They are often larger, mature early and are good producers, but they may not adapt to the local environment and may fall victim to various diseases.

cards.question: How can the adaptation and disease problems of exotic breeds be addressed?
cards.answer: Exotic breeds can be mated with local breeds to obtain cross-breeds that possess the most desirable qualities of both exotic and local breeds.

cards.question: List the advantages of breed introduction.
cards.answer: It introduces characteristics not originally present in local breeds; it enhances productivity; and crossbreeds may perform better than local breeds if adapted to the local environment.

cards.question: List the disadvantages of breed introduction.
cards.answer: It may introduce new diseases and pests to the area; exotic breeds may struggle to adapt to the new area; and exotic breeds may not reach full productivity in the new environment.

cards.text: Breed introduction is bringing {{c1::high-quality breeds}} of livestock into the farm or a country.
Before introducing animals from another farm or country, be sure the breeds possess {{c1::higher quality characteristics}} than the {{c2::local ones}}.
The different breeds of farm animals around the world are {{c1::local breeds}}, {{c2::exotic breeds}} and {{c3::cross breeds}}.
In Ethiopia, local breeds are usually {{c1::small}} animals, mature {{c2::slowly}} and are poor producers, but they are adapted to the local environment and {{c3::resistant to diseases}}.
Exotic breeds are not native to Ethiopia; they are often {{c1::larger}}, mature {{c2::early}} and are good producers, but may not {{c3::adapt to the local environment}}.
Mating exotic breeds with local breeds helps obtain {{c1::cross-breeds}} that possess the {{c2::most desirable qualities of both exotic and local breeds}}.

Advantages of breed introduction: characteristics not originally present in local breeds are {{c1::introduced}}, productivity is {{c2::enhanced}}, and adapted crossbreeds may {{c3::perform better than local breeds}}.

Disadvantages of introduction: it may introduce new {{c1::diseases and pests}}, exotic breeds may struggle to {{c2::adapt to the new area}}, and may not reach {{c3::full productivity}} in the new environment.

cards.question: Define selection as used in livestock improvement.
cards.answer: Selection is the process of allowing genetically superior animals to be parents of future generations while culling others. It is used as a tool for livestock improvement.

cards.question: What is culling?
cards.answer: Culling is the removal of animals that do not perform at the desired level from the herd.

cards.question: What is breeding stock, and what should it pass to offspring?
cards.answer: Animals with desirable characteristics are selected and make up the breeding stock. The breeding stock should pass its good qualities to offspring for better performance, such as higher milk production or growth, to improve the herd.

cards.question: What is the genetic effect of repeating selection over many generations?
cards.answer: Repeated selection increases the chances of forming desirable qualities in an animal: it increases the occurrence of desirable genes and decreases the occurrence of undesirable ones.

cards.question: Define natural selection.
cards.answer: Natural selection is the process in which animals better adapted to their environment get a better chance of surviving and producing more offspring than those that fail to adapt. Animals unable to adapt cannot survive or reproduce, and the offspring of adapted animals are more adapted than their parents.

cards.question: Define artificial selection and name its four methods described in this unit.
cards.answer: Artificial selection is when farmers select and mate the best animals, increasing animal health and productivity. Its four methods are mass selection, progeny selection, family selection and pedigree selection.

cards.question: Describe mass selection.
cards.answer: In mass selection, animals are selected or rejected on the basis of their own performance in the field. Animals with the desired characteristics are often chosen from a large group composed of a large number of animals.

cards.question: Describe progeny selection.
cards.answer: In progeny selection, animals are selected on the performance of their progeny or offspring. Mothers of the best performing offspring are retained, while mothers of offspring that do not perform well are culled (removed).

cards.question: Describe family selection and when it is usual.
cards.answer: In family selection, animals are selected or rejected on the basis of the performance of their relatives or family. It is usual when family size is large, that is, when the family has a large number of members.

cards.question: Describe pedigree selection.
cards.answer: In pedigree selection, animals are selected or rejected on the basis of the performance of their ancestors.

cards.question: List five advantages of selection.
cards.answer: It ensures that only the best naturally available animals are selected; animals with desirable characteristics are selected; animals from best breeds are bred for distribution; animals with undesirable characteristics are detected and culled; and it reduces the spread of diseases and parasites associated with breeding stocks.

cards.question: List four disadvantages of selection.
cards.answer: Selection is very costly in terms of time and money; it requires expertise which may not be readily available; it may eliminate or exclude some desirable traits of some parent stock; and it introduces no new desirable characteristics that do not occur in the existing stock.

cards.text: Selection is the process of allowing {{c1::genetically superior animals}} to be parents of future generations while {{c2::culling others}}.
Culling is the removal of animals which do not perform at the {{c1::desired level}} from the {{c2::herd}}.
Animals with desirable characteristics are selected and make up the {{c1::breeding stock}}, which should pass good qualities to their offspring for {{c2::better performance}}.
Selection increases occurrences of {{c1::desirable genes}} and decreases those of the {{c2::undesirable ones}}.
In natural selection, animals better {{c1::adapted to their environment}} get a better chance of {{c2::surviving and producing more offspring}}; animals unable to adapt cannot survive or reproduce.
In artificial selection, farmers select and mate the {{c1::best animals}}; the methods are {{c2::mass selection}}, {{c3::progeny selection}}, {{c4::family selection}} and {{c5::pedigree selection}}.
In mass selection, animals are selected or rejected on the basis of their {{c1::own performance in the field}}, often from a {{c2::large group}} of animals.
In progeny selection, animals are selected on the performance of their {{c1::progeny or offspring}}; mothers of the best performing offspring are {{c2::retained}} while the others are {{c3::culled}}.
Family selection selects or rejects animals on the basis of the performance of their {{c1::relatives or family}} and is usual when family size is {{c2::large}}.
Pedigree selection selects or rejects animals on the basis of the performance of their {{c1::ancestors}}.

Selection ensures only the {{c1::best naturally available animal}} is selected, detects and culls animals with {{c2::undesirable characteristics}}, and reduces the spread of {{c3::diseases and parasites}} associated with breeding stocks.

Disadvantages of selection: it is costly in {{c1::time and money}}, requires {{c2::expertise}}, may exclude some desirable traits of parent stock, and introduces {{c3::no new desirable characteristics}} not already in the existing stock.

cards.question: Define breeding in the context of this unit.
cards.answer: Breeding involves the development of animals by transferring inherited qualities from parents to offspring. This is achieved through mating.

cards.question: How are the different methods of breeding categorized?
cards.answer: They are categorized as related breeding systems and unrelated breeding systems.

cards.question: Define in-breeding and give the examples in the text.
cards.answer: In-breeding is mating animals that are more closely related than the average of the population from which they come. Examples are father to daughter, son to mother, and brother to sister mating.

cards.question: What are inbred lines used for, and what is in-breeding depression?
cards.answer: In-breeding produces inbred lines that can be used for cross breeding to produce hybrid vigour. It can also produce offspring with undesirable characteristics because recessive genes show up; this is known as in-breeding depression.

cards.question: Define line-breeding, give an example, and state its purpose and disadvantage.
cards.answer: Line-breeding is the mating of distantly related animals, for example cousins. It has the same disadvantages as in-breeding but takes a longer period for undesirable traits or in-breeding depression to appear. It is used to consolidate traits for a particular outstanding ancestor, and most high-quality commercial characters developed recently have resulted from line-breeding.

cards.question: Define out-breeding and state its effect.
cards.answer: Out-breeding is the mating of unrelated animals within the same breed. It is the opposite of in-breeding and produces offspring with greater vigour and productivity.

cards.question: Define cross-breeding and explain why it works.
cards.answer: Cross-breeding is the mating of proven quality animals of the same species but different breeds, because the parental animals differ in gene composition. It results in animals with higher production capacity than either parent.

cards.question: What are heterosis (hybrid vigour) and its effects in cross-bred offspring?
cards.answer: Heterosis or hybrid vigor is the higher production capacity of cross-bred offspring compared with any of the parents. It gives a greater rate of growth, enables offspring to withstand climatic variation, increases disease resistance, and promotes higher yields of eggs, meat and milk.

cards.question: What mating example illustrates in-breeding in the table of breeding systems?
cards.answer: An Afar ram mated with an Afar ewe that is the ram's daughter illustrates in-breeding, a related breeding system.

cards.question: What mating example illustrates cross breeding in the table of breeding systems?
cards.answer: An Arsi cow mated with a HF (Holstein-Friesian) bull illustrates cross breeding, an unrelated breeding system.

cards.question: State the advantages of related breeding systems.
cards.answer: Related breeding produces pure breeds or pure lines and helps to concentrate and preserve specific qualities in an animal.

cards.question: State the disadvantages of related breeding systems.
cards.answer: Related breeding causes reduction in vigour and performance, shown as a drop in productivity, slow growth rate, loss of fertility and poor resistance to diseases. It often gives rise to defective animals.

cards.question: State the advantages of unrelated breeding systems.
cards.answer: They promote heterosis or hybrid vigor, allow development of new breeds, produce animals that grow more rapidly and are more economical to rear, withstand environmental variations, and are more resistant to diseases.

cards.question: State the disadvantages of unrelated breeding systems.
cards.answer: Operating costs are higher than those for local breeds, and if the system is not systematic, sizing problems and associated delivery difficulties may occur.

cards.question: According to the unit summary, what is the incentive for cross breeding?
cards.answer: The incentive is exploitation of hybrid vigour, that is heterosis, as a result of which the performance of cross-breeds exceeds the average of the parental breeds.

cards.text: Breeding involves the development of animals by transferring {{c1::inherited qualities}} from parents to offspring through {{c2::mating}}.
Breeding systems can be categorized as {{c1::related breeding}} or {{c2::unrelated breeding}} systems.
In-breeding is the mating of {{c1::more closely related animals}} than the average of the population, for example {{c2::father to daughter}}, {{c3::son to mother}} or {{c4::brother to sister}}.
In-breeding helps produce {{c1::inbred lines}} used for cross breeding to produce {{c2::hybrid vigour}}, but when recessive genes show up it causes {{c3::in-breeding depression}}.

Line-breeding is the mating of {{c1::distantly related animals}}, such as {{c2::cousins}}, used to consolidate traits for a particular outstanding ancestor; undesirable traits appear after a {{c3::longer period}} than in in-breeding.
Out-breeding is the mating of {{c1::unrelated animals within the same breed}}; it is the opposite of in-breeding and produces offspring with greater {{c2::vigor and productivity}}.
Cross-breeding is the mating of {{c1::proven quality animals of the same species but different breeds}}, because parental animals differ in {{c2::gene composition}}.

Higher production capacity than any of the parents is called {{c1::heterosis}} or {{c2::hybrid vigor}}; cross-breeds grow faster, withstand {{c3::climatic variation}}, resist disease and yield more {{c4::eggs, meat and milk}}.
The related breeding example in the table is an {{c1::Afar ram}} mated with an {{c2::Afar ewe of the ram's daughter}} (in-breeding).
The unrelated breeding example in the table is an {{c1::Arsi cow}} mated with an {{c2::HF bull}} (cross breeding).
Related breeding gives production of {{c1::pure breeds or pure lines}} and helps to {{c2::concentrate and preserve specific qualities}} in an animal.
Related breeding causes reduction in {{c1::vigor and performance}}, including slow growth rate, loss of fertility and poor disease resistance, and often gives rise to {{c2::defective animals}}.

Unrelated breeding promotes {{c1::heterosis or hybrid vigor}}, develops new breeds, grows more rapidly and economically, withstands {{c2::environmental variations}} and gives more {{c3::resistance against diseases}}.
Unrelated breeding has higher {{c1::operating costs}} than local breeds and, if not systematic, may cause {{c2::sizing problems and associated delivery difficulties}}.
The incentive for cross breeding is exploitation of {{c1::hybrid vigour (heterosis)}}, so the performance of cross-breeds exceeds the {{c2::average of the parental breeds}}.

cards.question: Why are reproductive techniques important in modern animal breeding?
cards.answer: They make safe and efficient breeding possible, improve and optimize breeding programs, allow dissemination of genes of interest, and increase the reproductive capacities of animals. Artificial insemination and embryo transfer are examples of biotechnology methods used to improve breeding stock.

cards.text: {{c1::Artificial insemination}} and {{c2::embryo transfer}} are examples of biotechnology methods used in improving the breeding stock of animals.

cards.question: Define artificial insemination.
cards.answer: Artificial insemination is the process of collecting sperm cells from male animals and depositing them into the reproductive tract of a female, that is the vagina, cervix or uterus, by a method other than natural mating. It is the most important reproduction technology for genetic improvement in domestic animals.

cards.question: How is semen collected, handled and stored for artificial insemination?
cards.answer: Semen is collected hygienically from superior males. The semen containing spermatozoa is carefully handled, diluted and stored in a freezer at a temperature of -196 °C in liquid nitrogen until required for use.

cards.question: What is a liquid nitrogen tank used for in AI?
cards.answer: A liquid nitrogen tank is used for preserving and storing semen for an extended period of time.

cards.question: On what does success in insemination timing depend?
cards.answer: Success in insemination timing depends on a good heat detection program. Effective AI work needs accurate herd supervision and heat detection.

cards.question: List the physical signs of oestrus (heat) in females given in the text.
cards.answer: The signs are loss of appetite; constant vocalizations; restlessness; rubbing up against herd-mates; lips of the vulva becoming redder and more moist than usual; swelling around the vulva; and a thin mucous discharge from the vulva.

cards.question: List the mounting-related signs of oestrus in females.
cards.answer: A female in oestrus stops when mounted by other animals and mounts other animals.

cards.question: What is the safe and best method of insemination in cattle?
cards.answer: The safe and best method of insemination in cattle is the recto vaginal method of insemination. Considerable skill and experience are required to perform AI successfully for large numbers of animals.

cards.question: Describe the conditions and personal preparation required before inseminating a cow.
cards.answer: Insemination is carried out in a sheltered area to eliminate unfavorable conditions such as wind, dust and rain. Instruments must be sterile, the cow in heat is well controlled in a crush, and the inseminator wears a plastic apron, gumboots and gloves.

cards.question: How is the semen straw thawed and loaded for insemination?
cards.answer: The semen straw is thawed by keeping it in tepid water for a minute so the frozen semen becomes liquid and the sperm become motile. It is then loaded into a sterilized AI gum and covered with a plastic sheath.

cards.question: Describe the rectal steps of the recto-vaginal AI procedure in cattle.
cards.answer: The inseminator inserts a gloved left hand into the rectum after applying soft soap or other lubricant to the glove and back-racking the animal. The hand is inserted further to catch hold of the cervix through the rectal wall, and then the AI gun loaded with the semen straw is passed.

cards.question: List six advantages of artificial insemination.
cards.answer: A wider variety of superior males can be used; more females can be bred to a superior male; it reduces the spread of infectious diseases such as contagious abortion and vibriosis; there is no need to keep a male on the farm because semen is brought from AI centers; it helps maintain accurate breeding and parturition records; and old, heavy and injured males can be used.

cards.question: List five disadvantages or limitations of artificial insemination.
cards.answer: AI requires well-trained operators; it requires specialist equipment and facilities; it requires more time than natural services; improper cleaning of instruments and unsanitary conditions may lead to lower fertility; and if the bull is not properly tested, the spreading of genital diseases will be increased.

cards.question: Compare AI and embryo transfer in terms of the superior parent each exploits.
cards.answer: According to the unit summary, AI aims to exploit superior males, while embryo transfer favors the rapid exploitation of superior females.

cards.text: Artificial insemination is collecting sperm cells from {{c1::male animals}} and depositing them into the reproductive tract of a female ({{c2::vagina, cervix or uterus}}) by a method other than {{c3::natural mating}}.
Semen is collected hygienically from {{c1::superior males}}, then carefully handled, diluted and stored in a freezer at {{c2::-196 °C}} in {{c3::liquid nitrogen}} until required.
A {{c1::liquid nitrogen tank}} is used for preserving and storing semen for an {{c2::extended period of time}}.
Success in insemination timing is dependent upon a good {{c1::heat detection program}}, and effective AI work needs accurate {{c2::herd supervision and heat detection}}.

Physical signs of oestrus include loss of {{c1::appetite}}, constant {{c2::vocalizations}}, {{c3::restlessness}}, rubbing against herd-mates, redder and moister vulva lips, swelling around the vulva and a thin {{c4::mucous discharge}}.
A female in oestrus will stop when {{c1::mounted by other animals}} and will also {{c2::mount other animals}}.
The safe and best method of insemination in cattle is the {{c1::recto vaginal method}} of insemination.

Insemination is done in a {{c1::sheltered area}} free of wind, dust and rain; instruments must be {{c2::sterile}}, the cow is controlled in a {{c3::crush}}, and the inseminator wears a plastic apron, gumboots and gloves.
The semen straw is thawed by keeping it in {{c1::tepid water for a minute}} so the sperm become {{c2::motile}}, then loaded in a sterilized {{c3::AI gum}} and covered with a {{c4::plastic sheath}}.

The gloved left hand is inserted into the {{c1::rectum}} after applying {{c2::soft soap or other lubricant}}, the {{c3::cervix}} is caught hold of through the rectal wall, and the AI gum loaded with semen straw is passed.

AI allows a wider variety of {{c1::superior males}} to be used, increases the number of females bred to a superior male, reduces spread of {{c2::contagious abortion and vibriosis}}, removes the need to keep a male on the farm, helps maintain accurate {{c3::breeding and parturition records}}, and allows old, heavy and injured males to be used.

AI requires well-trained {{c1::operators}} and specialist {{c2::equipment and facilities}}, takes more {{c3::time}} than natural services, and improper cleaning or unsanitary conditions may lead to lower {{c4::fertility}} while an untested bull increases spread of {{c5::genital diseases}}.

cards.question: Define embryo transfer.
cards.answer: Embryo transfer is an artificial method of breeding whereby newly formed embryos, prior to implantation, are removed from a female animal called the donor and transferred into the reproductive tract of another female of the same species called the recipient.

cards.question: Describe the donor and the recipient in embryo transfer.
cards.answer: Donors are highly productive or superior animals, while recipients are inferior in productivity. Embryo transfer disseminates desirable genes from superior female animals.

cards.question: In which species is embryo transfer used to disseminate desirable genes?
cards.answer: Embryo transfer is used in horses, cattle, sheep, goats and pigs. It has proved to be a powerful technology in the genetic improvement of farm animals.

cards.question: Describe the first steps of the embryo transfer process in cattle.
cards.answer: Cows receive a hormone treatment to produce more than one ovulation (egg) at a time. They are then artificially inseminated with bulls that also possess desirable genetics.

cards.question: How and when are embryos recovered in the cattle embryo transfer process?
cards.answer: Seven days later, a veterinarian recovers the embryos using a catheter and recovery fluid. The fluid passes through a specialized filter that catches the embryos. The recovered embryos are filtered into a lab and evaluated under a microscope.

cards.question: How many good embryos are produced per cow on average, and what happens to them?
cards.answer: The process produces an average of six good embryos per cow. Fertilized embryos captured can be transferred into a surrogate cow called a recipient that carries the pregnancy to term, or the embryos can be frozen for later use.

cards.question: List five advantages of embryo transfer.
cards.answer: It allows a producer to quickly multiply the number of offspring of top females; it makes exchange of genetic material between countries easier and more rapid; it involves no transport of live animals; it reduces risks of disease transmission; and it enhances storage and expansion of rare genetic stock.

cards.question: List three disadvantages of embryo transfer.
cards.answer: The technique requires a high cost, requires skilled technicians, and may be time consuming.

cards.text: Embryo transfer removes newly formed embryos prior to {{c1::implantation}} from a female {{c2::donor}} and transfers them into the reproductive tract of a {{c3::recipient}} of the same species.
In embryo transfer, donors are {{c1::highly productive or superior animals}}, while recipients are {{c2::inferior in productivity}}.
Embryo transfer is used to disseminate desirable genes from species including {{c1::horses}}, {{c2::cattle}}, {{c3::sheep}}, {{c4::goats}} and {{c5::pigs}}.
Cows receive a {{c1::hormone treatment}} to produce more than one {{c2::ovulation}} at a time, and are then artificially inseminated with bulls possessing {{c3::desirable genetics}}.

{{c1::Seven days}} later, a veterinarian recovers embryos using a {{c2::catheter and recovery fluid}}, which passes through a {{c3::specialized filter}}; the embryos are then evaluated under a {{c4::microscope}} in a lab.

The process produces an average of {{c1::six good embryos}} per cow; embryos are transferred to a {{c2::surrogate cow (recipient)}} that carries the pregnancy to term, or they can be {{c3::frozen}} for later use.

ET quickly multiplies offspring of {{c1::top females}}, allows rapid exchange of genetic material between countries with no transport of {{c2::live animals}}, reduces {{c3::disease transmission}} risks and enhances storage and expansion of {{c4::rare genetic stock}}.
Disadvantages of embryo transfer: high {{c1::cost}}, need for {{c2::skilled technicians}}, and the technique may be {{c3::time consuming}}.
AI aims to exploit {{c1::superior males}}, whereas ET favors the rapid exploitation of {{c2::superior females}}.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 6::6.4 Animal identification and record keeping

cards.question: Why are herd performance records one of the best management tools for a successful genetic improvement program?
cards.answer: Performance records help producers identify areas of weakness in overall herd or flock performance. Information on animal performance helps farmers make informed decisions about flock management, selection of new breeding stock and culling of low performing animals.

cards.question: How do identification and record keeping help with animal health and culling decisions?
cards.answer: Tracking animals that have been treated with medication is made easy through identification and record keeping. Keeping records of the medical histories of individual animals can also be used when making culling decisions.

cards.question: What is phenotypic data, and why is its accuracy important?
cards.answer: Phenotypic data are an individual's observable traits, such as height and color. Recording phenotypic data is the major driving force for genetic progress, and that progress depends very much on the accuracy of the data.

cards.question: What records does individual animal identification allow producers to keep?
cards.answer: Individual animal identification allows producers to keep records of an animal's parentage, birth date and production records.

cards.question: List the permanent methods of animal identification.
cards.answer: Permanent identifications include branding, ear tags, tattooing, ear notches or notching, and microchips.

cards.question: List the simple temporary methods used to mark animals.
cards.answer: Temporary methods include tail marking with a pen and chalk, clipping their hair, and dying their fur.

cards.question: What are the two basic types of animal identification given in the unit summary?
cards.answer: The two basic types are permanent identification and temporary identification. Animal identification and trait recording are fundamental to all breeding programs.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 6::6.4 Animal identification and record keeping

cards.text: Performance records help producers identify {{c1::areas of weakness}} in overall herd or flock performance and make informed decisions about flock management, selection of {{c2::new breeding stock}} and culling {{c3::low performing animals}}.

Identification and record keeping make it easy to track animals treated with {{c1::medication}}, and records of individual {{c2::medical histories}} can also be used when making {{c3::culling decisions}}.

Recording of {{c1::phenotypic data}}, an individual's observable traits such as {{c2::height and color}}, is the major driving force for genetic progress, which depends on the {{c3::accuracy of the data}}.
Individual animal identification allows producers to keep records of an animal's {{c1::parentage}}, {{c2::birth date}} and {{c3::production records}}.
Permanent methods of animal identification include {{c1::branding}}, {{c2::ear tags}}, {{c3::tattooing}}, {{c4::ear notches}} and {{c5::microchips}}.
Simple temporary identification methods are {{c1::tail marking with a pen and chalk}}, {{c2::clipping their hair}} and {{c3::dying their fur}}.
The two basic types of identification are {{c1::permanent}} and {{c2::temporary}}; animal identification and trait recording are fundamental to all {{c3::breeding programs}}.

cards.question: What is the overall significance of a good housing system in farm animal production?
cards.answer: A good housing system has a significant role in profitable animal production. Proper housing protects animals from health problems, enables them to perform better, and furnishes adequate comfort and protection from climatic stresses and potential diseases.

cards.question: Why can good feeding and breeding fail to produce maximum output even on a well-managed farm?
cards.answer: Good feeding and breeding will not result in maximum production if farm animals are not kept in a good house; housing must provide comfort and protection from climatic stresses and diseases.

cards.question: Which environmental variables can a good house help the farmer control, and how do animals respond to them?
cards.answer: Good housing improves control of temperature, relative humidity, air movement, sun radiation and rain. Animals respond to changes in these factors by changing their behavior, and their productivity or reproduction efficiency also drops.

cards.question: How does high temperature reduce animal production and reproduction?
cards.answer: At high temperature, feed intake is reduced to regulate body temperature. This reduces the quantity and quality of milk, meat, egg and wool production, and reproduction is also adversely affected by high temperature range.

cards.question: How does a well-ventilated, dry house control diseases and external parasites?
cards.answer: A well ventilated and dry house prevents the buildup of pathogens. Good housing facilitates strict sanitary control, is easy to clean and disinfect, minimizes animal mortality, and helps eliminate external parasites such as ticks, mite and lice.

cards.question: How does careful planning of buildings and equipment improve the efficient use of feed and labor?
cards.answer: Careful planning improves the efficiency of feeding, reduces feed wastage and labor cost, and allows efficient communication between feed stores and feeding points such as feed troughs.

cards.question: Which routine management activities become easier in a well-designed animal house, and what benefit is there for workers?
cards.answer: Watering, breeding, egg collection, milking and cleaning become easier. A well-designed house also protects laborers from various environmental stresses, which has an economic implication.

cards.question: Why is safeguarding farm animals against predators a purpose of housing?
cards.answer: All farm animals are prey animals, so keeping them inside a house is a major way to protect them from predators.

cards.text: A good housing system has a significant role in {{c1::profitable animal production}} and should furnish adequate {{c2::comfort}} and protection from {{c3::climatic stresses}} and potential diseases.

Farm animals respond to changes in temperature, relative humidity, air movement, sun radiation and rain by changing their {{c1::behavior}}, while their {{c2::productivity or reproduction efficiency}} also drops.
Protecting animals from environmental changes helps achieve the desired production level {{c1::throughout the year}}.
A well ventilated and dry house helps prevent the buildup of {{c1::pathogens}} and allows easy {{c2::cleaning and disinfecting}} to minimize animal mortality.
External parasites eliminated through good housing include {{c1::ticks}}, {{c2::mite}} and {{c3::lice}}.
Careful planning of buildings and equipment arrangements reduces {{c1::feed wastage}} and {{c2::labor cost}}, and makes routine work such as {{c3::milking}} easier.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 7::7.2 Types of Farm Animal Housing

cards.question: What factors should be considered when choosing a farm animal housing system?
cards.answer: Housing type should be chosen depending on the type of animals, climate conditions, local tradition, availability of building materials and economics.

cards.question: How do conventional barns and loose housing differ in climatic suitability?
cards.answer: The conventional barn system is not suitable to hot and humid climates, while the loose housing system is more suitable to Ethiopian conditions.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 7::7.2 Types of Farm Animal Housing

cards.text: Each housing system has its own {{c1::advantages and disadvantages}}, so the type should be chosen according to the animals, climate, local tradition, building materials and {{c2::economics}}.

cards.question: What are the structural and management features of a conventional barn?
cards.answer: Animals are kept in constructed houses, managed intensively and protected from adverse climatic conditions. Barns are completely roofed, with complete walls containing windows or ventilators at suitable places; continual air flow keeps the area comfortable.

cards.question: What advantages and climatic suitability are stated for conventional barns?
cards.answer: Animals and workers caring for them are less exposed to adverse weather conditions, barns remain hygienic and disease prevalence is less, and they are suitable in heavy rainfall and temperate climates.

cards.question: How are dairy cattle handled in a conventional barn, and why is a separate milking parlour unnecessary?
cards.answer: Dairy cattle are often kept tied in large stalls and cannot walk around the barn. They are provided with feed and water and are milked in the same barn, so there is no need for a separate milking parlour. Tie stalls have largely been phased out due to animal welfare concerns and are becoming less popular.

cards.question: What examples of conventional barns are given, and how does a deep litter system work?
cards.answer: Examples are conventional barns for dairy cattle and deep litter poultry housing. Deep litter poultry or pig housing repeatedly spreads straw or sawdust in indoor booths: an initial layer serves for bedding and defecation, and new layers are continuously added as litter becomes soiled.

cards.text: Conventional barns are {{c1::completely roofed}} and their walls are complete with {{c2::windows or ventilators}} at suitable places so that continual air flow keeps the area comfortable.
In conventional dairy barns, cows are often {{c1::tied in large stalls}}, cannot walk around, and are fed, watered and milked in the same barn, so no separate {{c2::milking parlour}} is needed.
Deep litter housing repeatedly spreads {{c1::straw or sawdust}} in indoor booths, and as the initial litter is soiled, {{c2::new layers}} of litter are continuously added.

cards.question: What is loose housing and what does it provide for animals and workers?
cards.answer: Loose housing allows animals to move freely and have free access over the whole area of the building or pen. It provides more comfort and free movement for both workers and animals, thus improving productivity and welfare.

cards.question: How are animals grouped and fed in a loose housing system?
cards.answer: Animals of equal line of production and similar age are usually kept in groups; group size depends on the type of animal and size of farm. Self-feeding is practiced, and animals have freedom to walk around the free stalls at will.

cards.question: What practical advantages make loose housing suitable for Ethiopian conditions?
cards.answer: Less bedding is required and less manure must be removed. It is very suitable for tropical climates such as most parts of Ethiopia, all types of livestock can be housed under it, and it is cheaper to construct, easier to expand and flexible in utility.

cards.text: Loose housing allows animals to move freely and have {{c1::free access over the whole area}} of the building or pen, improving productivity and welfare.
Animals of equal {{c1::line of production}} and similar age are usually kept in groups, and {{c2::self-feeding}} is practiced in loose housing.
Loose housing is very suitable for a {{c1::tropical climate}} such as most parts of Ethiopia, is cheaper to construct, easier to {{c2::expand}} and flexible in utility.

cards.question: What are the physical features of a free range system?
cards.answer: Stock animals are left in a large area of natural or cultivated pasture land with watering points and shelters. The farm headquarters is situated at the center, and animals run free in the large area throughout the year.

cards.question: What management, exercise and behavioral characteristics distinguish free range production?
cards.answer: An attendant moves with the animals to protect them from predators and thievery. Animals are less intensively managed than in modern farms, the farmer has less control over their environment, but the animals get more exercise, more time to graze and greater freedom to express their natural behaviour.

cards.question: Which animals suit free range systems, and how is the system practiced with chickens, sheep and goats in Ethiopia?
cards.answer: It suits animals not handled daily, such as beef cattle and fattening sheep. Local chickens in mixed flocks use an outdoor range during daylight and are housed in a shed at night, with little or no supplementary prepared feed, which limits productivity and exposes them to predators. Sheep and goats graze during the day and are kept in a barn at night.

cards.text: A free range system leaves stock animals in a large area of {{c1::natural or cultivated pasture land}} with {{c2::watering points}} and shelters, with the farm headquarters at the center.
An {{c1::attendant}} should move with free range animals to protect them from {{c2::predators and thievery}}.
Local chickens in mixed flocks use the outdoor range during {{c1::daylight hours}} and are housed in a {{c2::shed}} at night; sheep and goats graze by day and are kept in a {{c3::barn}} at night.

cards.question: How are animals housed and fed in modern farms?
cards.answer: Depending on the weather condition, animals can be kept in a full or half walled house in a separate pen or enclosure. Cut and carry or prepared feed is the main feed source, and the system is practiced with all common farm animals.

cards.question: Compare the investment cost and productivity of modern farms with conventional operations.
cards.answer: The investment cost per animal is more than in conventional operations, but productivity is better in the modern farm system.

cards.question: Which modern housing examples are given for egg laying chickens, and what trade-off is noted?
cards.answer: Battery cages such as enriched cages and hens-aviary systems are good examples of modern farms for egg laying chickens. Cage systems are the most efficient systems for egg production, but some people are concerned about the welfare of laying hens kept in cages.

cards.question: What are enriched cages?
cards.answer: Enriched cages are cages stacked on top of one another in row upon row, but they also provide limited facilities for nesting, perching and scratching.

cards.question: What are hens-aviary systems?
cards.answer: Hens-aviary systems, also called multi-tier systems, have tiers as their most typical feature; they provide living space at several levels and allow hens to disperse across several levels.

cards.question: When is an animal in a good state of welfare?
cards.answer: An animal is in a good state of welfare if it is healthy, comfortable, well-nourished, safe, able to express innate behavior, and not suffering from unpleasant states such as pain, fear and distress. Animal welfare is the well-being of non-human animals.

cards.text: Good animal welfare requires {{c1::disease prevention}} and veterinary treatment, appropriate shelter, management, nutrition, humane handling and {{c2::humane slaughter}}; protecting an animal's welfare means providing for its physical and mental needs and is a human responsibility.

The five freedoms of animal welfare are freedom from {{c1::thirst and hunger}}, freedom from {{c2::discomfort}} by providing adequate shelter, freedom from {{c3::disease, pain, or injury}}, freedom from {{c4::distress and fear}}, and freedom to {{c5::exhibit natural behaviors}}.
Depending on the weather condition, animals in modern farms can be kept in a {{c1::full or half walled house}} in a separate pen or enclosure.
{{c1::Cut and carry or prepared feed}} is the main feed source in modern farms, where investment per animal is higher but {{c2::productivity}} is better.
Battery cages like {{c1::enriched cages}} and {{c2::hens-aviary systems}} for egg laying chicken are good examples of modern farms.

cards.question: Why is location the first consideration when planning a new farm, and what does it refer to?
cards.answer: When planning an entirely new farm, the choice of location for constructing the building is the first consideration. Location refers to where animal housing is placed in relation to soil structure, drainage, road access and proximity to other farm houses.

cards.question: What topography and drainage requirements apply to an animal housing site?
cards.answer: Topography means the arrangement of the features of an area. The site should ideally be elevated but fairly level with no abrupt slopes, always in a well-drained area, with porous soil and a gentle slope so drainage is efficient.

cards.question: What water supply is required at an animal housing site?
cards.answer: A good source of clean water should be available cheaply and in plenty. A year-round supply is essential for the animals, sanitation, workers and residences, and fire protection.

cards.question: What service and input availability should a good animal housing site have?
cards.answer: The site should be in areas with adequate veterinary services and where feed is available at a cheaper price.

cards.question: What accessibility features should an animal housing site have, and why are roads important?
cards.answer: It should preferably have a good market outlet, power line, electric power source and all weather road, with provision for easy electricity connection. Outages are more likely far from the electric substation, and good roads ease supply; inadequate roads and transportation create problems producing and marketing fresh products such as milk, meat, fish and egg.

cards.question: What distance, health and size considerations apply when selecting an animal housing site?
cards.answer: Odors are inherent in livestock operations, especially when manure is not managed properly, so prevailing wind direction relative to non-owned residences matters; the site should not be near hospitals, schools, residential areas, slaughter houses or factories. It should preferably not be beside a national highway or main market road, to reduce disease transmission, and enough space should separate farm houses. The farm area should be adequate for future expansion: plan years ahead, consider doubling the present anticipated size, and avoid property lines or public-use areas that limit expansion.

cards.text: The topography of the site should ideally be {{c1::elevated but fairly level}} with no abrupt slopes, and the soil should be {{c2::porous}} with a gentle slope for efficient drainage.
A year-round supply of clean water is essential for the animals, {{c1::sanitation}}, workers and residences, and {{c2::fire protection}}.
The site should be located where there are adequate {{c1::veterinary services}} and where feed is available at a {{c2::cheaper price}}.
Good accessibility means a good {{c1::market outlet}}, power line and {{c2::all weather road}}, together with provision for easy electricity connection.
Inadequate road and transportation facilities create problems producing and marketing fresh farm products such as {{c1::milk, meat, fish and egg}}.
Prevailing {{c1::wind direction}} in relationship to non-owned residences is important because {{c2::odors}} are inherent in livestock operations, especially when manure is not managed properly.
Plan for expansion some years into the future, consider {{c1::doubling the size}} anticipated at present, and avoid locating facilities near {{c2::property lines}} or public-use areas.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 7::7.3.2 Guidelines for Construction of Animal House

cards.question: What general qualities should a well-constructed animal house have?
cards.answer: It should provide adequate space for feeding and exercise and proper ventilation, offer maximum comfort and protection from environmental stresses, be inexpensive to build and economical to operate and maintain, be easy to clean and disinfect to minimize animal mortality, protect animals from drafts, and have ventilation adequate to prevent dampness.

cards.question: Why is careful planning of buildings and equipment arrangements essential?
cards.answer: Careful planning develops an integrated and efficient layout for producing quality products such as milk, and gives due consideration to building and equipment arrangements for efficient use of labor and feed. Inadequate and improper planning results in additional labour charges and increased maintenance costs.

cards.question: What are the effects of East-West orientation of an animal house?
cards.answer: East-West orientation helps avoid direct sunlight, so feed and water troughs can be placed under shade all times of the day. Feed consumption increases and more manure is dropped in the shade.

cards.question: What are the effects of North-South orientation of an animal house?
cards.answer: In North-South orientation, the sun strikes every part of the floor area under and on either side of the roof at some time of the day, keeping the floor area dry. This orientation is preferred if paving is too costly.

cards.question: What are the construction requirements for a livestock house floor?
cards.answer: The floor should be laid on a solid and compact foundation; the foundation must be with stones but the inner side must be smooth. An ideal floor is well drained and made of cement concrete. It must facilitate hygienic feeding and effective removal of liquid and solid wastes, and should be non-slippery with grooves and a roughened surface.

cards.question: What are the wall requirements for an animal house?
cards.answer: Walls should protect animals from draft, be hard and durable and preferably made with cement concrete. Their inside should have a smooth hard cement finish that prevents lodgment of dust and moisture, and corners or projections where animals could injure themselves should be avoided. Walls may be solid or partially open depending on local conditions and animal type; wood and bamboo are inexpensive local alternatives, with wood painted in preservative solution every 3 to 5 years. Side walls often include windows covered with wire mesh for ventilation, especially in chicken and pig houses, and the shorter width side has to be solid.

cards.question: What are the roof requirements for an animal house?
cards.answer: A well designed roof reduces heat and cold stresses. It should preferably be galvanized iron-sheet for durability and comfort, though inexpensive local materials such as thatches can be used. It should be high enough to release excess heat, moisture and pollutants, sloped, and have an overhang of at least 60 cm for protection from sun and rain. Direct solar radiation increases heat load and adversely affects production and reproduction.

cards.question: What is ventilation and why must it be adequate in all farm animal houses?
cards.answer: Ventilation is the entry and circulation of air freely. Smooth air movement supplies fresh air for breathing and removes noxious and toxic gases such as CO2 and NH3. Adequate ventilation is a must in all farm animal houses to avoid dampness; continual airflow keeps the area comfortable and helps prevent and control disease-causing pathogens. Roof height should be a minimum of 3 m to allow sufficient air movement.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 7::7.3.2 Guidelines for Construction of Animal House

cards.text: A good animal house provides adequate space for {{c1::feeding and exercise}} and proper {{c2::ventilation}}, offers maximum comfort and protection, and protects farm animals from {{c3::drafts}}.

The objective is housing that is inexpensive to build, economical to operate and maintain, and easy to {{c1::clean and disinfect}} to minimize {{c2::animal mortality}}; flooring must facilitate hygienic feeding and effective removal of {{c3::liquid and solid wastes}}.

Careful planning of buildings and equipment arrangements gives efficient use of {{c1::labor and feed}}, whereas improper planning results in additional {{c2::labour charges}} and increased maintenance costs.
In the {{c1::East-West}} orientation, direct sunlight is avoided and feed and water troughs can be under shade all day; feed consumption increases and more {{c2::manure}} is dropped in the shade.
In the {{c1::North-South}} orientation, the sun strikes every part of the floor area at some time of the day, which keeps the floor {{c2::dry}}; it is preferred if paving is too costly.
The floor should be laid on a {{c1::solid and compact foundation}} made with stones whose inner side is {{c2::smooth}}.
An ideal livestock floor is well drained and made of {{c1::cement concrete}}, with {{c2::grooves and a roughened surface}} so that it is non-slippery.

The inside of walls should have a smooth hard finish of cement that will not allow any {{c1::lodgment of dust and moisture}}, and corners or projections where animals could injure themselves should be {{c2::avoided}}.
Walls may be built from inexpensive local materials such as {{c1::wood and bamboo}}; if wood is used, it should be painted with wood preservative solution every {{c2::3 to 5 years}}.
Side walls often include {{c1::windows}} which can be covered with {{c2::wire mesh}} for ventilation, especially in chicken and pig houses; the shorter width side has to be {{c3::solid}}.
A well designed roof is preferably made of {{c1::galvanized iron-sheet}} for durability and comfort, although inexpensive local materials such as {{c2::thatches}} may be used.
The roof should be sloped with an overhang of at least {{c1::60 cm}} to offer protection from sun and rain, and high enough to release excess {{c2::heat, moisture and pollutants}}.

Ventilation is the entry and circulation of air freely; it supplies fresh air and removes noxious and toxic gases such as {{c1::CO2 and NH3}}, and the roof height should be a minimum of {{c2::3 m}} to allow sufficient air movement.

To reduce the risk of disease transmission and support biosecurity, the site should preferably not be beside a {{c1::national highway or main market road}}, enough {{c2::space between farm houses}} should be left, and continual airflow helps prevent {{c3::disease causing pathogens}}.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 8::8.1 Introduction to Animal Health and Disease Control

cards.question: Define animal health as given in the textbook.
cards.answer: Health is the state of wellbeing of an animal.

cards.question: Define disease and list the consequences of animal diseases mentioned in the introduction.
cards.answer: Any departure from the state of health is called disease. Consequences include loss of appetite and weight, slow growth, reduction in production, reproduction loss and death of the animal.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 8::8.1 Introduction to Animal Health and Disease Control

cards.text: Health is the state of {{c1::wellbeing}} of an animal, and any departure from this state is called {{c2::disease}}.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 8::8.1.1 Routes of Transmission of Pathogens

cards.question: What is a pathogen?
cards.answer: Pathogens are disease-causing microorganisms.

cards.question: List all the routes by which animals can be infected with pathogens, as summarised in the unit.
cards.answer: Direct contact, ingestion, inhalation, the uro-genital tract (mating), the placenta (before birth), and vectors.

cards.question: How does direct contact transmit pathogens between animals?
cards.answer: Infection occurs through direct contact with an infected animal or with its tissues or fluids, for example blood, saliva, urine and droppings.

cards.question: Describe the ingestion route of pathogen transmission on a farm.
cards.answer: Animals ingest pathogens from contaminated feed, water and farm equipment such as feed and water troughs.

cards.question: Describe the inhalation route of pathogen transmission.
cards.answer: Animals are infected through inhalation of droplets or dust containing pathogens.

cards.question: What are vectors and how do they spread pathogens?
cards.answer: Vectors are living organisms, such as insects, that carry pathogens and transmit them to animals.

cards.question: Name the two routes of infection that involve reproduction or birth.
cards.answer: Pathogens may be spread during mating (the uro-genital tract) or before birth through the placenta.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 8::8.1.1 Routes of Transmission of Pathogens

cards.text: Pathogens are {{c1::disease-causing}} microorganisms.
One route of infection is direct contact with an infected animal or its tissues or fluids such as {{c1::blood}}, saliva, {{c2::urine}} and droppings.
Pathogens can be ingested from contaminated {{c1::feed}}, water and farm equipment such as feed and water {{c2::troughs}}.
Animals can be infected through inhalation of {{c1::droplets}} or {{c2::dust}} containing pathogens.
Vectors are {{c1::living organisms}}, such as {{c2::insects}}, that carry pathogens from one animal to another.
Pathogens may be spread during {{c1::mating}} or before birth through the {{c2::placenta}}.
The common routes of transmission are direct contact, {{c1::ingestion}}, inhalation, {{c2::uro-genital tract}}, placenta and {{c3::vectors}}.

cards.question: Define a symptom.
cards.answer: A symptom is a sign or indication of the existence of a disease or other disorder.

cards.question: List the general symptoms of sick animals given in the textbook.
cards.answer: Loss of appetite, weight loss, coughing, being unable to rise, slow movement, lameness, isolation from the herd or flock, head and neck down, tired or lazy look, watery/bad-smelling/blood-stained faeces and urine, discharges from body openings, sunken eyes, raised hair coat, rough skin, dry muzzle, swelling in joints, variation in body temperature, pulse rate and respiration rate, and death.

cards.question: Which symptoms describe the posture, movement and behaviour of a sick animal?
cards.answer: Being unable to rise, slow movement, lameness, isolation from the herd or flock, standing with head and neck down, and appearing tired or lazy.

cards.question: What abnormal faeces and urine signs may a sick animal show?
cards.answer: The faeces and urine may be watery, bad-smelling, or blood-stained.

cards.question: Name the visible body-condition signs of ill health involving openings, eyes, coat, skin, muzzle and joints.
cards.answer: Discharges from body openings, sunken eyes, raised hair coat, rough skin, dry muzzle and swelling in joints.

cards.question: Which vital signs may vary in a sick animal, and what is the most severe possible outcome?
cards.answer: Body temperature, pulse rate and respiration rate may vary; disease may also lead to death.

cards.question: A farm animal has separated itself from the rest of the flock. Which symptom is this?
cards.answer: Isolation from the herd or flock is a symptom of sickness.

cards.text: A symptom is a {{c1::sign}} or indication of the existence of a disease or other {{c2::disorder}}.
General symptoms include loss of {{c1::appetite}}, weight loss, {{c2::coughing}}, inability to rise, slow movement, lameness and isolation from the herd or flock.
A sick animal may stand with its {{c1::head and neck}} down or appear to have a tired or {{c2::lazy}} look.
Sick animals may have {{c1::watery}}, bad-smelling or {{c2::blood-stained}} faeces and urine.
Other signs of ill health are discharges from {{c1::body openings}}, {{c2::sunken eyes}} and a raised hair coat.
A sick animal may show rough skin, a {{c1::dry muzzle}} and swelling in the {{c2::joints}}.
There may be variation in body {{c1::temperature}}, pulse rate and {{c2::respiration rate}}, and disease may lead to {{c3::death}}.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 8::8.2 Major Diseases of Farm Animals

cards.question: How are diseases of farm animals categorized, and what are examples of each category?
cards.answer: They are categorized as infectious and non-infectious. Infectious diseases are caused by pathogenic organisms such as viruses, bacteria and protozoa and are communicable from one animal to another or to a human being; examples are anthrax, foot and mouth disease (FMD) and Newcastle disease. Non-infectious diseases are neither caused by pathogens nor passed from animal to animal; they may be caused by hereditary factors or the environment; examples are ketosis, rickets and poisoning.

cards.question: Define viruses, bacteria and protozoa as presented in the key terms box.
cards.answer: Viruses are very small acellular structures visible only with a powerful electron microscope; they multiply only within a living cell and can be transmitted from one organism to another. Bacteria are microscopically small, single-celled organisms found worldwide in most habitats. Protozoa are single-celled organisms that live within or on the animal, are found worldwide in most habitats, and only a few cause infections.

cards.question: List the major animal diseases in Ethiopia named in this unit.
cards.answer: Foot and mouth disease (FMD), anthrax, tuberculosis, brucellosis, contagious bovine pleuropneumonia (CBPP), mastitis, Newcastle disease, coccidiosis and trypanosomiasis.

cards.question: Give the causal agent, affected species, transmission, symptoms and control of foot and mouth disease (FMD).
cards.answer: FMD is a highly contagious, acute viral disease affecting cattle, sheep, goats and pigs. It is transmitted by contact with infected urine, faeces, milk and nasal discharge. It causes sores on feet, lips, tongue and cheek, fever, rough hair coat, salivation, foaming, inability to feed, weakness, lameness and death. Control uses quarantine, vaccination, good sanitation and elimination of infected animals.

cards.question: Give the causal agent, affected species, transmission, signs, productivity impact and control of contagious bovine pleuropneumonia (CBPP).
cards.answer: CBPP is described as a viral respiratory disease of cattle, goats, sheep and pigs, transmitted through contact with infected body fluids such as milk and urine. Signs are a dry and painful cough, loss of appetite, difficulty in breathing and inflammation of the lungs. It causes important productivity losses through high mortality and morbidity rates. Control includes vaccination, isolation and slaughtering of infected animals.

cards.question: Give the causative agent, alternative name, hosts, transmission, effects, symptoms and control of brucellosis.
cards.answer: Brucellosis is an infectious bacterial disease caused by Brucella abortus and is also called contagious abortion disease. It infects cattle, goats, sheep, camels and pigs through direct contact with infected animals, tissue or fluids and through ingestion. It causes abortion and infertility with heavy economic loss; symptoms are intermittent fever, reduced milk flow and enlarged testicles. Prevention uses good herd management, and dead animals should be burned or buried.

cards.question: Why is brucellosis a public-health concern, and how can humans acquire it?
cards.answer: Brucellosis threatens human health if people eat infected dairy products that are raw or unpasteurized.

cards.question: Give the causative agent, hosts, transmission, signs and prevention of anthrax.
cards.answer: Anthrax is an infectious bacterial disease whose causative agent is Bacillus anthracis. It afflicts ruminants and can also affect humans. Animals are infected through contact with infected animals or materials and by inhalation of spores. Signs are high fever, convulsion, rapid breathing and sudden death. Prevention is through isolation of infected animals and disposal of the dead ones.

cards.question: Give the cause, hosts, transmission, signs and control of Newcastle disease (NCD).
cards.answer: Newcastle disease is a well-known viral disease of poultry. Transmission can be airborne or through contaminated vaccines and farm equipment such as feeders and drinkers. Birds show lack of appetite, respiratory difficulties, twisted neck, paralysis of the legs or wings, laying of soft-shelled eggs and watery greenish diarrhea. Control uses culling of sick birds, quarantine and vaccination.

cards.question: Give the cause, hosts, transmission, symptoms and control of taeniasis.
cards.answer: Taeniasis, also known as tapeworm infection disease, affects cattle and pigs. The common mode of transmission is through the soil during feeding. Symptoms are anaemia, vomiting and discomfort. Regular de-worming and good sanitation are recommended control measures.

cards.question: Which diseases are given as examples of infectious diseases, and which as non-infectious diseases?
cards.answer: Infectious examples: anthrax, foot and mouth disease and Newcastle disease. Non-infectious examples: ketosis, rickets and poisoning.

cards.question: Which common Ethiopian diseases are listed in this section but not described in detail in the disease entries?
cards.answer: Tuberculosis, mastitis, coccidiosis and trypanosomiasis.

cards.question: What term is used for morbidity, and how does the textbook describe it?
cards.answer: Morbidity is having a specific illness; CBPP causes high morbidity along with high mortality.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 8::8.2 Major Diseases of Farm Animals

cards.text: Infectious diseases are caused by {{c1::pathogenic}} organisms such as viruses, bacteria and protozoa and are {{c2::communicable}} from one animal to another.
Non-infectious diseases are neither caused by {{c1::pathogens}} nor passed from one animal to another; they may result from {{c2::hereditary}} factors or the environment.
Viruses are very small {{c1::acellular}} structures, visible only with a powerful {{c2::electron microscope}}.
Bacteria are microscopically small, {{c1::single-celled}} organisms, while protozoa are also single celled and live within or on the {{c2::animal}}.
Foot and mouth disease is a highly contagious, acute {{c1::viral}} disease affecting cattle, sheep, {{c2::goats}} and pigs.
FMD is transmitted by contact with infected {{c1::urine}}, faeces, milk and {{c2::nasal discharge}}.
FMD is characterized by sores on the feet, {{c1::lips}}, tongue and cheek, with fever, salivation, {{c2::foaming}}, weakness and lameness.
FMD prevention and control measures are {{c1::quarantine}}, vaccination, good sanitation and {{c2::elimination of infected animals}}.
Contagious Bovine Pleuropneumonia is a {{c1::viral}} respiratory disease transmitted through contact with infected body fluids such as {{c2::milk}} and urine.
An animal with CBPP has a dry and painful {{c1::cough}}, loss of appetite, difficulty in breathing and inflammation of the {{c2::lungs}}.
CBPP control includes {{c1::vaccination}}, isolation and {{c2::slaughtering}} of infected animals.
Brucellosis is an infectious bacterial disease caused by {{c1::Brucella abortus}} and is also known as {{c2::contagious abortion}} disease.
Brucella can infect cattle, goats, sheep, {{c1::camels}} and pigs, and the disease causes {{c2::abortion}} and infertility.
Brucellosis symptoms include {{c1::intermittent fever}}, reduced milk flow and enlarged {{c2::testicles}}.
Anthrax is caused by {{c1::Bacillus anthracis}}; animals are infected by contact with infected materials or by inhalation of {{c2::spores}}.
Anthrax is accompanied by high {{c1::fever}}, convulsion, rapid breathing and {{c2::sudden death}}.
Newcastle disease is a well-known {{c1::viral}} disease of poultry, transmissible by air or through contaminated {{c2::vaccines}} and farm equipment.
NCD signs include respiratory difficulties, a twisted {{c1::neck}}, paralysis of legs or wings, soft-shelled eggs and watery {{c2::greenish diarrhea}}.
Recommended NCD control measures are {{c1::culling}} of sick birds, {{c2::quarantine}} and vaccination.
Taeniasis, also called {{c1::tapeworm}} infection disease, affects cattle and pigs and is transmitted through the {{c2::soil}} during feeding.
Taeniasis symptoms are {{c1::anaemia}}, vomiting and discomfort; control uses regular {{c2::de-worming}} and good sanitation.
The major animal diseases in Ethiopia include foot and mouth disease, anthrax, tuberculosis, brucellosis, CBPP, mastitis, Newcastle disease, {{c1::coccidiosis}} and {{c2::trypanosomiasis}}.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 8::8.3 Internal and External Parasites of Farm Animals

cards.question: Define a parasite and state how many species affect domestic animals.
cards.answer: A parasite is an organism that lives in or on another host organism to get its nourishment. Over 1,000 species of parasites affect domestic animals.

cards.question: How are parasites classified, and what are parasitic diseases?
cards.answer: Parasites are broadly classified as internal and external, depending on where they live. Diseases that occur due to parasites are called parasitic diseases.

cards.question: Where do internal parasites (endoparasites) live and what are the four examples given?
cards.answer: Endoparasites live in the blood or tissues of the animal's body. Examples are tape worm, round worm, trypanosome and liver fluke.

cards.question: What effects do internal parasites have on their host and on the farmer's income?
cards.answer: They interfere with digestion and assimilation of food, share the animal's food and cause diarrhea, anaemia and loss of condition. Often death results if there is no effective treatment, leading to loss of production and income.

cards.question: How do external parasites (ectoparasites) annoy or attack their hosts, and what are four examples?
cards.answer: Ectoparasites often bite, embed or irritate the skin, attacking the blood, skin or hair of the host. Examples are ticks, flies, lice and mites.

cards.question: List the effects of external parasites on animals.
cards.answer: They cause anemia, weight/condition loss, restlessness, skin irritation and skin destruction.

cards.question: Name the diseases that external parasites can cause or transmit, and give the vector example.
cards.answer: They may cause mange and scabies, or transmit red water and trypanosomiasis. For example, the bite of a tsetse fly transmits trypanosomiasis.

cards.question: Define mange, scabies and red water.
cards.answer: Mange is an infectious skin disease caused by mites, resulting in hair loss, scabs and itching. Scabies is a contagious skin disease marked by intense itching, inflammation and red papules. Red water is a disease characterized by the passage of reddish urine.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 8::8.3 Internal and External Parasites of Farm Animals

cards.text: A parasite is an organism that lives in or on another {{c1::host}} organism to get its {{c2::nourishment}}.
Internal parasites, or {{c1::endoparasites}}, live in the blood or tissues; examples are tape worm, round worm, {{c2::trypanosome}} and liver fluke.
Endoparasites interfere with digestion and {{c1::assimilation}} of food and cause diarrhea, {{c2::anaemia}} and loss of condition.
External parasites, or {{c1::ectoparasites}}, include ticks, {{c2::flies}}, lice and mites.
Ectoparasites attack the blood, skin or hair and cause anemia, weight loss, {{c1::restlessness}}, skin irritation and skin {{c2::destruction}}.
The bite of a {{c1::tsetse fly}} transmits {{c2::trypanosomiasis}}.
Mange is caused by {{c1::mites}} and results in hair loss, {{c2::scabs}} and itching, while red water is marked by reddish urine.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 8::8.4 Effects of Diseases and Parasites in Animal Production

cards.question: How do diseases and parasites reduce production and reproduction, and what is mortality?
cards.answer: Sick animals eventually fail to produce or reproduce to their ultimate capacity; this productivity loss is a loss to the farmer. Mortality is the fate of death of the sick animal, and both production loss and mortality are losses to a farmer.

cards.question: In what forms does economic loss from animal diseases and parasites arise?
cards.answer: Reduction in productivity and mortality cause money loss because the farmer has less product to sell and/or fewer animals; external parasites degrade the market value of hide, skin and wool; exports of live animals and their products are limited; and control, prevention, diagnosis and treatment are expensive.

cards.question: Beyond individual farm losses, what wider effects do disease and parasite outbreaks have?
cards.answer: They affect food and job security and can cause economic loss to both the farmer and the nation.

cards.question: What are zoonotic diseases, how many are known, and what examples does the textbook give?
cards.answer: Zoonotic diseases are animal diseases transmittable to humans, often through consumption of food products from infected animals. More than 150 are known; examples are brucellosis, anthrax, salmonellosis and taeniasis.

cards.question: Which product quality losses result specifically from external parasites attacking the coat?
cards.answer: The market value of hide, skin and wool is degraded.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 8::8.4 Effects of Diseases and Parasites in Animal Production

cards.text: Diseases and parasites cause {{c1::morbidity}} and {{c2::mortality}} as well as economic and zoonotic effects.
Sick animals fail to {{c1::produce}} or {{c2::reproduce}} to their ultimate capacity, and this loss of productivity is a loss for the farmer.
External parasites attack the coat and degrade the market value of {{c1::hide}}, skin and {{c2::wool}}.
Diseases and parasites limit the {{c1::export}} of live animals and their products, and the costs of control, prevention, {{c2::diagnosis}} and treatment are expensive.
Animal diseases transmittable to humans are called {{c1::zoonotic}}; more than {{c2::150}} such diseases are known.
Examples of zoonotic diseases are brucellosis, anthrax, {{c1::salmonellosis}} and {{c2::taeniasis}}.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 8::8.5.1 Prevention and Control of Diseases and Parasites

cards.question: Distinguish prevention from control of diseases and parasites.
cards.answer: Prevention refers to measures applied to prevent the occurrence of a disease. Control refers to measures applied to prevent transmission after the disease has occurred.

cards.question: What hygiene and sanitation practices are recommended for disease and parasite control?
cards.answer: Hygiene or sanitation is an effective strategy for controlling infectious disease and parasite infestations. Wash feed and water troughs well, separate sick animals from healthy ones, and burn or bury dead animals.

cards.question: What good-management practices help animals resist disease and parasite attacks?
cards.answer: Provide essential nutrients, keep animals' houses well ventilated and dry, follow rotational grazing in pasture, and avoid overcrowding.

cards.question: Describe the recommended quarantine and isolation procedure for new and sick animals.
cards.answer: Purchase only healthy-looking animals from reputable farms. At arrival, quarantine new animals by keeping them away from other animals for two weeks until you are sure they are not sick. Isolate any sick animals to prevent the illness from spreading.

cards.question: What does the medication measure for controlling farm animal diseases include?
cards.answer: Timely vaccination against diseases, quarantining diseased animals, and the use of drugs in the form of powder, liquid or solids.

cards.question: How are spraying and dipping used against external parasites?
cards.answer: Animals are sprayed with chemical solutions or dipped in them, and pens and animals are sprayed with veterinary chemicals; dipping in water containing chemicals such as wettable powders controls ticks, mites and lice. Regular dipping or spraying is encouraged.

cards.question: Define deworming and give the examples of dewormers and other internal-parasite treatments.
cards.answer: Deworming is giving appropriate drugs to expel internal parasites from animals. Dewormers include piperazine, which controls roundworm; internal parasites are also controlled with drugs, antibiotics or drenches.

cards.question: Define biosecurity and give the examples of biosecurity measures.
cards.answer: Biosecurity refers to measures taken to prevent the introduction and/or spread of harmful organisms to animals and plants. Examples are controlling animal mixing, restricting unnecessary personnel entry to farms, and using protective clothing.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 8::8.5.1 Prevention and Control of Diseases and Parasites

cards.text: {{c1::Prevention}} refers to measures applied to prevent the occurrence of a disease, while {{c2::control}} prevents transmission after the disease has occurred.
Hygiene measures include washing feed and water {{c1::troughs}}, separating sick animals from healthy ones, and {{c2::burning}} or burying dead animals.
Good management means providing essential {{c1::nutrients}}, keeping houses well ventilated and {{c2::dry}}, using rotational grazing and avoiding overcrowding.
New animals should be purchased from reputable farms and quarantined for {{c1::two weeks}}, while sick animals should be {{c2::isolated}}.
Medication includes timely {{c1::vaccination}}, quarantining diseased animals and using drugs in powder, {{c2::liquid}} or solid form.
Spraying or dipping animals with chemical solutions controls external parasites such as flies, lice, {{c1::mites}} and {{c2::ticks}}.
Deworming gives drugs to expel {{c1::internal}} parasites; {{c2::piperazine}} controls roundworm.
Biosecurity measures prevent the introduction and/or spread of {{c1::harmful organisms}} and include controlling animal mixing, limiting personnel entry and using {{c2::protective clothing}}.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 8::8.5.2 Indigenous Knowledge in Livestock Disease Treatment

cards.question: Why are plant-based remedies important in Ethiopia, and from whom do farmers mainly acquire ethno-veterinary knowledge?
cards.answer: In Ethiopia, plant-based remedies are the most important and sometimes the only method of managing livestock diseases; they are an inexpensive alternative to science-based treatments. Farmers mostly acquire ethno-veterinary knowledge from their elders.

cards.question: List the categories of indigenous veterinary practices and state where most medicinal plants are collected.
cards.answer: The practices include mechanical, physical, pharmacological, surgical, ritual and managerial methods of treatment. Several medicinal plant species of veterinary importance are documented, and most medicinal plants are collected from the wild.

cards.question: Which plant parts are used for livestock health treatment, and can they be combined?
cards.answer: Leaf, root, rhizomes, bulb, bark, seed, stem and whole parts may be used, alone or in combination.

cards.question: Name the preparation methods of traditional medicine and identify the major form.
cards.answer: Preparation methods are concoction, squeezing, crushing or pounding. Concoction, meaning mixing things together, is the major form of preparing herbal medicines.

cards.question: How do farmers determine doses and administer traditional medicines to livestock?
cards.answer: Farmers are aware of toxicity and provide antioxidants. They determine the dose using household utensils or their own hand. The oral route is the most common mechanism of application of traditional medicines.

cards.question: Which livestock diseases and parasite syndromes are treated by traditional practitioners, and what animal-fluid example is given?
cards.answer: Examples are anthrax, black leg, ectoparasites, endoparasites, rabies, foot and mouth disease, bloat and colic. Besides plant-based medications, some animal fluids are used: Somali pastoralists in Ethiopia immunize animals against rinder-pest using a solution of urine, milk and faeces from an animal with a mild case of rinderpest.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 8::8.5.2 Indigenous Knowledge in Livestock Disease Treatment

cards.text: In Ethiopia, {{c1::plant-based remedies}} are the most important and sometimes the only method of managing livestock diseases, an inexpensive alternative to {{c2::science-based treatments}}.
Indigenous veterinary practices include {{c1::mechanical}}, physical, pharmacological, {{c2::surgical}}, ritual and managerial methods of treatment.
Medicinal plant parts used may be leaf, root, {{c1::rhizomes}}, bulb, bark, {{c2::seed}}, stem or whole parts.
Traditional medicine is prepared by {{c1::concoction}}, squeezing, {{c2::crushing}} or pounding; concoction is the major form.
Farmers determine the dose using different {{c1::household utensils}} or their own hand, and the {{c2::oral route}} is the most common way of administering traditional medicines.
Traditional practitioners treat anthrax, {{c1::black leg}}, ectoparasites, endoparasites, rabies, foot and mouth disease, {{c2::bloat}} and colic.
Somali pastoralists in Ethiopia immunize animals against {{c1::rinder-pest}} using a solution of {{c2::urine}}, milk and faeces from an animal with a mild case.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 9::9.1 Introduction to dairy cattle production and management

cards.question: What are dairy type cattle raised for, and what makes them excellent at it?
cards.answer: They are raised for milk production and are excellent at converting feeds into high-quality milk.

cards.question: What are multi-purpose cattle?
cards.answer: Cattle that have typical dual-purpose milk and meat production plus some working-cattle features such as strong bones, sound constitution and a quiet temperament.

cards.question: At what age do female calves of modern breeds reach sexual maturity, and what are they called then?
