cards.answer: At seven or eight months; they are called heifers (before having their first calf or having only one calf).

cards.question: At what age are heifers usually mated, and what is that age called?
cards.answer: They are usually mated at 15 to 18 months old; this is the age at first service.

cards.question: At what age do heifers tend to give birth to their first calves?
cards.answer: At two to 2.5 years of age.

cards.question: What management practices are involved in good dairy farming practice?
cards.answer: Producing safe, high-quality milk from healthy animals through breeding, feeding, housing, health care and record keeping.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 9::9.1 Introduction to dairy cattle production and management

cards.text: Cattle raised for both meat and milk production are called {{c1::dual-purpose cattle}}.
Dairying (dairy cattle production) is a branch of {{c1::agriculture}} that raises dairy animals for {{c2::milk and milk products}}; milk is the primary product.
A heifer is a female cattle animal {{c1::before having her first calf or having only one calf}}.
The gestation period in cattle typically lasts {{c1::265 to 300 days}}.
After calving, cows are typically bred again {{c1::four to eight weeks}} later.
Good dairy farming practice involves producing {{c1::safe and high quality milk}} from {{c2::healthy animals}}.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 9::9.2 Dairy cattle breeds and their selection

cards.question: To which scientific family do all domestic cattle of the world belong?
cards.answer: All domestic cattle belong to the family Bovidae.

cards.question: How does the conformation of Bos indicus differ from that of Bos taurus?
cards.answer: Bos indicus have a much narrower body, longer legs, a very prominent dewlap and a hump; Bos taurus have a wider body, shorter legs, a less prominent dewlap and no hump.

cards.question: What production abilities characterize Bos indicus cattle?
cards.answer: Delayed maturity, long calving interval, slow growth rate, short lactation and low milk yield.

cards.question: Name representative breeds of Bos indicus given in the textbook.
cards.answer: Sahiwal, Red Sindhi, Tharparker (Pakistan), Gir, Kankrej, Hariana (India), Kenana, Butana (Sudan) and Ethiopian cattle breeds.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 9::9.2 Dairy cattle breeds and their selection

cards.text: Cattle are classified into two groups: {{c1::Bos indicus}} (indigenous/zebu type) and {{c2::Bos taurus}} (exotic type), which differ in conformation, fitness characters and production abilities.

Bos indicus are adapted to {{c1::tropical}} environments through natural selection in Africa and Asia, while Bos taurus are adapted to {{c2::temperate}} environments through artificial selection in Europe and the USA.
Bos taurus cattle mature early, have a short calving interval and fast growth, are milked up to {{c1::305 days}}, and have a high milk yield.
Representative Bos taurus breeds include Holstein Friesian, Jersey, Brown Swiss, Guernsey, Ayrshire, Milking Shorthorn and {{c1::Red Danish}}.

cards.question: How many recognized cattle breeds of Ethiopian origin are there, and how are they usually named?
cards.answer: There are around 27 recognized breeds, usually named after their place of origin (for example Horro, Fogera, Arsi, Barca, Sheko and Boran).

cards.question: Where is the Fogera breed found?
cards.answer: In the north-western part of Ethiopia around Fogera, Gondar.

cards.question: What is the milk yield and butterfat content of Fogera cattle?
cards.answer: About 915 litres of milk per lactation, with a butterfat content of 5.8%.

cards.question: Where did the Barca (Begait) breed originate, and where is it abundant?
cards.answer: It originated in the western part of Eritrea but is abundant in Tigray and Gonder.

cards.question: What is the milk yield of Barca cattle under extensive management, and how does intensive management affect it?
cards.answer: About 682 litres per lactation under extensive management; milk production is enhanced when managed intensively.

cards.question: Where are Arsi-Bale cattle predominantly found, and what is their coat colour?
cards.answer: In the highlands of the central region of Arsi and Bale; their coat colour is variable.

cards.question: What milk yield and butterfat percentage do selected Arsi cows produce?
cards.answer: Up to 516 litres per lactation, with milk containing 5.4 to 5.8% butterfat.

cards.question: Where did Horro cattle originate, and what is their dominant coat colour?
cards.answer: In western Ethiopia around Horro Guduru, Wollega; the dominant colour is brown, sometimes slightly lighter on the flanks and between the hind legs.

cards.question: How much milk can selected Horro cows produce per lactation?
cards.answer: Up to 543 litres per lactation.

cards.text: All indigenous Ethiopian cattle are {{c1::multi-purpose}} (milk, meat and draft), and there is {{c2::no specialized local cattle breed considered as dairy type}}.
The common coat color of Fogera cattle is {{c1::white with black spots or patches}}.
Fogera cattle are a {{c1::small sized}} breed producing about 915 litres of milk per lactation.
The coat colour of Barca cattle is variable, but two colours ({{c1::pied}}) including black are common.
Barca cattle are considered to be a {{c1::good milk cattle}} breed.
Arsi-Bale cattle have a {{c1::small body size}} and a compact body conformation.
Selected Arsi cows produce up to {{c1::516 litres}} per lactation, with high butterfat (5.4 to 5.8%).
Horro cattle are {{c1::medium sized}} animals mainly raised for meat and draft use.
Horro cattle originated around {{c1::Horro Guduru, Wollega}} in western Ethiopia.

cards.question: Name the major world dairy breeds and state where they originated.
cards.answer: Holstein-Friesian, Ayrshire, Brown Swiss, Guernsey and Jersey; all originated in Europe and are outstanding milk producers.

cards.question: Where did the Holstein Friesian originate, and what colour patterns does it have?
cards.answer: It originated in the Netherlands and has a Black and White or Red and White colour pattern.

cards.question: How much milk can Holstein Friesian cows produce per lactation?
cards.answer: More than 6600 litres of milk per lactation.

cards.question: Where did the Jersey breed originate, and what is its size and coat colour?
cards.answer: It originated on the Island of Jersey in the United Kingdom; it is small-sized with a light gray to dark fawn coat.

cards.question: What are the average butterfat and protein percentages of Jersey milk?
cards.answer: Butterfat averages 5% and protein 3.8%; Jersey milk is the richest among the major dairy breeds.

cards.question: Why is Jersey especially suitable in harsh Ethiopian environments?
cards.answer: It is the most heat-tolerant of the exotic breeds and is a good pasture animal in harsh environments.

cards.text: The most popular exotic cattle breeds in Ethiopia are {{c1::Holstein Friesian}} and {{c2::Jersey}}.
Holstein Friesians are {{c1::large, angular}} animals that require more feed than other dairy breeds.
Holstein Friesian milk is low in butterfat (average {{c1::3.6%}}) and protein (average {{c2::3.2%}}).
Jersey cattle are well known for their {{c1::well-shaped udders}}, stronger udder attachments and ease of calving.
Jersey cattle require {{c1::less feed}} than Holstein Friesians and are good foragers.
Friesian {{c1::teat size}} is often preferred by farmers for both hand and machine milking.

cards.question: What should a farmer consider about climatic conditions when choosing a dairy breed?
cards.answer: Choose hardy breeds tolerant of tropical conditions and popular in the community, which indicates suitability to ambient temperature, poor-quality feeds and the local parasite and disease situation.

cards.question: How does the production objective (market) influence breed choice?
cards.answer: Get information on the dairy product with a good local market: fresh milk or butter/cheese.

cards.question: How does the feeding system influence the choice of dairy breed?
cards.answer: Growing forage and grazing systems call for breeds with high grazing ability; cut-and-carry systems suit breeds with less grazing ability.

cards.question: How much difference in age of maturity exists among major dairy breeds?
cards.answer: There is at least a four to five month difference in age of maturity among the major dairy breeds.

cards.question: When do large-sized dairy breeds come to production, and how do local breeds mature?
cards.answer: Large-sized breeds do not come to production until 28 to 30 months, and local breeds are generally slow to reach maturity.

cards.question: How important should price be when choosing a breed, and why may local cattle be cheaper?
cards.answer: Price should be the last consideration within reasonable limits; locally grown cattle of equal quality are cheaper because of considerably lower transportation and incidental costs.

cards.question: Which physical characteristics indicate the productive potential of a dairy animal?
cards.answer: General appearance, dairy character, body capacity and mammary system, judged by close inspection of conformation.

cards.question: Describe the desirable body appearance of a high-yielding dairy cow.
cards.answer: A wedge-shaped body (front portion less deep than the rear), bright eyes and a lean neck.

cards.question: Why are performance records more reliable than visual appraisal in selection?
cards.answer: They give measured information on milk yield, composition, feeding efficiency, age at calving and condition at calving rather than appearance alone.

cards.question: What other breeding guide is useful when selecting foundation females?
cards.answer: The breeding ability of the sire or dam of the prospective foundation females.

cards.question: How can a buyer minimize the risk of contagious reproductive diseases when purchasing cattle?
cards.answer: By demanding negative results from high-quality and timely tests.

cards.text: Cross-bred animals with about {{c1::50% exotic inheritance}} are preferable to retain adaptability, heat tolerance and disease resistance of local animals.
If cheese and butter have a good market, select cows producing more cream such as {{c1::Jersey and local breeds}}; for fresh milk, select high yielders such as {{c2::Holstein Friesians}}.
A cut-and-carry feeding system makes a breed with {{c1::less grazing ability}} suitable.
Heifers of small breeds such as Jersey and Guernsey come to production soon after {{c1::24 months}} of age.
A farmer who wants milk production early should choose {{c1::small-sized breeds}} such as Jersey or Guernsey.
Locally grown cattle of equal quality should be cheaper due to lower {{c1::transportation and incidental costs}}.
High-yielding dairy cows are usually not large but have a {{c1::lean, angular form}} and a well-developed mammary system.
The udder of a good dairy cow should be healthy and large enough, with all four quarters well demarcated, well-placed teats, and attachment high to the abdomen to prevent {{c1::teat injury}}.
Performance records provide information on milk yield, milk composition, feeding efficiency, {{c1::age at calving}} and condition at calving.
Important contagious reproductive diseases of breeding cattle are tuberculosis, brucellosis, leptospirosis, vibriosis and mastitis in females and {{c1::trichomoniasis}} in bulls.
Selecting the right kind of {{c1::foundation animals}} is very important when starting a new dairy herd.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 9::9.3 Feeding management of dairy cattle

cards.question: Why is feeding management very important on a dairy farm?
cards.answer: Nutrition maintains health and productivity, and feed alone constitutes 60 to 70% of the cost of producing milk.

cards.question: What does feeding management involve, and what are the two types of feed?
cards.answer: It involves feeding a balanced diet and avoiding overfeeding; feeds are roughage and concentrates.

cards.question: What should concentrates contain, and are they a staple feed?
cards.answer: Concentrates are supplementary feeds, not a staple feed; they should contain high-energy feeds and protein supplements.

cards.question: How can feed costs be reduced for low-producing or late-lactation cows?
cards.answer: By reducing the amount of concentrates given to them.

cards.question: Which nutrients do lactating dairy cows need?
cards.answer: Energy, protein, fiber, vitamins, minerals and water.

cards.question: Why is maximizing dry matter intake important?
cards.answer: It supplies more nutrients to rumen microbes, which in turn provide more nutrients for milk production, milk composition, growth, reproduction and body condition.

cards.question: How much dry matter does a high-producing 450 kg cow producing over 25 L/day need?
cards.answer: More than 4% of body weight, i.e. 450 kg x 4% = 18 kg DM/day.

cards.question: List the indicators of inadequate daily dry matter intake in lactating cows.
cards.answer: Low milk yield and variable composition (mainly milk fat), cows appearing hungry and shouting or waiting for feed, rushing to fresh forage or troughs, eating all allocated feed and low body condition scores.

cards.question: Why must lactating cows receive abundant cool, clean and pure water?
cards.answer: To optimize feed and nutrient use; no animal requires clean drinking water as much as a milk-producing animal does.

cards.question: Which factors change a cow's water requirement?
cards.answer: Stress, weather conditions, heat, cold, disease, productive state, exercise, and the water and salt content of the feed.

cards.question: What are the recommended trough dimensions for dairy cattle water?
cards.answer: A minimum of 10 cm of trough length per cow at a height of 90 cm.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 9::9.3 Feeding management of dairy cattle

cards.text: Feed alone constitutes {{c1::60 to 70%}} of the production cost of milk, making feeding management vital to farm economy.
Roughages available on the farm include grazing, hay, silage and roots; Timothy, Clover and Alfalfa are kinds of {{c1::green fodder}} for dairy cattle.
The first four months of lactation require a higher percentage of {{c1::concentrates}} because production is high during that time.
In general, {{c1::two-third}} of the daily dry matter requirement should be supplied from roughages and the remaining portion from concentrates.
Nutrient requirements of lactating cows are determined for maintenance, milk production, the fat percentage in milk and {{c1::gestation}}.
An efficient milking cow needs a daily dry matter intake of at least {{c1::3% of its body weight}}; a 400 kg cow needs 12 kg DM/day.

Signs of adequate dry matter intake include milk yield and composition on target, lush pasture not fully eaten, feed left in troughs, cows not waiting to be fed and {{c1::body condition scores}} on target.
When dry matter intake is insufficient, cows rush to fresh forage and feed troughs and have low {{c1::body condition scores}}.
To produce one litre of fresh milk, a cow requires {{c1::five litres}} of clean and fresh water.
Water should be placed near feed sources and in {{c1::milking parlor return alleys}}.
Low quality or insufficient water greatly affects {{c1::milk production}}.

cards.question: What is the primary product of dairying, and what nutrients does it contain?
cards.answer: Milk; it contains calcium, iodine, potassium, phosphorous, fats and vitamins B2 and B12.

cards.question: What are the two types of milking systems, and what determines the choice between them?
cards.answer: Hand milking and machine milking; the choice depends on level of operation, economic efficiency and number of cows to be milked.

cards.question: How often can cows be milked, and why must the interval be regular?
cards.answer: Twice or three times a day; the interval must be regular because a sudden change in milking time affects total yield.

cards.question: What is the ideal milking duration for machines and for hand milking?
cards.answer: 5 to 6 minutes for machines and 7 minutes for hand milking.

cards.question: Which cows come third and fourth in the suggested milking order?
cards.answer: Third: cows with a history of mastitis but not showing symptoms; fourth: cows with quarters producing abnormal milk.

cards.question: What is the lactation cycle, and how often do cows usually calve?
cards.answer: The period between one calving and the next; mostly cows calve every twelve months because they must calve to produce milk.

cards.question: How long is a normal lactation, and what is the remaining period called?
cards.answer: Around 10 months (305 days); the remaining two months are the drying off period.

cards.question: Describe the normal shape of the lactation curve.
cards.answer: Milk yield rises during the first months after calving, followed by a long period of continuous decline.

cards.question: What is peak yield, and when is it normally reached?
cards.answer: The point of highest milk production during the entire lactation, normally reached four to ten weeks after calving.

cards.question: Why is the dry period the most important phase, and how long does it normally last?
cards.answer: It prepares the cow for the next calving or lactation and normally lasts 55 to 60 days.

cards.question: What should early-lactation feeding achieve?
cards.answer: Cows should maximize intake, reaching maximum dry matter intake no later than ten weeks after calving and eating at least 4% of their body weight.

cards.text: Milk is important for {{c1::food security}} and influences both income and nutrition.
The place selected for milking cows should be {{c1::calm and quiet}}.
The ideal interval between milkings is {{c1::12 hours}}, and the interval affects both quantity and composition of milk.
In the suggested milking order, the first cows milked are {{c1::first calf heifers free of mastitis}}, followed by older cows free of mastitis.
Newly introduced animals should be milked {{c1::separately}} until their status is determined.
The lactation cycle is split into four phases: early lactation, mid lactation, late lactation and the {{c1::dry period}}.
{{c1::Colostrum}} is the first milk produced by a cow after calving.
The shape of the lactation curve differs for each individual and breed, and feeding and management influence its shape and the {{c1::total amount of milk produced}}.
Peak yield is normally reached {{c1::four to ten weeks}} after calving.
Abnormalities during the {{c1::dry period}} negatively affect the cow's health and milk production after calving.
Cows should be fed a ration that maintains {{c1::peak production}} as long as possible.

cards.question: Why does milk spoil easily, and how can its shelf life be extended?
cards.answer: Milk is an excellent medium for microbial growth, causing spoilage and food-borne illness; shelf life can be extended by cooling, fermentation or processing.

cards.question: How is cooling of milk achieved?
cards.answer: By mechanical refrigeration or cooling tanks.

cards.question: Into which high-value products does milk processing convert raw milk?
cards.answer: Pasteurized liquid milk, cream, yoghurt, cheese, butter and ghee.

cards.question: What are the main reasons for processing milk?
cards.answer: To increase shelf life and palatability, reduce bulkiness (access to distant markets), satisfy consumer demands and create employment opportunities.

cards.question: What is pasteurized milk?
cards.answer: Dairy milk heated to a high temperature and cooled by a simple heating process to destroy harmful bacteria and microorganisms, also extending shelf life.

cards.question: What is the simplest equipment for pasteurization, and what shelf life results?
cards.answer: An open boiling pan over a fire; pasteurized milk lasts 2 to 3 days, up to 12 days at 4 °C depending on conditions.

cards.question: What is cream, and what is the milk left after separation called?
cards.answer: Cream is the higher-butterfat top layer that rises when milk stands; the remaining milk is skim milk.

cards.question: What are the fat concentrations of single/light cream and double/heavy cream?
cards.answer: Single or light cream contains 18% milk fat; double or heavy cream normally contains 48% milk fat.

cards.question: How are fermented milk products made and preserved?
cards.answer: Milk ferments with specific bacteria and sometimes yeast; the acidity prevents growth of microorganisms and preserves the milk.

cards.question: Which culture is used for yoghurt, and what does it do?
cards.answer: A mixed 1:1 culture of Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus, converting lactose (milk sugar) to lactic acid.

cards.question: Describe the temperature steps in yoghurt making after heating.
cards.answer: Cool the milk to 30 to 40 °C, add the culture, leave at 32 to 47 °C for approximately five hours to ferment, then immediately cool to 4 °C.

cards.question: From which kinds of milk can cheese be made, and which is cheapest?
cards.answer: From whole milk, sour milk, skim milk and buttermilk; the cheapest way is from buttermilk or skim milk.

cards.question: What are the objectives of cheese production, and what is its composition?
cards.answer: To prolong shelf life, reduce spoilage and load, and increase palatability; it is composed of concentrated milk fat, casein, salts, lactose and some albumin.

cards.question: What happens after coagulation in cheese making, and what are the solid and fluid parts called?
cards.answer: The coagulant is heated at about 50 °C for at least 20 minutes; the solid left is cheese and the fluid left over is whey.

cards.question: At what temperature can cheese be stored for a long time?
cards.answer: At 5 to 10 °C.

cards.question: When rennet or starter culture is absent, which reagents can be used for cottage cheese?
cards.answer: Lemon juice or lactic acid, acetic acid, or acid whey.

cards.question: Describe the remaining cottage cheese procedure after adding lemon juice.
cards.answer: Stop heat treatment and let the curd settle for 15 minutes; scoop out the curd and filter through a sieve; add 40 g salt per kg of cheese if necessary; fill molds, press overnight, remove and store; then clean and store all equipment.

cards.question: What is butter, and what is its approximate composition?
cards.answer: A semi-solid product made by churning fresh or fermented cream; approximately 80 to 85% milk fat, 15 to 16% water and 2% solid-non-fat (SNF).

cards.question: Which samples and equipment are used in butter making?
cards.answer: Sour whole milk and sweet cream; pH meter, thermometer, electrical churner, weighing balance, salt and plastic pails.

cards.question: What churning temperature is used in butter making, and how is the churn operated?
cards.answer: The temperature is adjusted to 14 to 17 °C; the outlet must be tightly closed and the churn switched on for agitation.

cards.question: How is the butter finished after churning?
cards.answer: Drain the buttermilk through the outlet, wash the butter with cold water 2 to 3 °C below the butter temperature, drain, soak or knead in cold water, add 16 g salt per kg of butter if needed, and determine buttermilk volume/fat and butter moisture.

cards.question: What is ghee and how is it prepared?
cards.answer: Ghee, also called clarified butter oil, is prepared from butter by direct heating to 110 to 120 °C after churning milk or cream and evaporating water.

cards.question: List the first four steps of the industrial method of milk processing.
cards.answer: Put on personal protective equipment and clothing; assemble and clean all necessary materials; prepare whole milk; separate whole milk into cream and skim milk with a cream separator (centrifugal/gravitational).

cards.question: What are the last steps of the industrial method after making ghee?
cards.answer: Heat skim milk at 50 °C for 20 minutes to obtain whey and cottage cheese, then clean all materials after processing.

cards.text: Milk should be cooled immediately after milking and kept at {{c1::4 °C or below}}, the best temperature for keeping it.
Cooling is the {{c1::most common}} choice for maintaining the original quality of milk for consumption and processing.
Hygiene at all stages of milk collection and processing is very important; milk can be transported in {{c1::milk cans or bulk tankers}} to a processing center.
Processing reduces {{c1::bulkiness}}, allowing producers to access distant markets.
Pasteurization heats milk to {{c1::63–65°C for 20–30 minutes}} or to {{c2::72–75°C for 15–30 seconds}}.
Supermarket milk is always {{c1::pasteurized}}.
Whole fresh milk can be separated into cream and skim milk using a {{c1::manual or powered centrifuge separator}}.
Cream is used in coffee, as a cake filling or in ice cream; fermented cream can be processed into {{c1::butter and buttermilk}}.
The best-known fermented dairy product is {{c1::yoghurt}}.
For yoghurt, milk is normally heated at {{c1::70 °C for 15–20 minutes}} using an open boiling pan or steam jacketed pan.
After fermentation, yoghurt is immediately cooled to {{c1::4 °C}}.
Cheese is a concentrated form of milk-fat and milk-protein, composed of concentrated milk fat, {{c1::casein}}, salts, lactose and some albumin.
Milk is coagulated in cheese making by direct acidification, lactic acid produced by bacteria, added rennet, or a {{c1::combination of acidification and rennet}}.
Hard cheeses have most of the {{c1::whey}} drained out and are pressed, while soft cheeses retain some whey and are not always pressed.
Cottage cheese can be made from {{c1::whole fresh/sour milk and skim milk}} using a pH meter, muslin cloth (cheese sieve), weighing balance, salt, plastic pails, molder with presser and scooper.
In cottage cheese making, milk is boiled at {{c1::83–85 °C for 20 minutes}}, then 30 ml of lemon juice diluted with an equal amount of pure water is added and stirred gently for three minutes.
In cottage cheese making, {{c1::40 g of salt per kg of cheese}} is added and the cheese is pressed overnight.
Butter may be yellow or white, has a bland flavour and slightly salty taste, and is a valuable high-demand {{c1::food ingredient}}.
The inside of the churner is cleaned with {{c1::iodized water or salted water}} before butter making.
During churning, the churn is opened at {{c1::30-second intervals for 10 minutes}} to remove gas, and agitation continues until butter grains form.
Butter is washed with cold water {{c1::2–3 °C below}} the butter temperature.
Ghee is almost entirely {{c1::butterfat}} with no or low moisture and SNF, which inhibits bacterial growth and makes storage easier without refrigeration.
In the industrial method, cream is churned into buttermilk and butter ({{c1::85% fat}}), and butter is heated to ghee (melted butter, {{c2::89% fat}}).
In the industrial method, skim milk is heated at {{c1::50 °C for 20 minutes}} to get whey and cottage cheese.

cards.question: Which two types of dairy houses are commonly used, and what determines the type?
cards.answer: Loose housing and the conventional barn; the choice depends on climate, local tradition and availability of building supplies.

cards.question: Why must housing be of appropriate size and well planned?
cards.answer: Cows must be able to stand or lie down easily; adequate housing and careful layout reduce respiratory infections and injuries and support efficient quality milk production.

cards.question: What floor and drainage specifications are recommended for dairy housing?
cards.answer: Good drainage is essential; the floor should have a rough concrete finish with a 1.5% slope towards the drain and should not be slippery.

cards.question: What floor area and trough length are recommended for non-pregnant cows?
cards.answer: 6 to 9 m² covered area, 24 to 30 m² open area, and 51 to 61 cm trough length per animal.

cards.question: What floor space and trough length are recommended for pregnant cows?
cards.answer: 30 to 36.5 m² covered area, 55 to 61 m² open area and 61 to 76 cm trough length per animal.

cards.question: Why is sanitation a key element in dairy farming?
cards.answer: It maximizes the quantity and quality of milk by minimizing contamination from unhygienic milking, equipment, milk contact surfaces, handlers, storage and packaging.

cards.question: Which routine cleaning tasks are part of dairy farm sanitation?
cards.answer: Regular cleaning of floors, bedding, walls and feeding surfaces.

cards.question: How do flies and other insects harm dairy cattle?
cards.answer: They disturb the animals and spread deadly diseases such as bovine Babesiosis and Theileriosis.

cards.question: Why is manure both valuable and potentially problematic?
cards.answer: It is a source of nutrients for crops and improves soil health, but if poorly managed it causes smell and contaminates groundwater and water courses because it contains nitrogen, phosphorous and carbon.

cards.question: How should a manure pit and channels be designed?
cards.answer: The pit should be large enough to hold the shed's manure produced over two or three days, and a concrete-lined channel should lead from the house floor to the pit.

cards.text: Loose housing with a {{c1::milking parlor}} is ideal for tropical regions like Ethiopia.
Buildings must provide proper {{c1::ventilation}} so barn air is fresh, pure and free of dust and dirt.
Floor slope should be {{c1::1.5%}} towards the drain, with a rough concrete, non-slippery finish.
Young stock require {{c1::4.5–6 m²}} covered area, 15 to 18 m² open area and 38 to 51 cm trough length per animal.
Bulls require {{c1::36.5–42.5 m²}} covered area, 61 to 76 m² open area and 61 to 76 cm trough length.
Ongoing {{c1::pen sanitation}} is an absolute necessity in preventing infections that debilitate dairy calves and cows.
Modern sanitation equipment with properly diluted chemicals helps prevent mastitis, ringworm, mange, foot rot and enteric diseases such as {{c1::E. coli and Salmonella}}.
Each large-breed dairy cow produces {{c1::20 to 30 kg faeces}} and {{c2::10 to 14 kg urine}} per day, plus shed effluent from washing floors.
The most common method of manure management is storage in a {{c1::pit}} and spreading.
Manure can be spread on forage fields before planting, composted, sold to local nurseries, or used for {{c1::biogas production}}.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 9::9.6 Major diseases of dairy cattle and their control methods

cards.question: Why is keeping dairy cows healthy economically important?
cards.answer: Good feeding and breeding will not give maximum production if cows are unhealthy, and the best economic returns occur when disease problems are minimized.

cards.question: Name the major internal and external parasites of dairy cattle.
cards.answer: Internal: liver fluke and schistosomiasis; external: ticks, fleas and tsetse flies.

cards.question: How can many dairy cattle diseases be prevented?
cards.answer: Through good herd management, proper nutrition, housing and vaccinations.

cards.question: What are the signs of Chronic Respiratory Disease, and how is it controlled?
cards.answer: Swollen face, nasal discharge and difficulty breathing; controlled by vaccination, good sanitation and good ventilation.

cards.question: How is bovine tuberculosis transmitted and controlled?
cards.answer: By inhaling droplets (aerosol) containing the bacteria or orally through contaminated feed; controlled by vaccination.

cards.question: How is blackleg transmitted and controlled?
cards.answer: By ingestion of bacterial spores while grazing; controlled by vaccination.

cards.question: How is mastitis transmitted, and what control measures are recommended?
cards.answer: Through contaminated feed and water, injury to udder and teat, and a dirty environment; control by disinfecting hands before milking, good sanitation, avoiding overcrowding and using antibiotics.

cards.question: How is trypanosomiasis transmitted and controlled?
cards.answer: Through the tsetse fly (Glossina species); controlled by insecticides and good sanitation measures.

cards.question: Which important dairy cattle diseases are covered in detail in Unit 8?
cards.answer: Foot and mouth disease (FMD), contagious bovine pleuropneumonia (CBPP), brucellosis, anthrax and taeniasis.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 9::9.6 Major diseases of dairy cattle and their control methods

cards.text: Major diseases that heavily affect dairy cattle include foot and mouth disease (FMD), blackleg, anthrax, brucellosis, chronic respiratory disease (CRD) and {{c1::contagious bovine pleuropneumonia (CBPP)}}.
Nutritional disorders of dairy cattle include bloat, diarrhea, acidosis, ketosis and {{c1::milk fever}}; reproductive diseases include dystocia, retention of placenta and vaginal prolapse.
Chronic Respiratory Disease is a {{c1::viral}} disease with swollen face, nasal discharge and difficulty in breathing, spread through contaminated feeds, water and bedding.
Bovine tuberculosis is a bacterial disease causing dry coughs with {{c1::blood-stained sputum}}, emaciation and death; it is spread by inhaling aerosol droplets or orally via contaminated feed.
Blackleg causes lameness, depression, loss of appetite and a hot painful limb swelling that {{c1::crackles}} when pressed.

Mastitis is a bacterial disease causing uneasiness during milking, traces of blood in milk, a swollen udder and pain around the udder; control includes disinfection of hands before milking, good sanitation, avoiding overcrowding and {{c1::antibiotics}}.
Trypanosomiasis is a protozoan disease causing drowsiness, severe {{c1::anaemia}}, loss of weight and death.
Reproductive disorders of dairy cattle include dystocia, retention of {{c1::placenta}} and vaginal prolapse.

cards.question: Why is dairy production an attractive business in Ethiopia?
cards.answer: Milk production, processing and marketing have profitable margins; demand rises with a growing economy and more urban middle-class consumers, attracting investors and creating employment, especially for the young.

cards.question: In the textbook example, calculate daily and monthly milk production for 10 cross-bred cows yielding 12 litres per day.
cards.answer: 10 x 12 = 120 litres per day, approximately 3600 litres per month.

cards.question: What monthly farm expenses are given in the profit example, and what do they include?
cards.answer: 125,250 birr, covering feeds, supplements, medications, labor and other expenses.

cards.question: Which management practices maximize profit margins on a dairy farm?
cards.answer: Farm forage production management, feed and nutrition management, fertility management, hygienic milk production and marketing.

cards.question: Why does green forage improve profitability?
cards.answer: It ensures year-round forage supply, produces more milk and saves feeding costs, contributing to better profitability.

cards.question: Summarize the unit's conclusions about dairy cow type and selection.
cards.answer: Dairy cattle are triangular in characteristics with a well-developed mammary system; high-yielding, resistant breeds that fit the environment are recommended, with disease resistance, adaptability and ability to feed on poor-quality feeds.

cards.text: The main purpose of a dairy farm is to earn income from {{c1::milk sales}}, and profit is calculated as income minus expenses.
At 50 birr per litre, 120 litres per day brings {{c1::6000 birr per day}} or about 180,000 birr per month.
Net profit in the example is 180,000 minus 125,250 birr, giving {{c1::54,750 birr per month}}.
Major dairy farm expenditure is feed (nearly {{c1::60 to 70%}}), so year-round forage and good grasses and legumes reduce costs.

Proper dairy cattle housing provides a {{c1::comfortable, well-drained and dry lying area}}; sanitation and manure management are essential, and the best economic returns come when health problems are minimized through improved management.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 10::10.1 Definition and Importance of Natural Resources

cards.question: Define natural resources.
cards.answer: Natural resources are objects or materials, creatures or energy found in nature which can be used by humans.

cards.question: Can humans produce natural resources?
cards.answer: No. Natural resources cannot be produced by humans, but they are used by humans.

cards.question: What are renewable resources? Give examples.
cards.answer: Renewable resources are capable of regenerating themselves after use. Examples include forests, soils, water, biodiversity and atmospheric air.

cards.question: What are non-renewable resources? Give examples.
cards.answer: Non-renewable resources cannot regenerate themselves after being used once. Examples include oil, coal and minerals that occur in the natural environment.

cards.question: How do natural resources benefit humans?
cards.answer: They provide both direct and indirect benefits; some benefits are current while others are only visible in the future. Most of our food and drink, clothes and shelters come from natural resources.

cards.question: Why is human survival dependent on natural resources?
cards.answer: Our survival, as a species, is dependent on the availability of natural resources.

cards.question: What is carrying capacity?
cards.answer: Carrying capacity is the maximum population level for which a given resource can satisfy the food and shelter requirement.

cards.question: Why must natural resources, especially non-renewable ones, be used wisely?
cards.answer: Their supply is fixed by nature; unless we use them wisely, our survival and the survival of coming generations will be questionable.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 10::10.1 Definition and Importance of Natural Resources

cards.text: Natural resources are {{c1::objects or materials, creatures or energy}} found in nature which can be used by humans.
Natural resources cannot be {{c1::produced by humans}}, but they are used by humans.
{{c1::Renewable resources}} are capable of regenerating themselves after use; examples include forests, soils, water, biodiversity and {{c2::atmospheric air}}.
Oil, coal and minerals are examples of {{c1::non-renewable resources}}, which cannot regenerate themselves after being used once.
Most of our food and drink are {{c1::directly or indirectly derived from natural resources}}, which are also the sources of our clothes and shelters.
Economic growth and development of a nation is highly determined by the magnitude and {{c1::quality of the management}} of natural resources available in the country.
{{c1::Sustainable use}} means using natural resources in a way that enables us to have and continue to have the resources for our current needs as well as the needs of future generations.
The supply of natural resources and the services we get from them is {{c1::fixed by nature}}.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 10::10.2 Major Types of Natural Resources

cards.question: Why are natural resources classified into categories?
cards.answer: Classification helps to identify and effectively execute sustainable management of the resources in order to improve the quality of life for both current and future generations.

cards.question: Which natural resources closely associated with agriculture are the focus of this unit?
cards.answer: Forests, soils and water are the natural resources closely associated with agriculture and the focus of this unit.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 10::10.2 Major Types of Natural Resources

cards.text: Classification of natural resources helps to identify and effectively execute {{c1::sustainable managements}} of the resources to improve the quality of life for both current and future generations.
{{c1::Forests, soils, and water}} are natural resources closely associated with agriculture and will be the focus of this unit.

cards.question: Describe the structure of a forest and its effect on the forest ecosystem.
cards.answer: Forests contain various plants or trees standing very close to each other. The leaves of tall trees form a continuous canopy that greatly reduces the amount and quality of light reaching the ground and influences other climatic variables, determining the number and types of plants, animals and microorganisms that live in the forest.

cards.question: List products humans obtain from trees.
cards.answer: Firewood, fruits, medicines, timber, food and construction materials.

cards.question: What habitats and non-timber products do trees provide?
cards.answer: Trees are important habitats for various wild animals and sources of various non-timber products, including honey.

cards.question: How do trees improve soil fertility and prevent flooding?
cards.answer: Trees improve soil fertility through their roots, add organic matter to the soil through falling leaves, protect the soil from erosion and prevent flooding.

cards.question: How do trees help regulate carbon and oxygen in the atmosphere?
cards.answer: Trees absorb carbon dioxide and water and produce oxygen through photosynthesis, keeping more carbon in their biomass and reducing its release to the atmosphere.

cards.text: In a forest, the leaves of tall trees form a continuous {{c1::canopy}}, which significantly reduces the amount and quality of light that reaches the ground level.
Trees provide us with {{c1::shade}} and protect us from a {{c2::strong wind}}; they also have aesthetic and spiritual value.
Trees are important habitats for various wild animals and sources of non-timber products including {{c1::honey}}.
Trees add organic matter to the soil through {{c1::leaves falling on the soil}} and protect the soil from {{c2::erosion}} and prevent flooding.
Through {{c1::photosynthesis}}, trees absorb carbon dioxide and water and produce oxygen, keeping more carbon in their {{c2::biomass}}.

cards.question: Define soil.
cards.answer: Soil is a mixture of mineral and organic particles of varying sizes.

cards.question: Describe how soils form.
cards.answer: Weathering processes on rock surfaces break rocks into smaller particles called soil parent materials. Air and water enter rock cracks and form chemical substances; bacteria and plants colonize the fragments, and decay of dead plants improves fertility, gradually forming soil.

cards.question: What is the composition of a typical mineral soil?
cards.answer: About 5% organic material, 45% minerals, 25% water and 25% air.

cards.question: What are pore spaces and why are they important?
cards.answer: Pore spaces are the spaces between soil particles that hold water and air; through them soils supply the water, oxygen and different nutrients required for plant growth.

cards.question: Which soil organisms live in soil, and how does soil help mitigate climate change?
cards.answer: Soils are a habitat for millions of organisms including earthworms, bacteria, fungi and other microscopic organisms. Soils are a major storehouse of carbon; storing carbon reduces the release of carbon dioxide, whose concentration in air causes climate change.

cards.question: Which soil properties affect crop yields?
cards.answer: Nutrient content, organic matter content, soil reaction (acidity and alkalinity), depth of top soil, soluble salt accumulation (salinity) and diversity of soil organisms.

cards.text: Soil is a mixture of {{c1::mineral and organic particles}} of varying sizes.
Soils are formed by {{c1::weathering processes}} that take place on the surface of rocks.
Typical mineral soils contain about {{c1::5%}} organic material, {{c2::45%}} minerals, {{c3::25%}} water and {{c4::25%}} air.
Soils contain water and air in the spaces between particles known as {{c1::pore spaces}}.
Soils serve as a habitat for millions of soil organisms including {{c1::earthworms, bacteria, fungi}} and other microscopic organisms, and are a major storehouse of {{c2::carbon}}.
Soil properties that affect crop yields include nutrient content, organic matter content, {{c1::soil reaction (acidity, alkalinity)}}, depth of top soil, salinity and diversity of soil organisms.

cards.question: How much of the earth's crust is covered by water and how is global water distributed?
cards.answer: Water covers 70% of the earth's crust. Approximately 97% of total global water is in oceans and seas, 2% is fresh water and 1% is frozen in ice caps and glaciers.

cards.question: Define surface water and give examples.
cards.answer: Any body of water aboveground, including lakes, rivers, streams and ponds, is called surface water.

cards.question: What are the uses of surface water?
cards.answer: Surface water is used in agriculture and industry; fish and wildlife need it to survive; it is used for electricity generation and for recreational and domestic purposes.

cards.question: Define ice caps and glaciers.
cards.answer: Ice caps are a mass of ice that covers a large area; glaciers are a huge mass of ice that slowly moves over land.

cards.question: Why is Ethiopia called the water tower of Africa, and how many basins does it have?
cards.answer: Ethiopia is endowed with a substantial amount of water resources and is often referred to as 'the water tower of Africa'. The country has eight river basins and one lake basin.

cards.question: Define a river basin.
cards.answer: A river basin is the portion of land drained by a river and its tributaries.

cards.question: What development potential do Ethiopia's water resources offer?
cards.answer: The country has a huge potential to expand small, medium and large scale irrigation, which can greatly improve agricultural productivity and food security, and an encouraging potential for hydropower to meet growing energy demand.

cards.question: For the Abbay, Baro-Akobo and Tekeze basins, give the sources and flow directions or terminals.
cards.answer: Abbay River: source Sekela, west Gojam; flows west to Sudan border. Baro-Akobo River: source Illubabor; flows west to Sudan border. Tekeze River: source Lasta/Gidan; flows west to 'Chew bahir'.

cards.question: For the Genale-Dawa and Wabishebele basins, give the sources and flow directions.
cards.answer: Genale-Dawa River: source Bale; flows east to Somali border. Wabishebele River: source Bale mountains; flows east to Somali border.

cards.question: Give the source and flow direction of the Rift valley Lakes basin.
cards.answer: Source: Lake Arsi mountain; flows south to the Sudan border.

cards.text: Water covers {{c1::70%}} of the earth's crust, and approximately {{c2::97%}} of total global water is found in oceans and seas.
Of the remaining global water, approximately {{c1::2%}} is fresh water and {{c2::1%}} is found as frozen in ice caps and glaciers.
Any body of water aboveground, including lakes, rivers, streams and ponds, is called {{c1::surface water}}.
Surface water is used in agriculture and industry, for electricity generation and for {{c1::recreational and domestic purposes}}.
An {{c1::ice cap}} is a mass of ice that covers a large area, while a {{c2::glacier}} is a huge mass of ice that slowly moves over land.
Ethiopia is often referred to as '{{c1::the water tower of Africa}}' and has {{c2::eight river basins}} and {{c3::one lake basin}}.
A {{c1::river basin}} is the portion of land drained by a river and its tributaries.
Ethiopia has substantial groundwater resources and huge potential for expansion of small, medium and large scale {{c1::irrigation}} and for developing {{c2::hydropower}}.
The Awash River originates at {{c1::Ginchi}} and flows {{c2::north-east}} to {{c3::border lakes}}.
The Omo-Gibe River originates at {{c1::Ambo}} and flows {{c2::south}} to {{c3::Rudolph lake}}, while the Mereb River originates at {{c4::Zalanbessa}} and flows west to the Eritrean border.

cards.question: Define natural resource degradation.
cards.answer: Natural resource degradation is any change or disturbance of the environment that causes deterioration, destruction or depletion of resources such as soil, trees, water or air.

cards.question: What severe outcomes can natural resource degradation cause?
cards.answer: It can result in the destruction of ecosystems and extinction of wildlife.

cards.text: Natural resource degradation is any change or disturbance of the environment that causes {{c1::deterioration, destruction or depletion}} of resources such as soil, trees, water or air.
Natural resource degradation can result in the destruction of {{c1::ecosystems}} and extinction of {{c2::wildlife}}.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 10::10.3.1 Soil Degradation: Causes and Consequences

cards.question: Define soil degradation.
cards.answer: Soil degradation is a long term decrease in the productivity of soils. It reduces their capacity to support healthy crop growth.

cards.question: What are the three major forms of soil degradation?
cards.answer: Water and wind erosion; chemical degradation including acidification, salinization and pollution by toxic chemicals; and physical degradation including soil compaction.

cards.question: Define soil erosion and explain where water versus wind erosion mainly occurs.
cards.answer: Soil erosion is the washing away of surface or top soil by the natural physical forces of water and wind. Water erosion dominates in the highlands where average annual rainfall is high, and wind erosion in the lowlands where vegetation cover is low. Erosion is a natural process but human activities accelerate it.

cards.question: Which human activities accelerate soil erosion?
cards.answer: Removal of vegetation, high intensity of tillage, overgrazing, mining and construction activities.

cards.question: What are the consequences of soil erosion?
cards.answer: It removes valuable top soil, the most productive part for agriculture, washing away essential nutrients and causing lower yields and increased production costs. Eroded soil can pollute lakes, rivers and streams, and sediment accumulation in dams reduces power generation from hydro dams.

cards.question: What does soil chemical degradation include and what are its major causes?
cards.answer: It includes loss of essential plant nutrients, soil acidification, soil salinization and soil fertility decline. Major causes are human activities such as deforestation, agricultural mismanagement and industrial pollution.

cards.question: What is soil acidification and what causes it?
cards.answer: Acidification is a common chemical degradation form in Ethiopian highlands with high rainfall. It is caused by removal of basic nutrient ions such as potassium, calcium, magnesium and sodium from top soils by water (leaching) or in crop harvest, and by improper use of acid forming mineral fertilizers, which gradually lower soil pH below 7.

cards.question: Why are acid soils a problem, what is the suitable pH for most crops, and how widespread is acidity in Ethiopia?
cards.answer: Acid soils are not suitable for plant growth or for the activities of numerous soil organisms. Most crops grow best at soil pH between 6.5 and 7.2; below this range agricultural productivity declines. Approximately 40% of Ethiopian soils are affected by different levels of soil acidity.

cards.question: What is soil salinization and how does it develop?
cards.answer: Soil salinization is excessive accumulation of soluble salts in surface soils. It results from salt-rich irrigation and insufficient drainage; in warm lowlands with low rainfall high evapotranspiration leaves dissolved salts behind, visible as a white thin layer on the soil surface.

cards.question: What are the impacts of salinization and where is it particularly common in Ethiopia?
cards.answer: With high salt accumulation water may move from plant roots back to the soil, causing dehydration, yield decline or plant death. It restricts cropping options because few crop species grow well in saline soils. Salinization is particularly common in the Ethiopian rift valley region.

cards.question: What is soil physical degradation and what causes it?
cards.answer: It is the deterioration of the natural composition and structure of the soil, often producing compacted soils with poor structure. Causes include erosion by water and wind, intensive (repeated) tillage with oxen or heavy agricultural machinery, overgrazing and loss of cultivated land due to urban expansion.

cards.question: What are the consequences of physical soil degradation?
cards.answer: Reduced root growth, reduced water and air movement in soils, reduced uptake of nutrients by plants, reduced microbial activities, reduced water storage capacity, increased flooding and hence reduced plant growth and yields.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 10::10.3.1 Soil Degradation: Causes and Consequences

cards.text: Soil degradation is a {{c1::long term decrease in the productivity of soils}}, reducing their capacity to support healthy crop growth.
The three major forms of soil degradation are water and wind erosion, {{c1::chemical degradation}} and {{c2::soil physical degradation}}.
Soil erosion is mainly caused by {{c1::water}} in the highlands where rainfall is high, and by {{c2::wind}} in the lowlands where vegetation cover is low.
Human activities that accelerate soil erosion include removal of vegetation, high intensity of tillage, {{c1::overgrazing}}, mining and construction activities.
Erosion removes the most productive {{c1::top soil}}, washes away essential nutrients and increases sediment accumulation in {{c2::dams}}, reducing power generation from hydro dams.
Major causes of soil chemical degradation include deforestation, {{c1::agricultural mismanagement}} and {{c2::industrial pollution}}.

Soil acidification is caused by removal of basic nutrient ions such as {{c1::potassium, calcium, magnesium and sodium}} by {{c2::leaching}} or in crop harvest and by improper use of acid forming mineral fertilizers.
For most crops the most suitable soil pH is between {{c1::6.5 and 7.2}}, and approximately {{c2::40%}} of Ethiopian soils are affected by different levels of acidity.
Soil salinization refers to excessive accumulation of {{c1::soluble salts}} in surface soils, visible as a {{c2::white thin layer}} on the soil surface.
High soluble salt accumulation causes {{c1::dehydration of plants}} and restricts cropping options; salinization is particularly common in the {{c2::Ethiopian rift valley region}}.
Soil physical degradation often results in {{c1::compacted soils with poor structure}}, caused by intensive tillage, overgrazing and loss of cultivated land due to urban expansion.
Physically degraded soils have reduced root growth, reduced water and air movement, reduced nutrient uptake and reduced {{c1::microbial activities}}, leading to reduced plant growth and yields.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 10::10.3.2 Water Pollution: Causes and Consequences

cards.question: Define water pollution.
cards.answer: Water pollution refers to the presence of unacceptable levels of harmful substances or chemicals in water; pollution spoils the quality of water.

cards.question: How can industrial waste water pollute water, and how can its acidity be treated?
cards.answer: Industries use acid and alkaline chemicals in their processes; untreated waste water pollutes the environment. If waste water is acidic, adding a base neutralizes the acid and brings its pH to around 7 before it is discharged.

cards.question: What pH range do most rivers and lakes have, and why does a change matter?
cards.answer: Most rivers and lakes have pH values ranging from 6 to 8. Aquatic organisms have specific pH requirements and may not survive if this natural range changes.

cards.question: Which organic wastes pollute water and what harm do they cause?
cards.answer: Organic wastes generated by living organisms, including wastes from humans, animals, agriculture and food processing. If these reach water bodies they can kill aquatic animals like fish.

cards.question: Which inorganic substances and metals pollute water?
cards.answer: Phosphorus and nitrogen used as fertilizers in crop production are inorganic pollutants. Metals from kitchen tools, paints and fuels can enter water bodies by erosion; above acceptable concentrations the water becomes toxic to aquatic organisms.

cards.question: How do chlorine and toxic organic substances pollute water?
cards.answer: Chlorine is used in producing disinfectants that kill harmful bacteria and viruses but also kill useful organisms like fish. Gasoline, oil, diesel and the pesticide 2-4D are toxic pollutants causing health problems in humans and aquatic organisms.

cards.question: How do solid particles affect water bodies?
cards.answer: Solid particles such as sands, silts, clays and plant fragments reduce visibility and cause problems for fish and other aquatic organisms; settled solids harm bottom-dwelling organisms, and too much solid makes water treatment difficult and expensive.

cards.question: How do bacteria and viruses enter water and what problems do they cause?
cards.answer: They enter water bodies through direct dumping of wastes or flood water from areas with a high concentration of animals. They harm aquatic organisms and, if the polluted water is drunk, cause diseases in humans and livestock.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 10::10.3.2 Water Pollution: Causes and Consequences

cards.text: Water pollution refers to the presence of {{c1::unacceptable levels of harmful substances or chemicals}} in water.
If waste water is acidic, adding a {{c1::base}} will neutralize the acid and bring its pH value to around {{c2::7}} before discharging it to the environment.
Most rivers and lakes have pH values ranging from {{c1::6 to 8}}, and aquatic organisms may not survive if this natural range changes.
Organic wastes from human, animal, agricultural and {{c1::food processing}} sources can kill aquatic animals like fish.
{{c1::Phosphorus and nitrogen}} used as fertilizers are inorganic pollutants, while metals from kitchen tools, paints and fuels can enter water bodies by {{c2::erosion}}.
The pesticide {{c1::2-4D}}, gasoline, oil and diesel are toxic pollutants that can cause health problems in humans as well as in {{c2::aquatic organisms}}.
Too much solid in water reduces {{c1::visibility}}, harms organisms living at the bottom of water bodies and makes treating the water {{c2::difficult and expensive}}.

Bacteria and viruses enter water bodies through direct dumping of wastes or {{c1::flood water}} from areas with high concentrations of animals, and can cause diseases in {{c2::humans as well as in livestock}}.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 10::10.3.3 Forest and Wildlife Degradation: Causes and Consequences

cards.question: What benefits do forests provide?
cards.answer: Forests provide firewood, construction materials, fruits, medicines, timber and food for animals. They store carbon in their biomass, reducing carbon release to the atmosphere, and are habitats for wildlife.

cards.question: What does scientific data say about tropical forest degradation since the 1960s?
cards.answer: Approximately over 50% of the tropical forests have been degraded since the 1960's.

cards.question: What processes are responsible for forest degradation?
cards.answer: Increasing forest fires and diseases, logging, and climate change with high temperature and variable weather conditions.

cards.question: Define logging and explain the role of fire in forest clearing.
cards.answer: Logging is a situation in which forests are cleared for firewood, timber or to obtain additional land for crop cultivation. Fires are often used to clear the forest so the land can be used for agriculture.

cards.question: What are the consequences of losing trees or forests?
cards.answer: The loss of trees or forest contributes to climate change, expansion of desertification and soil erosion. These in turn result in reduced food production both for humans and for livestock.

cards.question: Define desertification and give the rainfall limits for arid and semi-arid areas.
cards.answer: Desertification is a situation in which vegetation in drylands, arid and semi-arid areas such as grasslands or shrub lands decreases and eventually disappears. Arid areas receive less than 25 mm rainfall per year; semi-arid areas less than 50 mm annual rainfall.

cards.question: Define wildlife degradation and distinguish endangered from threatened species.
cards.answer: Wildlife degradation refers to a reduction in population size and types of wildlife species. An endangered species is at risk of extinction or disappearance throughout its range of habitats; a threatened species can become endangered in the near future.

cards.question: List the major causes of wildlife degradation.
cards.answer: Expansion of agriculture, environmental pollution, loss of habitat, loss of mobility and limitation of expansion of vegetation; also introduction of non-native species, international trade in animal fur, bones and horns (ivory), and medicinal plants.

cards.question: What are the consequences of wildlife degradation?
cards.answer: It results in total loss of wildlife resources and reduces their population and diversity, diminishing ecological roles and aesthetic, recreational and scientific values. A healthy forest has diverse tree species, whereas a deforested area has sparse vegetation and low species diversity.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 10::10.3.3 Forest and Wildlife Degradation: Causes and Consequences

cards.text: Forests provide firewood, construction materials, fruits, medicines, timber and food for animals, and reduce the release of carbon to the atmosphere by storing carbon in their {{c1::biomass}}.
Scientific data shows that approximately over {{c1::50%}} of the tropical forests have been degraded since the {{c2::1960's}}.
Forest degradation is caused by increasing forest fires and diseases, {{c1::logging}} and climate change with high temperature and variable weather conditions.
Forests are cleared by {{c1::logging}} for firewood, timber or additional land for crop cultivation, and fires are often used to clear land for {{c2::agriculture}}.
Loss of trees contributes to climate change, expansion of {{c1::desertification}} and soil erosion, resulting in reduced food production for humans and {{c2::livestock}}.
Arid areas receive less than {{c1::25 mm}} rainfall per year, while semi-arid areas receive less than {{c2::50 mm}} annual rainfall.
{{c1::Wildlife degradation}} refers to a reduction in population size and types of wildlife species; {{c2::threatened species}} are those that can become endangered in the near future.
Major causes of wildlife degradation include expansion of agriculture, environmental pollution, loss of habitat, loss of {{c1::mobility}} and limitation of expansion of vegetation.

International trade in animal fur, bones and horns ({{c1::ivory}}) and medicinal plants are important causes of wildlife degradation, whose consequences include loss of ecological roles and {{c2::aesthetic}}, recreational and scientific values.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 10::10.3.4 Causes and Consequences Air Pollution

cards.question: Describe the composition of the atmosphere.
cards.answer: The atmosphere is the thin layer of air surrounding the earth. It is composed of nitrogen gas (78%) and oxygen (21%), while other gases make up only 1% (water vapor in clouds, carbon dioxide and other minor gases); nitrogen and oxygen together make up 99%.

cards.question: When is air considered polluted?
cards.answer: We say the air is polluted when there is an abnormally high concentration of harmful and poisonous substances or chemicals in the atmosphere.

cards.question: Which natural particles reduce the cleanness of air?
cards.answer: When air moves across the earth's surface it picks up dust from the land, pollen and spores from plants and other particles, reducing the cleanness of the air.

cards.question: List the human activities and substances that cause air pollution.
cards.answer: Gases emitted from cars, chemicals from industries, dust from agriculture and construction activities, soot and smoke from biomass burning, pollen and spores suspended in air, and ozone, which can be toxic to plants and animals.

cards.question: What health and environmental problems does air pollution cause?
cards.answer: Breathing polluted air introduces toxic substances that cause respiratory problems, heart diseases and lung cancer, reducing quality of life and life expectancy. Air pollution also harms livestock and plants by reducing their health and productivity.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 10::10.3.4 Causes and Consequences Air Pollution

cards.text: The atmosphere is composed of nitrogen gas ({{c1::78%}}) and oxygen ({{c2::21%}}), with other gases constituting only {{c3::1%}}.
Air is polluted when there is an {{c1::abnormally high concentration of harmful and poisonous substances or chemicals}} in the atmosphere.
Air moving across the earth's surface picks up {{c1::dust}} from the land and pollen and spores from plants, reducing the cleanness of the air.
Air pollution can be caused by high concentrations of {{c1::solid particles (particulate materials)}} and harmful gases, including soot and smoke from {{c2::biomass burning}}.
Air pollution causes {{c1::respiratory problems}}, heart diseases and lung cancer in humans and reduces the health and productivity of {{c2::livestock and plants}}.
Ozone, when present in the atmosphere, can be {{c1::toxic for plants and animals}}.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 10::10.3.5 Environmental Impact of Mineral Exploitation

cards.question: Give examples of mineral resources and explain their economic importance.
cards.answer: Mineral resources such as gold, bronze, iron ore and aluminum contribute to the growth of the national economy. Mining provides raw materials for different industries and is vital for the growth of the industrial sector.

cards.question: How does surface excavation during mining pollute the air?
cards.answer: During the mining process surface excavation is often carried out to expose the mineral material, and dust particles from the excavation process can pollute the air.

cards.question: How do mining wastes pollute soil and water?
cards.answer: After excavation, rocks are crushed to smaller sizes and the minerals are separated. Leftover materials are disposed or dumped as wastes, polluting soils and water in the area.

cards.question: Which chemicals used in mineral separation can pollute water?
cards.answer: The separation processes use water and chemicals, especially heavy metals and naturally occurring radionuclides (radiation emitting elements like uranium), which can pollute water resources.

cards.question: What are the environmental and health consequences of mineral exploitation?
cards.answer: Air pollution from mining can cause serious human and animal health problems. Water and soil pollution from mineral exploitation can harm soil, aquatic organisms and humans when the polluted water is used for domestic uses.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 10::10.3.5 Environmental Impact of Mineral Exploitation

cards.text: Mineral resources like {{c1::gold, bronze, iron ore and aluminum}} contribute to the growth of the national economy.
Dust particles from the {{c1::surface excavation}} process can pollute the air.
After rocks are crushed and minerals separated, leftover materials are disposed or dumped as wastes that pollute {{c1::soils and water}} in the area.
The separation processes use water and chemicals, especially {{c1::heavy metals}} and naturally occurring {{c2::radionuclides}} like uranium, which can pollute water resources.
Water and soil pollution from mineral exploitation can harm soil, {{c1::aquatic organisms}} and humans when the polluted water is used for {{c2::domestic uses}}.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 11::11.1 Concepts of natural resource use

cards.question: What does carrying capacity mean in natural resource management?
cards.answer: Carrying capacity is the maximum population level for which a given resource can satisfy the food and shelter requirement.

cards.question: According to the text, what happens when a population exceeds an ecosystem's carrying capacity?
cards.answer: It is coupled with starvation leading to the emergence of diseases and predators that will eventually reduce the population.

cards.question: Define sustainable use of natural resources.
cards.answer: Sustainable use refers to natural resource use that creates and maintains a condition in which humans use resources to fulfill their social, economic and other requirements.

cards.question: Which finite natural resources are given as examples, and what results from failure to use natural resources wisely?
cards.answer: Coal, natural gas and mineral ores exist in finite amounts; failure to use natural resources wisely results in their depletion in a short time, and lessening the amount available markedly affects the fate of future generations.

cards.question: How can intensive crop and livestock production affect the ability of a resource to be passed to the next generation?
cards.answer: In the process of increasing carrying capacity, the capacity of the resource to pass onto the next generation and provide services to fulfill human needs can be highly damaged.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 11::11.1 Concepts of natural resource use

cards.text: A hectare of grassland that can produce sufficient food for {{c1::100 sheep}} is at its carrying capacity; keeping {{c2::150 or more sheep}} on this grassland is far beyond the carrying capacity of the land.

Farming has increased the carrying capacity of the world by increasing the amount of {{c1::food}} that can be produced on the land, and {{c2::intensive crop and livestock production}} has increased the carrying capacity of the land.
Sustainable use refers to natural resource use that creates and maintains a condition in which humans use resources to fulfill their {{c1::social, economic and other}} requirements.
Sustainability enables us to have and continue to have {{c1::water, soils, forests, minerals}} and other resources to protect human health and the environment without interruption.

Sustainable use is sets of {{c1::processes and techniques}} to handle resources to satisfy the needs and demands of the current generation without affecting the needs and demands of future generations.

cards.question: What is the aim of soil management?
cards.answer: Soil management aims at reducing soil degradation and maintaining or improving the productive capacity of soils; different management practices reduce the effects of soil degradation on crop productivity.

cards.question: How does repeated cultivation lead to soil erosion?
cards.answer: Repeated cultivation presses soil particles together (compaction), so rainwater does not enter the soil; instead runoff is created, which often causes soil erosion.

cards.question: Why does leaving soil bare or removing all plants at harvest degrade the soil?
cards.answer: Bare soils without crops, grasses or other vegetation are easily washed away by rainwater or wind; complete removal of plants during harvest or using fire during land preparation leaves the soil without cover and causes nutrient depletion and a decline in soil fertility.

cards.question: Which agronomic measures are used in annual crop production to protect soils from water or wind erosion?
cards.answer: Mulching, mixed cropping, contour cultivation or strip cropping; crop rotation and increasing organic matter content are also listed as soil management practices. Their objective is to protect the soil by covering it with vegetation or residues.

cards.question: How do plant cover and mulch protect soil from erosion?
cards.answer: The plant cover or mulch absorbs the energy from raindrops and prevents loosening and removal of soil particles by erosion; the cover need not be living plants, since dry crop residues or various forms of mulch also effectively protect soil.

cards.question: Define mulching and state how it reduces erosion.
cards.answer: Mulching is spreading organic materials like crop residues or inorganic materials like plastic on the soil surface. The mulch prevents direct exposure of the soil to raindrops and runoff water and absorbs their energy, reducing their eroding capacity.

cards.question: Why is maize grown mixed with beans in many maize producing areas of Ethiopia?
cards.answer: Crops grown in mixture provide better soil coverage and reduce erosion more than monocropping: the maize canopy protects the soil against raindrops and the beans provide additional canopy coverage.

cards.question: Define contour cropping and contour cultivation and state their purpose.
cards.answer: Contour cropping is planting long lines of plots with different crops along the contour to control soil erosion; contour cultivation is cultivation of the soil opposite the slope direction. Both reduce the speed of runoff water and the transport of soil particles down the slope.

cards.question: Why are crops with different canopy nature used in contour cropping?
cards.answer: Crops with different canopy nature (growth habit) are used; having different plant strips reduces sediments transported down the slope and reduces the speed of runoff water, resulting in reduced soil erosion.

cards.question: How do legumes, manure, compost and inorganic fertilizers affect soil fertility and erosion?
cards.answer: Including legume crops in cereal plantings and applying manure, compost or other organic fertilizers improve soil fertility and reduce nutrient depletion; inorganic fertilizers also increase fertility, while a greater variety of crop types adds more organic matter. Higher organic matter increases resistance to erosion and structural deterioration, improves plant growth and canopy coverage, and thus reduces soil erosion.

cards.question: Define liming and explain how it reduces soil acidity.
cards.answer: Liming is adding calcium and magnesium-rich materials such as limestone to the soil to increase the pH value and reduce soil acidity. The calcium and magnesium replace acidic nutrients from soils and increase pH; when acidity is reduced, plants absorb essential nutrients and crop yield increases depending on crop type.

cards.question: Name four acid-tolerant crops and the traditional material farmers add to acidic soils.
cards.answer: Rice, cowpea, cassava and mango are acid-tolerant crops; traditionally farmers in acidic-soil areas add wood ash, which reduces soil acidity to some extent.

cards.question: How are saline soils managed and which crops are relatively salt-tolerant or sensitive?
cards.answer: Accumulated soluble salts are removed from surface soils by washing (leaching) with good quality water, and organic fertilizers such as compost and animal manure improve the physical properties and productivity of salt-affected soils. Sorghum, barley and wheat are relatively salt-tolerant, while rice is sensitive.

cards.question: Why is increasing soil organic matter important for both fertility and erosion control?
cards.answer: Increased organic matter gives soils better resistance to soil erosion and structural deterioration, increases fertility and improves plant growth; better plant growth gives better canopy coverage for the soil, resulting in reduced soil erosion.

cards.question: Which practice corresponds to conservation tillage in the text, and what is its purpose?
cards.answer: Contour cultivation, cultivation of the soil opposite the slope direction, reduces the speed of runoff water and hence the transport of soil particles down the slope.

cards.text: Soil management aims at reducing {{c1::soil degradation}} and maintaining or improving the {{c2::productive capacity of soils}}.
When soil particles are highly pressed together ({{c1::compaction}}), rainwater does not enter the soil; instead a {{c2::runoff}} which often causes soil erosion is created.

Complete removal of plants during harvest or using {{c1::fire}} during land preparation leaves the soil empty, without any cover, and also causes {{c2::nutrient depletion}} and a decline in soil fertility.
Agronomic measures such as {{c1::mulching}}, {{c2::mixed cropping}} and {{c3::contour cultivation or strip cropping}} are usually soil management practices used in annual crops production.
The plant cover or mulch absorbs the energy from {{c1::raindrops}} and prevents loosening and removal of {{c2::soil particles}} by erosion.

Mulching refers to spreading {{c1::organic materials like crop residues}} or {{c2::inorganic materials like plastic}} on the soil surface to prevent direct exposure of the soil to raindrops and runoff water.
Growing beans mixed with maize protects the soil well because the {{c1::maize canopy}} protects the soil against raindrops and the {{c2::beans}} provide additional canopy coverage.

Contour cropping refers to planting long lines of plots with different crops along the {{c1::contour}} to control soil erosion, while contour cultivation is cultivation of the soil {{c2::opposite the slope direction}}.
Having different plant strips reduces {{c1::sediments transported down the slope}}, and contour cropping reduces the {{c2::speed of runoff water}}, which usually results in reduced soil erosion.
Including {{c1::legume crops}} in cereal crop plantings, applying {{c2::manure, compost or other organic fertilizers}} improve soil fertility and help control soil nutrient depletion.
Liming is the practice of adding {{c1::calcium and magnesium-rich materials}} such as {{c2::limestone}} to the soil in order to increase the {{c3::pH value}} and reduce soil acidity.
Farmers in areas with acidic soil traditionally add {{c1::wood ash}} to the soil, which reduces soil acidity to some extent; acid tolerant crops include {{c2::rice, cowpea, cassava and mango}}.

Management of saline soils includes removal of accumulated soluble salts from surface soils by washing ({{c1::leaching}}) with {{c2::good quality water}}; {{c3::sorghum, barley and wheat}} are relatively salt-tolerant while {{c4::rice}} is sensitive.

When organic matter content of soils is increased, soils have better resistance to {{c1::soil erosion and structural deterioration}}, and better plant growth means better {{c2::canopy coverage}} for the soil, resulting in reduced soil erosion.

In the unit summary, {{c1::crop rotation}} is listed together with mulching, contour cultivation, contour farming, {{c2::mixed cropping}} and increasing the organic matter content of soils as soil management practices.

cards.question: Why is agricultural water management needed, particularly in semi-arid areas?
cards.answer: Agriculture is the major sector using water resources and in developing countries is mainly based on rainfall. In semi-arid areas total rainfall is low and rainfall patterns are unpredictable, so plants often face water shortage during critical growth stages; conserving rainfall reduces water loss and sustains productivity.

cards.question: Name four ways in which water received from rain can be lost.
cards.answer: Evaporation, transpiration, runoff and deep percolation.

cards.question: Define transpiration.
cards.answer: Transpiration occurs when plants absorb liquid water from the soil and release water vapor into the atmosphere through their leaves.

cards.question: Define deep percolation.
cards.answer: Deep percolation is the movement of water downward through the soil below the depth which plant roots cannot reach.

cards.question: How does contour cultivation in sloping areas conserve water for plant growth?
cards.answer: Cultivating the soil opposite the slope slows water running down the slope, raising the likelihood that water enters the soil; the water available in the soil can then be used to grow plants.

cards.question: Describe the water harvesting technique using a soil pit and how the stored water is used.
