cards.answer: In arid and semi-arid areas a soil pit can be prepared with plastic sheets lining to store rainwater on the farm; the stored water can be used when crops face water shortage.

cards.question: How can excess water collected from roof tops be used, and what further benefit does the text mention?
cards.answer: Excess water collected from roof tops of houses can be used for various purposes including irrigation in droughts of short duration; this reduces carbon loss to the atmosphere and improves carbon stock and sequestration.

cards.question: When is evaporative loss of water from soils particularly high and how can it be reduced?
cards.answer: It is particularly high when soils are bare, with no vegetation cover, or when coverage is low; spreading organic materials on the surface (mulching) reduces such losses, and leaving some biomass standing during crop harvest can also reduce soil loss.

cards.question: List the soil conservation practices that also improve water conservation and explain how they work.
cards.answer: Contour farming, contour bunding, bench terrace on steep slopes and storing runoff water. They reduce the speed of runoff water, allow water to enter the soil, reduce water loss and make water available for growing crops.

cards.question: What is the role of the bench terrace in Konso?
cards.answer: The bench terrace in Konso is used to reduce flooding and soil erosion and contributes to soil conservation by slowing runoff and allowing water to enter the soil.

cards.question: Why is selection of appropriate crops important in dry areas?
cards.answer: Crops that tolerate drought give adequate yield with low water requirement and low transpiration, so selecting such crops is an important water management method in dry areas.

cards.question: How should irrigation water use be managed to minimize water losses?
cards.answer: Water losses linked to the efficiency of the irrigation method used should be minimized; the amount of water used, the frequency of use and the irrigation time should be adjusted to properties of the soil, crop types and climatic conditions.

cards.question: What are the major agricultural water management practices listed in the unit summary?
cards.answer: Rain water conservation, reducing evaporative loss of water, and soil conservation practices.

cards.text: In developing countries agriculture is mainly based on water received from {{c1::rainfall}}, and in semi-arid areas total rainfall is low and rainfall patterns are {{c2::unpredictable}}.
Water received from the rain can be lost through {{c1::evaporation}}, {{c2::transpiration}}, {{c3::runoff}} and {{c4::deep percolation}}.
Transpiration occurs when plants absorb {{c1::liquid water}} from the soil and release {{c2::water vapor}} into the atmosphere through their leaves.
Deep percolation is the movement of water {{c1::downward}} through the soil below the depth which {{c2::plant roots cannot reach}}.
When soils in sloping areas are cultivated {{c1::opposite the slope}}, water running down the slope is {{c2::slowed down}}, which raises the likelihood of water entering the soils.
In rain water harvesting, a soil pit can be prepared with {{c1::plastic sheets lining}} to store rainwater on the farm, and the stored water can be used when crops face {{c2::water shortage}}.

Excess water collected from roof tops of houses can be used for various purposes, including {{c1::irrigation in droughts of short duration}}; this reduces carbon loss to the atmosphere and improves {{c2::carbon stock and sequestration}}.

Water loss through evaporation is particularly high when soils are {{c1::bare, with no vegetation cover}} or when the coverage is low; spreading {{c2::organic materials}} on the surface (mulching) can reduce such losses.

Practices that conserve agricultural soils also improve water conservation; these include {{c1::contour farming}}, {{c2::contour bunding}}, {{c3::bench terrace}} on steep slopes and {{c4::storing runoff water}}.

Bench terrace in Konso is used to reduce {{c1::flooding and soil erosion}} and contributes to soil conservation because it reduces the speed of runoff water and allows the water to {{c2::enter the soil}}.

In dry areas, crops that tolerate drought give adequate yield with {{c1::low water requirement}} and {{c2::low transpiration}}, making selection of appropriate crops an important water management method.

If irrigation is used, water losses linked to the {{c1::efficiency of the irrigation method}} used should be minimized, and the amount of water used, {{c2::frequency of use}} and {{c3::irrigation time}} should be adjusted to properties of the soil, crop types and climatic conditions.
Major agricultural water management practices include {{c1::rain water conservation}}, {{c2::reducing evaporative loss of water}} and {{c3::soil conservation practices}}.

cards.question: What are the benefits of maintaining and improving forest cover?
cards.answer: It increases the amount of carbon trees store in aboveground biomass and roots, reduces carbon emission to the atmosphere, protects soils against erosion and provides habitat for wildlife.

cards.question: What forest management interventions are listed in the text?
cards.answer: Planting of trees (afforestation) and replanting of depleted forests, planning carefully ways to harvest and transport timber, increasing forest cover through planting trees in areas where there are no forests, and adapting techniques to prevent wild forest fires.

cards.question: Why are forest management practices needed?
cards.answer: To provide fuel wood to meet demands sustainably, allow more productive use of forest vegetation, create employment and income for rural communities, contribute to biodiversity conservation, reduce deforestation and desert expansion, minimize vulnerability to climate change and reduce carbon emission.

cards.question: What is the principal objective of wildlife management and what usually causes wildlife destruction?
cards.answer: Wildlife destruction usually occurs due to destruction of natural habitats; the principal objective of wildlife management is protection of the habitats of wildlife including grasslands, forests and grazing lands.

cards.question: Give the Ethiopian example of a practice that violates the principal objective of wildlife management.
cards.answer: Humans allow their domestic animals to graze in national parks in Ethiopia, which violates the objective of protecting wildlife habitats including grasslands, forests and grazing lands.

cards.question: Name two endangered endemic wild animals in Ethiopia and the main cause of their endangerment.
cards.answer: Walia Ibex and Ethiopian Wolf are among the most endangered endemic wild animals in Ethiopia, mainly due to habitat destruction.

cards.question: List the integral parts of wildlife management mentioned in the text.
cards.answer: Reducing agricultural encroachment into wildlife habitats, prevention of introduction of invasive plant species, creating a buffer zone between settlements and wildlife habitats, and controlling population growth.

cards.question: How are forest management and wildlife management related?
cards.answer: Forests provide habitat for wildlife, so maintaining forest cover protects soils and wildlife habitat; both contribute to biodiversity conservation and to reducing deforestation and habitat destruction.

cards.text: Maintaining and improving forest cover increases the amount of carbon trees store in their {{c1::aboveground biomass and roots}}, reduces {{c2::carbon emission}} to the atmosphere, protects soils against erosion and provides habitat for wildlife.

Forest management practices include planting of trees ({{c1::afforestation}}) and replanting of {{c2::depleted forests}}, careful planning of timber harvesting and transport, and adapting techniques to prevent {{c3::wild forest fires}}.

Forest management practices are needed to provide {{c1::fuel wood}} sustainably, create {{c2::employment and income}} for rural communities, contribute to {{c3::biodiversity conservation}}, reduce deforestation and desert expansion, minimize vulnerability to climate change and reduce carbon emission.

Wildlife destruction usually occurs due to the destruction of their {{c1::natural habitats}}; protection of wildlife and their habitats is an integral part of management and conservation of wildlife resources.

Humans allow their domestic animals to graze in {{c1::national parks}} in Ethiopia, which violates the principal objective of wildlife management: protection of habitats including {{c2::grasslands, forests and grazing lands}}.
{{c1::Walia Ibex}} and {{c2::Ethiopian Wolf}} are among the most endangered endemic wild animals in Ethiopia mainly due to {{c3::habitat destruction}}.

Integral parts of wildlife management include reducing {{c1::agricultural encroachment}} into wildlife habitats, prevention of introduction of {{c2::invasive plant species}}, creating a {{c3::buffer zone}} between settlements and wildlife habitats and controlling population growth.

Forest management supports wildlife management because forests provide {{c1::habitat for wildlife}}, and both aim to conserve {{c2::biodiversity}} and reduce {{c3::deforestation}} and habitat destruction.

cards.question: Define environment as used in the unit.
cards.answer: Environment refers to the climatic, biological and chemical conditions that may affect the growth and welfare of organisms.

cards.question: What are environmental management practices?
cards.answer: Humans should use environmental resources in ways that do not harm the future use of the resources; practices that support such human interactions with the environment are called environmental management practices.

cards.question: State the main objectives of environmental management.
cards.answer: To ensure the protection of human health and wellbeing, and conservation and preservation of all life forms and their habitats.

cards.question: What is the major goal of environmental management concerning chemicals?
cards.answer: The major goal is to prevent the release of harmful chemicals into the environment.

cards.question: How can air pollution from agriculture be prevented and acceptable air quality achieved?
cards.answer: By improving management of agricultural wastes such as manure.

cards.question: How can water pollution from agricultural areas be minimized?
cards.answer: By reducing erosion from agricultural areas which could pollute water, in order to meet water quality standards.

cards.question: How can health and environmental risks of agricultural pesticides be reduced?
cards.answer: By proper use of the pesticides.

cards.question: What solid waste management practice is introduced and what pollution does it reduce?
cards.answer: A sound solid waste management practice is introduced, reducing pollution from solid wastes such as animal manure.

cards.question: What does the unit say about identifying environmental impacts of agricultural outputs and farmers obligations?
cards.answer: The aims include identifying core processes of major outputs in agriculture and their environmental impacts and ensuring that farmers meet the requirements of the environmental regulations.

cards.question: According to the unit summary, through which pollution types does environmental management protect health and welfare?
cards.answer: Through prevention of air, water and soil pollution and implementation of sound waste management strategies.

cards.text: Environment refers to the {{c1::climatic, biological and chemical}} conditions that may affect the growth and welfare of organisms.

Humans should use environmental resources in ways that do not harm the {{c1::future use}} of the resources; practices that support such interactions are called {{c2::environmental management practices}}.
The main objectives of environmental management are to ensure the protection of {{c1::human health and wellbeing}} and conservation and preservation of all life forms and their {{c2::habitats}}.
The major goal of environmental management is to prevent the release of {{c1::harmful chemicals}} into the environment.
Preventing air pollution and having acceptable air quality can be achieved through improving management of {{c1::agricultural wastes such as manure}}.
Water pollution is minimized to meet {{c1::water quality standards}} by reducing {{c2::erosion}} from agricultural areas which could pollute water.
Health and environmental risks of agricultural pesticides are reduced by their {{c1::proper use}}.
Introducing sound {{c1::solid waste management}} practice reduces pollution from solid wastes such as {{c2::animal manure}}.

The aims of environmental management include identifying core processes of major outputs in agriculture and their {{c1::environmental impacts}} and ensuring that farmers meet the requirements of the {{c2::environmental regulations}}.

Environmental management protects human health and welfare and other organisms through prevention of {{c1::air, water and soil pollution}} and implementation of {{c2::sound waste management strategies}}.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 11::11.6 Indigenous knowledge applicable in natural resources

cards.question: How does indigenous knowledge contribute to natural resource management in Ethiopia?
cards.answer: Ethiopia has diverse altitudes, climates and natural vegetation; indigenous knowledge contributes to forest conservation, north Shewa farmers use indigenous soil and water conservation practices, and the Gumuz have a knowledge system for managing natural resources. Indigenous knowledge plays a vital role in managing soil, water, vegetation and wildlife.

cards.question: Why do farmers in north Shewa apply indigenous soil and water conservation practices?
cards.answer: They apply these practices to respond to land degradation in their area.

cards.question: Describe the wide water way practice of north Shewa, including its exact width and purpose.
cards.answer: A wide water way 40 to 50 cm wide is constructed between adjacent farms to control runoff coming from upper slopes.

cards.question: What is the medium-sized traditional ditch and what does it do?
cards.answer: It is a ditch that dissects the farm and connects two wide water ways; it reduces runoff speed by diverting excess water.

cards.question: Describe the single line of stones practice, including the slope limit and its purposes.
cards.answer: A single line of stones is constructed across the farm on slopes of up to 2%, which reduces runoff speed and retains soils (sediments) from the runoff water.

cards.question: How do tree species on the edge of the farm and local vegetative barriers protect the soil?
cards.answer: Planting some tree species on the edge of the farm protects the soil from erosion, while local vegetative barriers filter out sediments from runoff waters and reduce runoff speed.

cards.question: How can traditional stone bunds be combined with vegetation to control erosion?
cards.answer: Grasses or perennial species can be combined with traditional stone bunds to control soil erosion on steep slopes.

cards.question: Describe the natural resource base and livelihood of the Gumuz community.
cards.answer: The Gumuz community in northwestern Ethiopia has fertile soils, enormous vegetation with diverse plant and animal species, and abundant mineral resources such as gold. Their livelihood is highly based on natural resources and they have a special relationship with their land and environment.

cards.question: How did the Gumuz develop their indigenous knowledge system?
cards.answer: Through observation and experience; their indigenous knowledge about management of natural resources is associated with their traditional belief systems.

cards.question: List the traditional beliefs of the Gumuz about natural resources.
cards.answer: Vital natural resources are sacred; natural resources are an indigenous gift, blessing and creation of Yamba (God); Yamba provided the knowledge of proper use, management and responsibility to pass them to future generations; natural resources are ancestral heritage; ownership is vested upon the whole community so they cannot be privately possessed or controlled by single members.

cards.question: In what form is Gumuz indigenous knowledge institutionalized and who enforces it?
cards.answer: It constitutes mostly norms, values, ethics and taboos institutionalized as customary laws and conventions within the community, and the elders enforce these institutions.

cards.question: Which natural resources do indigenous knowledge practices help manage according to the unit summary?
cards.answer: Soil, water, vegetation and wildlife.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 11::11.6 Indigenous knowledge applicable in natural resources

cards.text: Ethiopia is a land of diverse altitudes and climates covered by various types of natural vegetation, and {{c1::indigenous knowledge}} contributes to forest conservation.
Farmers in {{c1::north Shewa}} apply indigenous soil and water conservation practices to respond to {{c2::land degradation}} in their area.
A wide water way {{c1::40 to 50 cm wide}} is constructed between adjacent farms to control runoff coming from {{c2::upper slopes}}.
A medium-sized traditional ditch dissects the farm and connects {{c1::two wide water ways}}, reducing runoff speed by {{c2::diverting excess water}}.
A single line of stones is constructed across the farm on slopes of up to {{c1::2%}}, which reduces runoff speed and retains {{c2::soils (sediments)}} from the runoff water.
Planting some {{c1::tree species}} on the edge of the farm protects the soil from erosion, while local {{c2::vegetative barriers}} filter out sediments from runoff waters and reduce runoff speed.
Combining traditional {{c1::stone bunds}} and vegetation, that is {{c2::grasses or perennial species}}, can be used to control soil erosion on steep slopes.

The Gumuz community of northwestern Ethiopia has fertile soils, enormous vegetation with diverse plant and animal species and abundant mineral resources such as {{c1::gold}}; their livelihood is highly based on {{c2::natural resources}}.
Through {{c1::observation and experience}} the Gumuz developed an indigenous knowledge system associated with their {{c2::traditional belief systems}}.

The Gumuz believe natural resources are an indigenous gift, blessing and creation of {{c1::Yamba (God)}} and perceive them as {{c2::ancestral heritage}}, with ownership vested upon the {{c3::whole community}}.

Indigenous Gumuz knowledge constitutes mostly {{c1::norms, values, ethics and taboos}} institutionalized as {{c2::customary laws and conventions}}, and these institutions are enforced by the {{c3::elders}}.
Different indigenous knowledge practices play a vital role in the management of natural resources like {{c1::soil, water, vegetation and wildlife}}.

cards.question: Define biodiversity.
cards.answer: Biodiversity refers to the range of all forms of life on earth, including plants, animals, humans, bacteria and other organisms.

cards.question: Which groups of organisms are explicitly named in the definition of biodiversity?
cards.answer: Plants, animals, humans, bacteria and other organisms.

cards.question: Give two examples of habitats in which different species, sub-species and communities exist.
cards.answer: A rainforest and a grassland.

cards.question: List the four components of biodiversity given in the textbook.
cards.answer: 1) The number of species (plants, animals and other organisms); 2) the genetic diversity of different species found in an area; 3) the population of each species; and 4) the diversity of habitats and landscapes of the species (forests, grasslands and others) in an area.

cards.question: What is meant by genetic diversity as a component of biodiversity?
cards.answer: It is the genetic diversity of the different species found in an area, that is, the genetic variation within species.

cards.question: What does the biodiversity of an area show?
cards.answer: It shows how rich the area is in terms of the total number of species present and their populations and habitats.

cards.question: Why does Ethiopia have a high diversity of plant and animal species?
cards.answer: Ethiopia has high geographic and climatic diversity, which has resulted in high diversity of plant and animal species inhabiting the different agro ecologies.

cards.question: What are endemic plants or animals?
cards.answer: They are plants and animals found in a given country or area that are not found elsewhere; Ethiopia possesses a large number of such species.

cards.question: What three levels of biodiversity are represented by the components listed in the text?
cards.answer: Genetic diversity (genetic diversity of species), species diversity (number of species and their populations), and ecosystem or habitat diversity (diversity of habitats and landscapes such as forests and grasslands).

cards.question: What determines whether individual species and ecosystems develop healthily in an area?
cards.answer: The way biodiversity of the given area is managed determines whether or not there is healthy development of individual species and ecosystems.

cards.text: Biodiversity refers to the range of all forms of life on earth, including plants, animals, humans, bacteria and other {{c1::organisms}}.
Biodiversity includes the different species, {{c1::sub-species}} and communities that exist in a given habitat like a rainforest or grassland.
A rainforest or a {{c1::grassland}} is an example of a habitat containing different species, sub-species and communities.
One component of biodiversity is the number of {{c1::species}} (plants, animals and other organisms) in an area.
One component of biodiversity is the {{c1::genetic diversity}} of different species found in an area.
The {{c1::population}} of each species and the diversity of habitats and landscapes are components of biodiversity.
The biodiversity of an area shows how rich it is in terms of the total number of {{c1::species}} present and their {{c2::populations}} and {{c3::habitats}}.
Ethiopia's high geographic and climatic diversity has resulted in high diversity of plant and animal species inhabiting the different {{c1::agro ecologies}}.
Plants and animals that are not found elsewhere are called {{c1::endemic}} plants/animals.
The three levels of biodiversity are genetic diversity, species diversity and {{c1::ecosystem (habitat) diversity}}.
cards.extra: Ecosystem diversity is the diversity of habitats and landscapes such as forests and grasslands.

cards.text: The way biodiversity of a given area is {{c1::managed}} determines whether or not there is healthy development of individual species and ecosystems.

cards.question: What does biodiversity deal with regarding plant species?
cards.answer: It deals with the diversity of plant species, including crop genetic resources and forest genetic resources.

cards.question: What does biodiversity deal with regarding animal species?
cards.answer: It deals with the diversity of animal species, including farm animal genetic resources and wildlife genetic resources.

cards.question: Which microbial component is included in the scope of biodiversity?
cards.answer: Microbial genetic resources.

cards.question: Besides genetic resources, what other kind of diversity falls within the scope of biodiversity?
cards.answer: Habitat diversity, that is, the diversity of habitats and landscapes such as forests and grasslands.

cards.question: At which different scales can assessment of biodiversity be made?
cards.answer: Assessment can be made at specific sites or regions, at country level, or at global level.

cards.question: What determines the scale at which biodiversity is assessed?
cards.answer: The scale of assessment depends on the objective of the evaluation.

cards.question: How would biodiversity be evaluated if one needs to know its level in a forest area or a water resource?
cards.answer: By evaluating the biodiversity in that specific forest or water body.

cards.question: What does assessment of general national biodiversity status include?
cards.answer: Assessment at country level includes biodiversity in all kinds of habitats and the different species of plants, animals and other organisms.

cards.text: Plant species in the scope of biodiversity include {{c1::crop genetic resources}} and {{c2::forest genetic resources}}.
Animal species in the scope of biodiversity include {{c1::farm animal genetic resources}} and {{c2::wildlife genetic resources}}.
{{c1::Microbial genetic resources}} are included in the scope of biodiversity alongside plant and animal genetic resources.
Besides genetic resources, the scope of biodiversity includes the diversity of {{c1::habitats and landscapes}}.
Assessment of biodiversity can be made at scales varying from specific {{c1::sites or regions}} to {{c2::country}} or {{c3::global}} level.
The scale of assessment of biodiversity depends on the {{c1::objective of the evaluation}}.
To know the level of biodiversity of a forest area or a water resource, evaluate the biodiversity in that specific {{c1::forest}} or {{c2::water body}}.
Assessment of general national biodiversity status has to be made at a {{c1::country}} level and covers all kinds of {{c2::habitats}} and the different species of plants, animals and other organisms.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 12::12.3 Values and services of biodiversity

cards.question: What provisioning products and services does biodiversity provide according to the text?
cards.answer: Food production (cropping, livestock, food from wild plants and animals); firewood, fiber and construction materials from various plant species; and medicinal resources, since various plant and animal species are important sources of medicines.

cards.question: In what way are plant and animal species important as medicinal resources?
cards.answer: Various plant and animal species are important sources of medicines.

cards.question: How do soil and forests contribute to climate regulation?
cards.answer: Soil and forests store a large amount of carbon, preventing its release to the atmosphere, and thus contribute to climate regulation.

cards.question: What role do natural predators play among the regulatory services of biodiversity?
cards.answer: Some natural predators control some disease-causing pests.

cards.question: Which organisms assist in pollination and in the dispersal of seeds and plant reproduction?
cards.answer: Different organisms, including bees and other insects, assist in the dispersal of seeds and plant reproduction.

cards.question: How do organisms contribute to purification of drinking water and air?
cards.answer: Organisms decompose (detoxify) toxic substances that can pollute water and air, and this contributes to water and air purification.

cards.question: Which regulatory service is provided by forests in relation to soil?
cards.answer: Soil erosion control by forests.

cards.question: What is the role of waste decomposition among the services of biodiversity?
cards.answer: Various organisms in the environment decompose wastes, enhance nutrient cycling and prevent accumulation of wastes.

cards.question: List the cultural services of biodiversity given in the textbook.
cards.answer: Recreation, sports, hunting; a source of foreign currency; and education and research.

cards.question: What are supporting services of biodiversity, and give the example described in the text.
cards.answer: Supporting services underpin the other services; for example, decomposition of wastes enhances nutrient cycling, and pollination through seed dispersal supports plant reproduction.

cards.question: In the review exercise, pollination, soil erosion control by forests and waste decomposition are all examples of which kind of service?
cards.answer: Regulatory services; the correct answer to the multiple-choice question is 'All of these'.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 12::12.3 Values and services of biodiversity

cards.text: Provisioning services of biodiversity include food production through cropping, livestock, and food from {{c1::wild plants and animals}}.
Firewood, {{c1::fiber}} and construction materials are provisioning products obtained from various plant species.
Various plant and animal species are important sources of {{c1::medicines}}.
Soil and forests store a large amount of {{c1::carbon}}, preventing its release to the atmosphere and contributing to climate regulation.
Some natural predators control some {{c1::disease causing pests}}, providing disease and pest control.
Different organisms including {{c1::bees}} and other insects assist in the dispersal of seeds and plant reproduction through pollination.
Organisms decompose (detoxify) {{c1::toxic substances}} that can pollute water and air, contributing to water and air {{c2::purification}}.
{{c1::Soil erosion control}} by forests is a regulatory service provided by biodiversity.
Waste decomposition by various organisms enhances {{c1::nutrient cycling}} and prevents accumulation of wastes.
Cultural services of biodiversity include recreation, {{c1::sports}}, hunting, a source of {{c2::foreign currency}}, and education and research.
Supporting services such as {{c1::nutrient cycling}} and waste decomposition underpin the provision of other biodiversity services.
Pollination and dispersal of seeds support plant {{c1::reproduction}}, a supporting role of biodiversity.
In the review exercise, pollination, soil erosion control by forests and waste decomposition are all {{c1::regulatory services}}, so the correct choice is All of these.

cards.question: Name the major threats to biodiversity listed in the unit summary.
cards.answer: Habitat destruction, overexploitation, invasive species, climate change, pollution and population growth.

cards.question: What is land use change, and why is it usually done?
cards.answer: It is the conversion of forests, grasslands and woodlands to cultivated land, usually done to expand cultivated land for crop production.

cards.question: How does land use change affect plant and animal species?
cards.answer: It destroys the natural habitats of various plant and animal species and results in the loss of several plant and animal species.

cards.question: What does unsustainable use of resources refer to?
cards.answer: It refers to overexploitation of resources, including overgrazing, hunting and harvesting of biological resources.

cards.question: How does overgrazing lead to the loss of species and ecosystem services?
cards.answer: Overgrazing exposes soils to erosion, which can result in the loss of plant and animal species; together with the species, ecosystem services can also be lost.

cards.question: Give three further examples of unsustainable resource use mentioned in the text.
cards.answer: Uncontrolled fishing, overuse of water resources and overharvesting of tree species.

cards.question: Which tree species in Ethiopia has been threatened by overharvesting for timber production?
cards.answer: Hagenia abyssinica.

cards.question: What happened to Lake Haramaya because of over exploitation of water, and what is its current trend?
cards.answer: Lake Haramaya disappeared for many years due to over exploitation, and it is only starting to come back as a result of restorative efforts.

cards.question: How do invasive species cause loss of biodiversity and ecosystem services?
cards.answer: Some invasive species compete against local species for resources and habitats, which causes loss of biodiversity and ecosystem services.

cards.question: Name the three invasive species given as threats to biodiversity in Ethiopia, with their scientific names.
cards.answer: Parthenium weed (Parthenium hysterophorus), the shrub Prosopis juliflora L., and water hyacinth (Eichornia crossipes L., 'Emboch').

cards.question: What does Parthenium weed invade, and what problem does it cause?
cards.answer: Parthenium weed invades forage and croplands and causes yield losses.

cards.question: Where has Prosopis juliflora invaded in Ethiopia, and what has it caused?
cards.answer: It has invaded rangelands in the Awash Valley, in Afar and Somali regions, and has caused losses of forage species in these areas.

cards.question: Where has water hyacinth become a major threat in Ethiopia?
cards.answer: In the Awash river basin and Lake Tana.

cards.question: How does the dense canopy of water hyacinth affect aquatic plants, animals, people and lakes?
cards.answer: It limits boat traffic and recreation, shades native aquatic plant species and prevents their growth, negatively affects aquatic animals that feed on those plants, reduces oxygen availability and fish production, and reduces the volume of water in lakes, eventually threatening the existence of lakes.

cards.question: How has climate change manifested itself in Ethiopia?
cards.answer: The average maximum as well as the minimum temperatures have increased, and there has been a change in the rainfall distribution pattern in the country.

cards.question: What effects of climate change on crop growing and yields are described in Ethiopia?
cards.answer: The crop growing season has shortened in many areas, crop varieties requiring long growing seasons have substantially decreased, and early or late coming of rain usually affects yields of some crops.

cards.question: What is usually the context of environmental pollution in Ethiopia?
cards.answer: Pollution is usually related to improper management of both solid and liquid wastes, which often contain toxic substances that enter water resources, forests or soils.

cards.question: What consequences does pollution of habitats have for species?
cards.answer: It destroys natural habitats, reduces the number of species and the populations of different organisms, and can even cause total loss of some species.

cards.question: How do agricultural runoff and eroded soils pollute water resources and harm aquatic animals?
cards.answer: Irrigation with runoff water containing dissolved pesticides and fertilizers can affect soil and aquatic organisms; eroded soils containing high nitrogen and phosphorus pollute water resources, harming fish and possibly resulting in their extinction.

cards.question: How does unchecked population growth threaten biodiversity?
cards.answer: It increases demand for food and other basic services, leading to expansion of agricultural lands, overexploitation of resources, and use of marginal and unsuitable lands for production.

cards.question: In the review exercise, which option correctly lists major threats to biodiversity in Ethiopia: habitat destruction, invasive species, deforestation, or all of these?
cards.answer: All of these.

cards.text: The major threats to biodiversity include habitat destruction, overexploitation, invasive species, climate change, pollution and {{c1::population growth}}.
The conversion of forests, grasslands and woodlands to cultivated land is called {{c1::land use change}}.
Land use change destroys the natural {{c1::habitats}} of various plant and animal species and results in the loss of several species.
Unsustainable use of resources refers to {{c1::overexploitation}} of resources including overgrazing, hunting and harvesting of biological resources.
Overgrazing exposes soils to {{c1::erosion}}, which can result in the loss of plant and animal species and of ecosystem services.
Uncontrolled fishing, overuse of water resources and overharvesting of {{c1::tree species}} are further examples of unsustainable resource use.
Overharvesting for timber production has threatened the tree species {{c1::Hagenia abyssinica}} in Ethiopia.
Lake Haramaya disappeared for many years due to over exploitation and is only starting to come back as a result of {{c1::restorative efforts}}.
Invasive species compete against {{c1::local species}} for resources and habitats, causing loss of biodiversity and ecosystem services.

Invasive species that threaten biodiversity in Ethiopia include Parthenium weed ({{c1::Parthenium hysterophorus}}), the shrub {{c2::Prosopis juliflora}} L. and water hyacinth (Eichornia crossipes L., 'Emboch').
Parthenium weed invades {{c1::forage and croplands}} and causes yield losses.
Prosopis has invaded rangelands in the {{c1::Awash Valley}}, in Afar and Somali regions, causing losses of {{c2::forage species}}.
Water hyacinth has become a major threat to the {{c1::Awash river basin}} and {{c2::Lake Tana}}.
By establishing a dense canopy, water hyacinth limits boat traffic and {{c1::recreation}} and shades native aquatic plant species, preventing their growth.
Water hyacinth reduces {{c1::oxygen}} availability, can result in reduced fish production and reduces the volume of water in lakes.
Due to climate change, the average maximum as well as the minimum {{c1::temperatures}} have increased in Ethiopia, and the {{c2::rainfall distribution pattern}} has changed.
Climate change has shortened the {{c1::crop growing season}} in many areas of Ethiopia and decreased crop varieties that require long growing seasons.
cards.extra: Early or late coming of rain usually affects yields of some crops.

cards.text: Pollution in the Ethiopian context is usually related to improper management of both {{c1::solid}} and {{c2::liquid}} wastes containing toxic substances.
Pollution of habitats destroys natural habitats and leads to a reduction in the number of {{c1::species}} and in the population of different organisms.
cards.extra: A total loss of some species could even be the consequence.

cards.text: Irrigation of croplands with runoff water containing dissolved {{c1::pesticides}} and {{c2::fertilizers}} can affect soil and aquatic organisms.
Eroded soils containing high {{c1::nitrogen}} and {{c2::phosphorus}} pollute water resources and may cause the extinction of fish.
Unchecked population growth results in the expansion of {{c1::agricultural lands}} and overexploitation of resources.
cards.extra: Using marginal and unsuitable lands for production is another undesirable consequence.

cards.text: In the review exercise, habitat destruction, invasive species and deforestation are all major threats to biodiversity in Ethiopia, so the correct choice is {{c1::All of these}}.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 12::12.5 Biodiversity conservation and its status in Ethiopia

cards.question: Define biodiversity conservation.
cards.answer: Biodiversity conservation refers to the planned management of biodiversity in a particular ecosystem to prevent overexploitation, pollution, destruction and to ensure biodiversity is maintained.

cards.question: List the three major objectives of biodiversity conservation.
cards.answer: To maintain: 1) a sustainable use of species and the ecosystem; 2) life supporting systems; and 3) essential ecological processes.

cards.question: In the review exercise, which answer is correct for the objectives of biodiversity conservation: sustainable use of species/ecosystems, functioning of ecological processes, both, or neither?
cards.answer: Both A and B.

cards.question: Why is conservation of biodiversity needed?
cards.answer: Human activities such as habitat destruction, introduction of invasive species and harvesting of species have caused huge losses; species diversity enables development of improved plant and animal varieties, provides food and raw materials for medicines, and supplies regulatory and cultural services.

cards.question: What proportion of Ethiopia's population lives in rural areas, and why is conservation vital for their livelihood?
cards.answer: Approximately 85% of the population lives in rural areas, and the livelihood of most of this population depends directly or indirectly on natural resources, so conservation is vital.

cards.question: List the plant genetic resources found in Ethiopia's diverse ecosystems.
cards.answer: Field crops; horticultural crops such as fruits and vegetables; wild plants; medicinal plants (wild plants used for treating human diseases); forests; rangelands and forage plants.

cards.question: What animal genetic and wildlife resources does Ethiopia possess?
cards.answer: Ethiopia has rich animal genetic resources and wildlife genetic resources; animal genetic resources include farm animal genetic resources such as indigenous breeds of cattle and other domestic animals.

cards.question: How many mammal types and bird species are endemic to Ethiopia?
cards.answer: About 29 mammal types and 18 bird species are endemic to Ethiopia.

cards.question: What threats are described for forest resources in Ethiopia?
cards.answer: Deforestation, habitat destruction and poor regeneration, expansion of invasive species, clearing forest for agriculture, forest fires and illegal tree harvest; these have threatened many tree species including medicinal plants.

cards.question: What are the major threats to forage resources in Ethiopia?
cards.answer: Overgrazing and over-browsing of shrubby vegetation, invasive species, and conversion of grazing lands to cultivated lands.

cards.question: What efforts are being made in Ethiopia to reduce threats to forage resources?
cards.answer: Clearing invasive species, selecting and multiplying locally adapted forage species, enclosing degraded rangelands and banning open grazing.

cards.question: What forms of habitat degradation threaten wild animals in Ethiopia?
cards.answer: Expansion of agriculture and grazing areas near wildlife habitats, deforestation, habitat destruction, overgrazing, overharvesting (fish), unbalanced water use and siltation of water resources.

cards.question: Name three endangered wild animals in Ethiopia with their scientific names.
cards.answer: Walia Ibex (Capra walie), Mountain Nyala (Tragelaphus buxtoni) and Ethiopian Wolf (Canis simensis).

cards.question: What community-based efforts reduce destruction of forest resources in Ethiopia?
cards.answer: Efforts involve local communities in the management of forest resources, and in some places forests were closed to reduce human interference.

cards.question: List the protected areas in Ethiopia mentioned in the text.
cards.answer: National and regional parks; wildlife sanctuaries; wildlife reserves; botanical gardens and herbariums; and controlled hunting centers.

cards.question: Why is biodiversity conservation important in general?
cards.answer: It is important to reduce losses of vital plants, animals and microbial resources for the sustainability of agriculture, forestry, wildlife and other similar sectors.

cards.question: What is in-situ conservation, and which Ethiopian measures from the text are examples of it?
cards.answer: In-situ conservation is conservation of biodiversity in its natural habitats. Ethiopian examples are national and regional parks, wildlife sanctuaries, wildlife reserves, controlled hunting centers and forests closed to reduce human interference.

cards.question: What is ex-situ conservation, and which measures named in the text are examples of it?
cards.answer: Ex-situ conservation is conservation of biodiversity outside its natural habitats; botanical gardens and herbariums, together with gene banks, are examples.

cards.question: What is the role of gene banks in biodiversity conservation?
cards.answer: Gene banks conserve genetic diversity ex-situ by storing seeds and other genetic material of crop plants, farm animals and wild species so the material remains available for future use, breeding and research.

cards.question: What role do laws and regulations play in biodiversity conservation?
cards.answer: Laws and regulations protect species and habitats by controlling hunting, harvesting, land conversion and pollution, and by supporting protected areas and sustainable use of resources.

cards.question: In the review exercise, which wild animals are identified as threatened due to habitat destruction?
cards.answer: Ethiopian Wolf and Walia Ibex; the correct choice is 'Both A and B'.

cards.question: In the review exercise, biodiversity refers to a range of different species of which groups?
cards.answer: Plants, animals and microorganisms; the correct choice is 'All of these'.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 12::12.5 Biodiversity conservation and its status in Ethiopia

cards.text: Biodiversity conservation refers to the {{c1::planned management}} of biodiversity in a particular ecosystem to prevent overexploitation, pollution and destruction.
The major objectives of biodiversity conservation are to maintain sustainable use of species and ecosystems, life supporting systems and {{c1::essential ecological processes}}.

The review exercise states that the objectives of biodiversity conservation include sustainable use of species/ecosystems and functioning of ecological process, so the correct choice is {{c1::Both A and B}}.
Human activities like habitat destruction, introduction of {{c1::invasive species}} and harvesting of species has caused huge losses of biodiversity.
The presence of diversity in species of plants and animals enables researchers to develop {{c1::improved varieties}} of plants and animals for human use.
Approximately {{c1::85%}} of the Ethiopian population lives in rural areas, and their livelihoods depend directly or indirectly on {{c2::natural resources}}.
Ethiopia's plant genetic resources include field crops, {{c1::horticultural crops}} (fruits and vegetables), wild plants, {{c2::medicinal plants}}, forests, rangelands and forage plants.
Medicinal plants are wild plants used for {{c1::treating human diseases}}.
Animal genetic resources include farm animal genetic resources such as indigenous breeds of {{c1::cattle}} and other domestic animals.
About {{c1::29}} mammal types and {{c2::18}} bird species are endemic to Ethiopia.
Forest resources in Ethiopia are seriously threatened by deforestation, habitat destruction and poor {{c1::regeneration}}, as well as invasive species, forest fires and illegal tree harvest.
Overgrazing and over-browsing of {{c1::shrubby vegetation}}, invasive species and conversion of grazing lands to cultivated lands are major threats to forage resources.

Efforts to reduce threats to forage resources include clearing invasive species, selecting and multiplying {{c1::locally adapted forage species}}, enclosing degraded rangelands and banning open grazing.
Unbalanced water use and {{c1::siltation}} of water resources are forms of habitat degradation threatening wild animals in Ethiopia.
Endangered wild animals in Ethiopia include the Walia Ibex ({{c1::Capra walie}}), Mountain Nyala ({{c2::Tragelaphus buxtoni}}) and Ethiopian Wolf ({{c3::Canis simensis}}).
Efforts to reduce destruction of forest resources involve {{c1::local communities}} in management, and in some places forests were {{c2::closed}} to reduce human interference.
Protected areas in Ethiopia include national and regional parks, wildlife sanctuaries, wildlife reserves, {{c1::botanical gardens and herbariums}} and controlled hunting centers.
Biodiversity conservation reduces losses of vital plants, animals and {{c1::microbial resources}} for the sustainability of agriculture, forestry and wildlife.
In-situ conservation protects biodiversity in its natural habitats; Ethiopia's national and regional parks, wildlife sanctuaries and wildlife reserves are {{c1::in-situ}} conservation measures.
Ex-situ conservation conserves biodiversity outside its natural habitat; {{c1::botanical gardens and herbariums}} and gene banks are ex-situ measures.
Gene banks conserve genetic diversity ex-situ by storing {{c1::seeds and other genetic material}} of crop, farm animal and wild species.
Laws and regulations support biodiversity conservation by controlling hunting, harvesting, land conversion and {{c1::pollution}} and by establishing protected areas.
In the review exercise, both the Ethiopian Wolf and the Walia Ibex are threatened species due to habitat destruction, so the correct choice is {{c1::Both A and B}}.
In the review exercise, biodiversity refers to a range of different species of plants, animals and {{c1::microorganisms}}, so the correct choice is {{c2::All of these}}.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 13::13.1 Definitions of climate change and variability

cards.question: What is climate change according to the textbook?
cards.answer: Climate change refers to a long term change (for example, over decades) in temperatures and in the patterns of the weather.

cards.question: What is climate variability?
cards.answer: Climate variability refers to the short term (days, weeks or months) variability in the climate.

cards.question: Why can organisms adapt to climate variability but not necessarily to climate change?
cards.answer: Climate variability does not cause fundamental changes in the ecosystem, and its changes are not long-term, so organisms can adapt to them. Climate change, by contrast, leads to fundamental changes in the ecosystem.

cards.question: Give the textbook example of climate variability involving rainfall.
cards.answer: Some years can have below average rainfall while others have average or above the average rainfall.

cards.question: What are the major greenhouse gases identified in Unit 13?
cards.answer: The major greenhouse gases are carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O).

cards.question: Define greenhouse gases using the key term definition.
cards.answer: Greenhouse gases are gases that can absorb heat radiation emitted from the earth's surface and reradiate it to the earth, causing global warming by trapping heat that should be released out of the atmosphere into space.

cards.question: What are fossil fuels, and give three examples.
cards.answer: Fossil fuels are fuels formed from fossilized plants and animals. Examples are coal, oil and natural gas.

cards.question: Which human activities release greenhouse gases into the atmosphere?
cards.answer: Human activities like agriculture, forest clearing, forest burning and fossil fuel burning release greenhouse gases into the atmosphere.

cards.question: Besides global warming, what other problem does climate change cause?
cards.answer: Climate change also causes depletion of the ozone layer and exposes the earth to harmful radiation that can cause skin cancer in humans.

cards.question: List six fundamental ecosystem changes that climate change can lead to.
cards.answer: A decrease in crop and animal productivity; plant and animal species threatened or extinct; changes in water availability; changes in storm patterns and frequencies; increased flooding of coastal areas; changes in rainfall amount and patterns. (Also increased frequency of drought, drying of surface water resources, increased soil erosion and increased desertification.)

cards.question: Which extreme weather events can become more common with climate change?
cards.answer: Unusual floods in some areas, droughts that stay for long periods, wildfires, unusual snowfalls, intense hurricanes and warming of the earth.

cards.question: What is the major cause of climate change, and what role do natural processes play?
cards.answer: The major cause is the production and release of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere from different sources; their accumulation causes climate change. Natural processes can also produce the gases, but it is generally agreed that climate change is mainly caused by human activities.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 13::13.1 Definitions of climate change and variability

cards.text: Climate change refers to a {{c1::long term}} (e.g. decades) change in {{c2::temperatures}} and the patterns of the weather.
Climate variability refers to the {{c1::short term}} variability in the climate, occurring over {{c2::days, weeks or months}}.
Climate variability does not cause {{c1::fundamental changes}} in the ecosystem, and organisms can {{c2::adapt}} because the changes are not long-term.
Climate change leads to {{c1::fundamental changes}} in the ecosystem, unlike climate variability.
The major greenhouse gases are {{c1::carbon dioxide (CO2)}}, {{c2::methane (CH4)}} and {{c3::nitrous oxide (N2O)}}.
Greenhouse gases trap {{c1::heat}} in the atmosphere and cause {{c2::global warming}}.
Human activities like {{c1::agriculture}}, forest clearing, forest burning and {{c2::fossil fuel burning}} release greenhouse gases into the atmosphere.
Fossil fuels are fuels formed from {{c1::fossilized plants and animals}}; examples include coal, oil and {{c2::natural gas}}.
In addition to global warming, climate change causes depletion of the {{c1::ozone layer}} and exposes the earth to harmful radiation that can cause {{c2::skin cancer}} in humans.
It is generally agreed that climate change is mainly caused by {{c1::human activities}}, although natural processes can also produce greenhouse gases.
As the concentration of greenhouse gases increases in the atmosphere, {{c1::heat is trapped}}, and this results in {{c2::global warming}}.
Examples of fundamental changes from climate change include decreased {{c1::crop and animal productivity}}, changes in water availability and increased {{c2::desertification}}.
Some years can have {{c1::below average rainfall}} while others have average or {{c2::above the average rainfall}}.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 13::13.2 Climate change and its effects

cards.question: What changes in rainfall and temperature does climate change cause?
cards.answer: Climate change causes changes in rainfall amounts and patterns, an increase in global temperatures, and the melting of icecaps and glaciers. Rise in sea level and droughts that increase evaporation are also consequences.

cards.question: In areas where agriculture depends mainly on rainfall, how does decreased rainfall affect farming?
cards.answer: A decrease in rainfall reduces water availability, leading to water shortage for growing crops and for animals and human consumption.

cards.question: How does an increase in temperature affect water resources used in agriculture?
cards.answer: Increased temperature increases water losses from soils and surface water resources, creating water shortage for crops, animals and people.

cards.question: How can increased rainfall reduce crop yields and animal productivity?
cards.answer: Increased rainfall may increase soil erosion; nutrients plants need are washed away with the soil, reducing nutrient availability for field crops and forages and thus decreasing crop yields and animal productivity.

cards.question: Besides reducing productivity, what other damage can increased rainfall cause?
cards.answer: Increased rainfall can also lead to damage of croplands and household properties.

cards.question: How does global warming affect crop and animal diseases?
cards.answer: Global warming could increase the incidence of some crop and animal diseases, resulting in reduced crop and livestock yields.

cards.question: Through which pathways does climate change affect animal production?
cards.answer: Through reduced forage yields, heat stress from increased temperature, water shortage, and increased incidence of existing and new diseases and parasites, all causing reduced animal growth and productivity.

cards.question: Why is Ethiopian agriculture highly vulnerable to climate change effects?
cards.answer: It is mainly small scale with very low use of production enhancing technologies such as improved seeds/breeds, fertilizers, pesticides, irrigation and agricultural machineries, so productivity is low compared to potential. More than 90% of crop production is rainfed, with very low production under irrigation.

cards.question: What are the effects of climate change on forestry?
cards.answer: Global warming and reduced water availability cause reduced vegetation growth, reduced productivity and loss of some tree species, reducing the forest's capacity to absorb carbon through photosynthesis and to regulate climate through carbon storage. Loss of forest or species causes loss of plant and animal biodiversity.

cards.question: How does environmental degradation enhance desertification?
cards.answer: Degradation in the form of deforestation, soil erosion and disappearance of wildlife enhances desertification in arid and semi-arid areas.

cards.question: How does climate change affect sea level and coastal communities?
cards.answer: Increased global temperature has already caused melting of polar ice caps, which causes sea level to rise and coastal communities to become more vulnerable to flooding. Flooding destroys communities and can damage the overall ecosystems.

cards.question: Explain ocean acidification and why it is harmful.
cards.answer: Oceans absorb about 30% of the carbon dioxide released to the atmosphere. Dissolved carbon dioxide produces carbonic acid; as more carbon dioxide dissolves, oceans become more acidic, which is harmful to organisms living in the oceans.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 13::13.2 Climate change and its effects

cards.text: Climate change causes changes in rainfall {{c1::amounts and patterns}} and an increase in {{c2::global temperatures}}.
Increase in global temperature has caused melting of {{c1::icecaps and glaciers}} and polar ice caps, causing {{c2::sea level}} to rise.
A decrease in rainfall reduces {{c1::water availability}}, while an increase in temperature increases {{c2::water losses}} from soils and surface water resources.
Increased rainfall may result in increased {{c1::soil erosion}}, which washes away {{c2::nutrients}} that plants use for growth.
Eroded soils reduce nutrient availability for {{c1::field crops and forages}}, with the consequence of decreased {{c2::crop yields and animal productivity}}.
Global warming could increase the incidence of some {{c1::crop and animal diseases}}, resulting in the reduction of {{c2::crop and livestock yields}}.
Animal production is affected through reduced {{c1::forage yields}}, heat stress, water shortage and increased {{c2::diseases and parasites}}.
More than {{c1::90%}} of crop production in Ethiopia is {{c2::rainfed}}, with very low production under irrigation.
Ethiopian agriculture has very low use of production enhancing technologies including {{c1::improved seeds/breeds}}, fertilizers, pesticides, {{c2::irrigation}} and agricultural machineries.
Global warming and reduced water availability cause reduced {{c1::vegetation growth}}, reduced productivity and loss of some {{c2::tree species}}.
Degradation in the form of {{c1::deforestation}}, soil erosion and disappearance of wildlife enhances {{c2::desertification}} in arid and semi-arid areas.
Any loss of the forest or species in it causes loss of {{c1::plant and animal biodiversity}} and reduces the forest's capacity to regulate climate through {{c2::carbon storage}}.
Rise in sea level makes {{c1::coastal communities}} more vulnerable to {{c2::flooding}}, which destroys communities and can damage ecosystems.
Oceans absorb about {{c1::30%}} of carbon dioxide released to the atmosphere; when dissolved in water it produces {{c2::carbonic acid}}, making oceans more acidic.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 13::13.3 Strategies of mitigating climate change

cards.question: What is climate change mitigation?
cards.answer: Climate change mitigation refers to the activities implemented to either reduce or remove the emissions of greenhouse gases to the atmosphere.

cards.question: In which two ways do mitigation practices reduce or remove greenhouse gas emissions?
cards.answer: 1. Reducing greenhouse gas emissions. 2. Enhancing removal of greenhouse gases by carbon sinks.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 13::13.3 Strategies of mitigating climate change

cards.text: Climate change mitigation refers to the activities implemented to either {{c1::reduce}} or {{c2::remove}} the emissions of greenhouse gases to the atmosphere.
Mitigation practices reduce or remove greenhouse gas emissions in two ways: {{c1::reducing greenhouse gas emissions}} and {{c2::enhancing removal of greenhouse gases by carbon sinks}}.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 13::13.3.1 Reducing greenhouse gas emissions from sources

cards.question: Why is there a need to shift away from fossil fuel burning for energy?
cards.answer: Fossil fuel burning has long been a source of energy in industries and has been the largest source of human-induced carbon dioxide emission to the atmosphere.

cards.question: Which renewable energy sources are mentioned as alternatives to reduce carbon emission?
cards.answer: Solar energy, wind energy and hydropower.

cards.question: How does clearing forests contribute to global warming?
cards.answer: Clearing forests releases stored carbon into the atmosphere as carbon dioxide, contributing to global warming.

cards.question: Why are forests usually cleared, and what mitigation action does the textbook recommend?
cards.answer: Forests are usually cleared to get additional agricultural land, firewood and timber. The reduction of deforestation is an important way of reducing carbon emission from forests.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 13::13.3.1 Reducing greenhouse gas emissions from sources

cards.text: Fossil fuel burning has long been a source of energy in industries and the largest source of {{c1::human-induced carbon dioxide emission}} to the atmosphere.
There is a growing need to shift to {{c1::renewable energy sources}} like solar energy, wind energy and {{c2::hydropower}} in order to reduce carbon emission.
Clearing of forests results in the release of {{c1::stored carbon}} into the atmosphere as {{c2::carbon dioxide}}.
The reduction of {{c1::deforestation}} is an important way of reducing {{c2::carbon emission}} from forests.

cards.question: Define carbon sinks using the key term definition.
cards.answer: Carbon sinks are any processes, activities or mechanisms that remove greenhouse gases from the atmosphere.

cards.question: Where do forests store carbon?
cards.answer: Forests store a large amount of carbon, through photosynthesis, in their biomass, forest floor and in soils.

cards.question: What is afforestation, and how does it mitigate climate change?
cards.answer: Afforestation means planting new forests. It enhances the carbon storage capacity (sink capacity) and helps to mitigate climate change.

cards.question: What vital role do forests play in mitigating climate change?
cards.answer: Forests remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere through photosynthesis and store it in biomass, forest floor and soils, helping to mitigate climate change.

cards.text: Carbon sinks are any processes, activities or mechanisms that {{c1::remove greenhouse gases}} from the atmosphere.
Forests store a large amount of carbon through {{c1::photosynthesis}} in their {{c2::biomass}}, forest floor and soils.
Afforestation means {{c1::planting new forests}}, which enhances the {{c2::carbon storage capacity (sink capacity)}} and helps mitigate climate change.
Forests play a vital role by removing {{c1::carbon dioxide}} from the atmosphere, which helps to mitigate {{c2::climate change}}.

cards.question: How much more carbon is stored in soil compared with the total amount in the atmosphere?
cards.answer: About 2 times more carbon is stored in the soil compared to the total amount in the atmosphere.

cards.question: Why is conservation and management of soils important for climate change mitigation?
cards.answer: Conservation and management of soils through best practices enhances the carbon storage capacity of soils, so a high proportion of the carbon removed from the atmosphere by plants remains in the soil.

cards.question: List the soil conservation practices named in section 13.3.3.
cards.answer: Crop rotation, mixed cropping, reduced soil tillage, mulching, and use of terraces and other physical soil conservation structures.

cards.question: How do soil conservation practices help mitigate climate change?
cards.answer: They keep a high proportion of the carbon removed from the atmosphere by plants in the soils, enhancing soil carbon storage.

cards.text: About {{c1::2 times}} more carbon is stored in the soil compared to the total amount in the {{c2::atmosphere}}.
Conservation and management of soils through implementing {{c1::best practices}} enhances the {{c2::carbon storage capacity}} of soils.
Soil conservation practices include {{c1::crop rotation}}, mixed cropping, {{c2::reduced soil tillage}}, mulching and use of terraces and other physical soil conservation structures.
A high proportion of the carbon removed from the atmosphere by plants remains in {{c1::soils}} through implementing {{c2::soil conservation practices}}.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 13::13.4 Climate change adaptation strategies in Ethiopia

cards.question: What is climate change adaptation?
cards.answer: Climate change adaptation refers to the adjustments that farmers and other communities make in response to actual or expected climate change. Farmers modify their ways of doing crop production and animal rearing to reduce the harmful effects of the changing climate.

cards.question: How do changing crop rotation and changing crop type help farmers adapt?
cards.answer: Farmers change crop rotation and involve more drought adapted crops in the cropping pattern, and change to crops better adapted to drought conditions with lower water demand.

cards.question: How does intercropping legumes and cereals help adaptation to climate change?
cards.answer: Intercropping, mixing legumes and cereals, reduces soil erosion and reduces water loss by evaporation.

cards.question: What does changing the crop calendar mean in climate adaptation?
cards.answer: It means planting early or late following the onset of rainfall as the climate changes.

cards.question: How do perennial crops such as fruit crops mixed with legumes and cereals help?
cards.answer: Using perennials like fruit crops mixed with legumes and cereals protects the soil from erosion and reduces water loss.

cards.question: What qualities should animal breeds have for climate adaptation?
cards.answer: Breeds better adapted to increased temperatures and water stress, and possessing better feed conversion efficiency.

cards.question: What are the benefits of grazing land enclosures?
cards.answer: Grazing land enclosures reduce land degradation, increase animal forage production and reduce incidence of animal diseases.

cards.question: What are non-conventional feed resources used in adaptation?
cards.answer: Locally available, non-conventional or unusual feed resources including agro-industrial by-products.

cards.question: How does expansion of perennial crops reduce the risk of total yield loss?
cards.answer: Planting enset and tree species that better tolerate climate change effects gives farmers food from enset or income from selling tree products to purchase food when field crops fail, reducing the risk of total yield loss.

cards.question: What is income diversification and how does it help households facing climate change?
cards.answer: Instead of depending totally on agriculture, farmers take part in off farm activities like trading, paid labor work and other activities. These reduce the chance of total income loss for the household, particularly during climate change.

cards.question: How do drought tolerant crop varieties reduce risk during moisture shortage years?
cards.answer: Farmers select varieties adapted to moisture shortage; these tolerate drought through a short maturity period or efficient use of available water, reducing the risk of total yield loss.

cards.question: How does mixed cropping reduce the risk of total crop loss?
cards.answer: More than one crop species is planted on the same farmland, using the soil resource efficiently. Crops have different tolerance to drought, so if one species fails the other still provides some yield.

cards.question: Why do farmers select or breed more suitable animals?
cards.answer: Increased temperature and drought reduce animal productivity and increase susceptibility to parasites and diseases, but impacts depend on breed. Replacing low producing animals with fewer highly productive, disease resistant breeds adapted to local climate conditions and feeds improves productivity.

cards.question: Which animal management practices can reduce greenhouse gas emissions?
cards.answer: Using animal manure for biogas production, improving animal nutrition, implementing a cut and carry system for feeding, and limiting free grazing.

cards.question: What is Climate Smart Agriculture (CSA)?
cards.answer: Climate Smart Agriculture is an integrated approach where crop production, animal production and natural resources are managed to address the changing climate.

cards.question: What are the three aims of Climate Smart Agriculture?
cards.answer: a. Increase sustainable productivity. b. Reduce vulnerability to climate related risks and improve capacity to adapt to climate change. c. Reduce greenhouse gas emissions from agricultural production.

cards.question: Why is integrated use of CSA practices important?
cards.answer: A single practice may not achieve all three objectives; a combination of crop and animal production and natural resources management practices is needed. Some practices contribute to more than one CSA objective, so integrated use achieves the triple objectives.

cards.question: Which CSA practices contribute to productivity, adaptation and mitigation respectively?
cards.answer: Productivity: agricultural input management, water and soil management. Adaptation: crop diversification, integrated crop-livestock management, improved grazing. Mitigation: planting trees/agroforestry. Some practices contribute to more than one objective.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 13::13.4 Climate change adaptation strategies in Ethiopia

cards.text: Climate change adaptation refers to the {{c1::adjustments}} that farmers and other communities make in response to {{c2::actual or expected climate change}}.
To cope with climate change impacts, farmers need to modify their ways of {{c1::crop production}} and {{c2::animal rearing}}.
Farmers change crop rotation by involving more {{c1::drought adapted crops}} in the cropping pattern.
{{c1::Intercropping}}, mixing legumes and cereals, reduces {{c2::soil erosion}} and reduces water loss by evaporation.
Changing crop type means using crops better adapted to {{c1::drought conditions}} and crops with {{c2::lower water demand}}.
Changing the crop calendar means planting {{c1::early or late}} following the {{c2::onset of rainfall}}.
Using perennials like {{c1::fruit crops}} mixed with legumes and cereals protects the soil from erosion and reduces {{c2::water loss}}.
Adapted animal breeds tolerate increased {{c1::temperatures}} and {{c2::water stress}} and possess better feed conversion efficiency.
{{c1::Grazing land enclosures}} reduce land degradation and increase {{c2::animal forage production}} and reduce incidence of animal diseases.
Farmers utilise locally available, {{c1::non-conventional}} or unusual feed resources including {{c2::agro-industrial by-products}}.
Expansion of perennial crops includes planting {{c1::enset}} and tree species; farmers may sell tree products and {{c2::purchase food}} when field crops fail.
Income diversification means taking part in {{c1::off farm activities}} such as trading and {{c2::paid labor work}} to reduce the chance of total income loss.
Drought tolerant varieties tolerate drought through a {{c1::short maturity period}} or {{c2::efficient use of the available water}}.
In mixed cropping, crops with different {{c1::tolerance to drought}} are planted on the same farmland, reducing the risk of {{c2::total crop loss}}.
Farmers replace low producing animals with fewer highly productive, {{c1::disease resistant}} breeds adapted to local {{c2::climate conditions and feeds}}.
Globally, {{c1::animal production}} is the major source of methane (CH4) emission; using manure for {{c2::biogas production}} can reduce greenhouse gas emission.
Implementing a {{c1::cut and carry system}} for animal feeding and limiting {{c2::free grazing}} are strategies to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from animal production.
Climate Smart Agriculture is an {{c1::integrated approach}} where crop production, animal production and {{c2::natural resources}} are managed to address the changing climate.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 13::13.5 Indigenous knowledge in climate change mitigation strategies

cards.question: What indigenous knowledge practice is described for the Gedeo community?
cards.answer: Gedeo environmental protection: the Gedeo community in southern Ethiopia have a rich culture and indigenous knowledge that encourages environmental protection and conservation, with great respect for nature.

cards.question: How do the Gedeo regard mountains, trees, hillsides and riversides?
cards.answer: They are recognized as intermediates connecting the creator (God) and the creation (man). According to elders, protecting these natural resources expresses human desire and prayers to God.

cards.question: Which natural resources should be respected among the Gedeo, and what happens to some forest patches?
cards.answer: Forests, wildlife and water resources should be respected just like humans. Some forest patches are considered sacred and therefore are protected.

cards.question: What has the Gedeo tradition maintained, and what is its climate mitigation significance?
cards.answer: It has maintained the Gedeo agroforestry systems for hundreds of years, contributing greatly to enhancing the climate mitigation potential of the agroforestry systems in the community.

cards.question: What indigenous soil conservation practice is used by the Konso community, and where?
cards.answer: The Konso community in south western Ethiopia have a traditional landscape characterized by indigenous stone terraces, used for soil conservation for hundreds of years.

cards.question: How do Konso stone terraces protect soils and manage water?
cards.answer: They protect soils from erosion, collect the maximum amount of water and discharge the excess, and create suitable spaces for agriculture.

cards.question: How does Konso soil conservation contribute to climate change mitigation?
cards.answer: Erosion protection improves soil capacity; improved soil stores carbon, and the carbon helps in the mitigation of changes in the climate.

cards.question: Define agroforestry using the key term definition.
cards.answer: Agroforestry is the deliberate integration of trees and shrubs with crops and livestock in agricultural systems.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 13::13.5 Indigenous knowledge in climate change mitigation strategies

cards.text: The {{c1::Gedeo}} community in southern Ethiopia have rich culture and {{c2::indigenous knowledge}} that encourages environmental protection and conservation.
Mountains, trees, hillsides and riversides are recognized as {{c1::intermediates}} connecting the creator (God) and the {{c2::creation (man)}}.
Protecting natural resources is a way of expressing human {{c1::desire and prayers}} to God among the Gedeo.
Some {{c1::forest patches}} are considered sacred and therefore are {{c2::protected}}.
This tradition has maintained the {{c1::Gedeo agroforestry systems}} for {{c2::hundreds of years}}, enhancing their climate mitigation potential.
The Konso community in {{c1::south western Ethiopia}} have a traditional landscape characterized by {{c2::indigenous stone terraces}}.
Konso stone terraces protect soils from {{c1::erosion}}, collect the maximum amount of water and {{c2::discharge the excess}}.
The effect of soil erosion protection is improved soil capacity; improved soil stores {{c1::carbon}}, which helps in the {{c2::mitigation of changes in the climate}}.

cards.question: Define mechanization.
cards.answer: Mechanization is the use of machinery to replace human or animal labor.

cards.question: What activities does mechanization in agriculture cover?
cards.answer: It involves the use of tools and machines for agricultural land development, crop production, harvesting, storage, animal rearing, and processing of products at the farm gate.

cards.question: Why is mechanized agriculture needed in place of simple farm tools or crude implements?
cards.answer: Simple farm tools or crude implements slow down farming activities, so mechanized agriculture is needed to replace them.

cards.question: List four advantages of farm mechanization.
cards.answer: Farm mechanization saves time, reduces the difficulty in farming, saves labour, and reduces farm health hazards.

cards.question: How does farm mechanization affect the scale of farming and farm income?
cards.answer: It encourages large-scale farming and increases on-farm output and income.

cards.question: How does farm mechanization encourage cooperation among farmers?
cards.answer: It encourages cooperation because farmers buy the machinery together.

cards.question: Name three disadvantages of farm mechanization.
cards.answer: Machinery can be expensive to purchase or hire; machines driven by fossil fuels cause environmental pollution; and tyre trafficking by heavy machines causes soil compaction and poor root growth.

cards.question: Which disadvantage of mechanization involves fossil fuels, and which involves soil?
cards.answer: Machinery driven by fossil fuels causes environmental pollution, while trafficking by the tyres of heavy farm machines causes soil compaction and poor root growth.

cards.question: What well-established social capitals of farmers may mechanization hamper?
cards.answer: It may hamper social capitals such as Debo or Guza.

cards.question: What are the labour and energy disadvantages of farm mechanization?
cards.answer: It reduces the amount of manual farm work available for workers and requires continuous supplies of energy from fuel and electricity.

cards.question: What are the three levels of mechanization and the three main power sources involved?
cards.answer: The levels are low, fair, and high mechanization. The three main power sources are human, animal, and mechanical power.

cards.question: What characterizes low level mechanization?
cards.answer: In low level mechanization, manual power used exceeds 33%.

cards.question: What characterizes fair level mechanization?
cards.answer: In fair level mechanization, animal power used is 34 to 66%.

cards.question: What characterizes high level mechanization?
cards.answer: In high level mechanization, mechanical power used is 67 to 100%.

cards.question: According to the unit summary, what does agricultural mechanization do to agricultural and food production?
cards.answer: Agricultural mechanization boosts agricultural and food production.

cards.question: True or false: mechanization has no maintenance cost.
cards.answer: False. Machinery is costly to purchase or hire and needs continuing energy and upkeep; the statement that mechanization has no maintenance cost is not correct.

cards.question: Why do different tools and equipment are needed at different stages of production?
cards.answer: Different tools are needed at the different stages of production because each tool serves a different purpose, from land preparation through planting, harvesting, irrigation, and feed processing.

cards.text: Mechanization is the use of {{c1::machinery}} to replace human or animal labor.

Mechanization in agriculture involves tools and machines for {{c1::agricultural land development}}, {{c2::crop production}}, {{c3::harvesting}}, {{c4::storage}}, {{c5::animal rearing}} and {{c6::processing of products at farm gate}}.
Simple farm tools or crude implements {{c1::slow down}} farming activities, so mechanized agriculture is needed to replace them.
Farm mechanization {{c1::saves time}}, {{c2::reduces the difficulty in farming}} and {{c3::saves labour}}.
