Farm mechanization reduces farm {{c1::health hazards}} and encourages {{c2::large-scale farming}}.
Farm mechanization increases {{c1::on-farm output}} and {{c2::income}} and encourages cooperation among farmers.
Farmers cooperate in mechanization by {{c1::buying the machinery together}}.
Machinery can be {{c1::expensive to purchase or hire}}.
Machineries driven by {{c1::fossil fuels}} cause {{c2::environmental pollution}}.
Trafficking by the tyres of heavy farm machines causes {{c1::soil compaction}} and {{c2::poor root growth}}.
Mechanization may hamper the well-established social capitals of farmers like {{c1::Debo}} or {{c2::Guza}}.
Farm mechanization reduces the amount of {{c1::manual farm work}} available for workers.
Farm mechanization requires continuous supplies of energy from {{c1::fuel}} and {{c2::electricity}}.
Mechanization in any area is categorized into three levels: {{c1::low}}, {{c2::fair}} and {{c3::high}} level.
The three main power sources involved in levels of mechanization are {{c1::human}}, {{c2::animal}} and {{c3::mechanical}}.

In {{c1::low}} level mechanization, {{c2::manual}} power used exceeds {{c3::33%}}; in {{c4::fair}} level mechanization, {{c5::animal}} power used is {{c6::34 to 66%}}; in {{c7::high}} level mechanization, {{c8::mechanical}} power used is {{c9::67 to 100%}}.
Agricultural mechanization boosts {{c1::agricultural and food production}}.
Based on the unit summary, {{c1::different tools}} are used in farming, each serving {{c2::different purposes}}.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 14::14.2 Types of Farm Tools and Equipment

cards.question: Give the range of agricultural equipment used on mechanized farms.
cards.answer: It ranges from the biggest combine harvesters to a hypodermic syringe for administering animal medication.

cards.question: On what basis are mechanized farm equipment divided into several categories?
cards.answer: They are divided into categories based on their functions.

cards.question: What are soil cultivation implements used for, and give three examples.
cards.answer: They are used for ploughing the soil and preparing it for cultivation. Examples include tilers, disk harrows, and moldboard ploughs.

cards.question: What are planting machines used for, and what is a good example?
cards.answer: They are used for planting saplings and seeds after the soil has been cultivated; a seeder is a good example.

cards.question: What is the function of harvesting equipment, and list four examples.
cards.answer: Harvesting equipment is used to gather crops once they have reached full maturity. Examples are combine harvester, diggers, trailers, and pickers.

cards.question: What is irrigation machinery used for, and give two examples.
cards.answer: Irrigation machinery is used for watering crops on large farms; examples are central pivot irrigation systems and pump units.

cards.question: List the equipment named as important in the feed processing industry.
cards.answer: Weighing scale, shovel, wheelbarrow, baler, hacker, chopper, millers or grinders, and mixers.

cards.question: List the dairy machinery mentioned in the textbook.
cards.answer: Buckets, milk containers, automatic milking machines, coolers, pasteurizers, homogenizer, cream separator, batch mixers, continuous freezers, butter churner, and cheese molder.

cards.question: What activities does miscellaneous agricultural equipment carry out, and what other materials are listed?
cards.answer: It carries out activities such as hay-making, shredding, and loading. Other materials listed are forestry machines, aerosols, middle level machinery, sophisticated materials, remote sensing, and fruit pickers.

cards.question: Which functional category includes central pivot irrigation systems and pump units?
cards.answer: Irrigation machinery, used for watering crops on large farms.

cards.question: Which functional category includes pasteurizers, homogenizers, and cheese molders?
cards.answer: Dairy machinery.

cards.question: Which categories of farm equipment are given as examples of functions needing machinery in the unit summary?
cards.answer: Soil cultivation, planting, harvesting, irrigation, and feed processing.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 14::14.2 Types of Farm Tools and Equipment

cards.text: Mechanized farm equipment ranges from the biggest {{c1::combine harvesters}} to a {{c2::hypodermic syringe}} for administering animal medication.
Mechanized farm equipment can be divided into several categories based on their {{c1::functions}}.
Soil cultivation implements are used for {{c1::ploughing the soil}} and preparing it for cultivation; examples include {{c2::tilers}}, {{c3::disk harrows}}, and {{c4::moldboard ploughs}}.
Planting machines are used for planting {{c1::saplings}} and {{c2::seeds}} after the soil has been cultivated; a good example is the {{c3::seeder}}.
Harvesting equipment gathers crops once they have reached {{c1::full maturity}}; examples are {{c2::combine harvester}}, {{c3::diggers}}, {{c4::trailers}}, and {{c5::pickers}}.
Irrigation machinery is used for {{c1::watering crops on large farms}}; examples are {{c2::central pivot irrigation systems}} and {{c3::pump units}}.
Feed processing equipment includes {{c1::weighing scale}}, {{c2::shovel}}, {{c3::wheelbarrow}}, {{c4::baler}}, {{c5::hacker}}, {{c6::chopper}}, {{c7::millers or grinders}}, and {{c8::mixers}}.
Dairy machinery includes {{c1::buckets}}, {{c2::milk containers}}, {{c3::automatic milking machines}}, {{c4::coolers}}, and {{c5::pasteurizers}}.
Other dairy machinery includes the {{c1::homogenizer}}, {{c2::cream separator}}, {{c3::batch mixers}}, {{c4::continuous freezers}}, {{c5::butter churner}}, and {{c6::cheese molder}}.
Miscellaneous agricultural equipment is used for activities such as {{c1::hay-making}}, {{c2::shredding}}, and {{c3::loading}}.

Other agricultural materials listed include {{c1::forestry machines}}, {{c2::aerosols}}, {{c3::middle level machinery}}, {{c4::sophisticated materials}}, {{c5::remote sensing}}, and {{c6::fruit pickers}}.
Examples of functions for which machinery and equipment are needed include {{c1::soil cultivation}}, {{c2::planting}}, {{c3::harvesting}}, {{c4::irrigation}}, and {{c5::feed processing}}.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 14::14.3 Uses of Some Farm Tools and Equipments

cards.question: Why is the tractor a key piece of farm equipment, and name three modern uses of tractors.
cards.answer: A tractor is one of the most popular and most essential pieces of farming equipment. Modern tractors can be used for planting, tilling, and spreading fertilizer.

cards.question: What is the function of a plough, and how is it pulled in modern times?
cards.answer: The plough is one of the most ancient agricultural tools; it cultivates the soil and prepares it for sowing. In modern times, ploughs are pulled by tractors mainly in the developed world.

cards.question: What is a subsoiler and what benefit does it give?
cards.answer: A subsoiler is a tractor-mounted implement used to break up and loosen the soil during deep tillage. It improves crop growth in areas where soil compaction is a problem.

cards.question: What is a cultivator used for, and what kind of motion does it usually have?
cards.answer: A cultivator carries out secondary tillage. It is usually equipped with rotary motion and is used for removing weeds and for pulverizing and stirring the soil before planting.

cards.question: What does a cultipacker do to the soil?
cards.answer: A cultipacker crushes soil clods, eliminates cracks, presses small stones, and removes air pockets to form a smooth, firm seedbed.

cards.question: What is the function of a harrow?
cards.answer: A harrow smoothes out and breaks up the surface of the soil, breaking up lumps of soil and producing soil structure suitable for seedbeds.

cards.question: What is a seed drill used for?
cards.answer: A seed drill is a machine used for planting seeds at equal distance and at the proper depth.

cards.question: What is a sprinkler used for on a crop farm?
cards.answer: A sprinkler is used to irrigate a field of crops; it helps irrigate large areas and maintain the needed level of humidity.

cards.question: What is a combiner (combine) harvester and which four operations does it combine?
cards.answer: It is a versatile machine designed to efficiently harvest a variety of grain crops. It combines reaping, threshing, gathering, and winnowing into a single process.

cards.question: What is the difference between a straw collector and a baler?
cards.answer: A straw collector collects straw or hay into small or large stacks, while a baler compresses hay or straw into bales for easy transport and storage.

cards.question: Why is a bale important for marketing?
cards.answer: A bale is the simplest minimum package for marketing hay or straw.

cards.question: What is a feed miller or grinder used for?
cards.answer: A feed miller or grinder is a power grinding-mill for reducing maize, wheat, barley, etc. to coarse meal suitable for animal feeding.

cards.question: What is a feed mixer used for during ration formulation?
cards.answer: A feed mixer is the appropriate equipment used to thoroughly and hygienically mix feed ingredients during ration formulation.

cards.question: Why is the milking machine the most important piece of equipment on a dairy farm?
cards.answer: It is used to harvest milk automatically.

cards.question: State the milk cooling rule given for dairy farms.
cards.answer: Milk should be cooled down to below 4°C within 2 hours of milking to avoid rapid deterioration; a milk cooler helps achieve this.

cards.question: What is a churner used for in dairy processing?
cards.answer: A churner is used to convert cream into butter and buttermilk.

cards.question: Describe an incubator and its purpose.
cards.answer: An incubator is a device with a fan and heater that keeps fertile eggs warm for 21 days of incubation.

cards.question: What can a sprayer be used for, and on what?
cards.answer: A sprayer is used for spraying liquid such as insecticides, herbicides, pesticides, and water on a crop farm, or on animals to control external parasites.

cards.question: What are pruning shears and what are they used for?
cards.answer: Pruning shears are sharp, heavy-duty scissors used for cutting branches of trees and plant stems.

cards.question: Besides milk cooling, mention two handling or hygiene practices stated in the text.
cards.answer: Feed ingredients must be mixed thoroughly and hygienically in a feed mixer, and sprayers are used on animals to control external parasites.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 15::15.1 Definition of basic terms in human nutrition

cards.question: What is nutrition according to the textbook?
cards.answer: Nutrition is the science of ingestion, digestion, absorption, assimilation and biosynthesis of nutrient in the body.

cards.question: Define food.
cards.answer: Food is any nutritious substance that is culturally acceptable and that people eat and drink to maintain life and growth.

cards.question: What does diet refer to?
cards.answer: Diet refers to the way people feed themselves and the foodstuffs they use. It is concerned with the eating patterns of individuals or a group and the sequence of meals in a day.

cards.question: What factors influence a person's diet?
cards.answer: Diet is strongly influenced by people's traditions and religion; people's economic position, their place in society and the possibilities offered by their natural surroundings are also important considerations.

cards.question: Distinguish macronutrients from micronutrients and give examples of each.
cards.answer: Macronutrients are needed in large amounts to maintain the body's structure and systems: carbohydrates, fat and protein. Micronutrients are needed in small quantities for a healthy life: minerals and vitamins; they are used to produce enzymes, hormones and other substances essential for proper growth and development.

cards.question: What does healthy eating mean, and what does a healthy diet provide?
cards.answer: Healthy eating means eating a variety of foods that give us all the essential nutrients needed to maintain health, feel good and have energy. A healthy diet provides sufficient nutrients, balance and variety, with different foods that provide optimal functioning of the body.

cards.question: Define a balanced diet.
cards.answer: A balanced diet is a diet that gives the body the right proportion of nutrients and calories needed to maintain a healthy body, with the desired proportion of carbohydrates, proteins and micronutrients.

cards.question: What are the six main classes of nutrients the human body needs?
cards.answer: The six main classes of nutrients are carbohydrates, lipids (fats and oils), proteins, vitamins, minerals and water.

cards.question: Which diet is described as containing a variety of foods that provide sufficient levels of calories and essential nutrients?
cards.answer: A balanced diet.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 15::15.1 Definition of basic terms in human nutrition

cards.text: Nutrition is the science of {{c1::ingestion}}, digestion, absorption, assimilation and biosynthesis of nutrient in the body.
Food is any {{c1::nutritious substance}} that is culturally acceptable and that people eat and drink to maintain {{c2::life and growth}}.
People may eat {{c1::twice, three or four times}} in a day, and this is strongly influenced by people's traditions and religion.
Carbohydrates, fat and protein are {{c1::macronutrients}}, while minerals and vitamins are {{c2::micronutrients}}.
Micronutrients are used by the body to produce {{c1::enzymes, hormones, and other substances}} essential for proper growth and development.
A healthy diet provides sufficient nutrients, {{c1::balance}}, and {{c2::variety}}.
A balanced diet gives the body the right proportion of {{c1::nutrients and calories}} needed to maintain a healthy body.
The main functions of nutrients are to {{c1::build and maintain body cells}}, regulate body functions and provide energy.
Minerals and vitamins regulate body function and serve as a {{c1::defending force for diseases}}, while water is needed for {{c2::optimal hydration}}.

cards.question: What are carbohydrates?
cards.answer: Carbohydrates are sugars, starches or fibers that provide energy to all the cells and tissues in the body.

cards.question: How much energy does one gram of carbohydrate generate?
cards.answer: One gram of carbohydrate generates four kilocalories of energy.

cards.question: What percentage of daily calories should carbohydrates constitute for optimal nutrition?
cards.answer: Carbohydrates should constitute 45 to 65% of the daily calorie for optimal nutrition.

cards.question: What are the limits recommended for free sugar intake?
cards.answer: Free sugar should be limited to 5% of total energy intake in children and 10% of total energy intake for adults.

cards.question: In what forms do carbohydrates exist in the human diet, and where do most calories in human diets come from?
cards.answer: Carbohydrates in the human diet exist mainly in the form of starches and various forms of sugars. Most of the calories in human diets are obtained from carbohydrates.

cards.question: In the review exercise, which nutrients primarily provide calories to meet energy needs?
cards.answer: Carbohydrates and fats.

cards.text: Carbohydrates are {{c1::sugars, starches or fibers}} that provide energy to all the cells and tissues in the body.
One gram of carbohydrate generates {{c1::four kilocalories}} of energy.
Carbohydrates should constitute {{c1::45 to 65%}} of the daily calorie for optimal nutrition.
Free sugar should be limited to {{c1::5%}} of total energy intake in children and {{c2::10%}} for adults.

cards.question: What are lipids, and how do oil and fat differ at room temperature?
cards.answer: Lipids include all fats and oils that occur in human diets. Usually oil refers to a liquid lipid and fat to a solid lipid at room temperature.

cards.question: How much energy does a gram of fat or oil generate?
cards.answer: A gram of fat/oil generates 9 kilocalories upon combustion, making lipids a concentrated source of energy for the human body.

cards.question: What share of daily calories should fat comprise?
cards.answer: Fat should comprise 20 to 35% of the daily calories of energy.

cards.question: What are the digestion products of dietary lipids and what functions do lipids serve?
cards.answer: Digestion of dietary lipid products consists of smaller molecules called fatty acids and glycerol. Lipids make the diet more palatable, serve as energy storage and in structural functions; stored fats are fuel reserves that store excess calories, and excess calories from carbohydrates, protein and lipids are stored as fat. The best fats are plant-based uncooked oils.

cards.text: Usually oil refers to {{c1::liquid}} and fat to {{c2::solid}} lipids at room temperature.
A gram of fat/oil generates {{c1::9 kilocalories}} upon combustion.
Fat should comprise {{c1::20 to 35%}} of the daily calories of energy.
Digestion of dietary lipid products consists of smaller molecules called {{c1::fatty acids and glycerol}}, and excess calories are stored in the form of {{c2::fat}}.
The best fats are {{c1::plant-based uncooked oils}}.

cards.question: What functions does protein carry out in the body?
cards.answer: Protein ensures the growth and development of muscles, bones, hair and skin, contributes to the formation of antibodies and hormones, and serves as a fuel source for cells and tissues when needed.

cards.question: What is the energy yield of protein and its recommended share of daily calories?
cards.answer: A gram of protein yields 4 kilocalories of energy, and proteins comprise 10 to 35% of the daily calorie for optimal nutrition.

cards.question: Which animal-source foods contain protein?
cards.answer: Red meat, eggs, dairy products and fish contain protein.

cards.question: Which plant foods are good sources of protein?
cards.answer: Beans, legumes, soy, nuts and some grains are good sources of protein.

cards.question: What are complete and incomplete proteins?
cards.answer: Protein is made up of organic compounds called amino acids. Proteins that contain all 20 amino acids required by the body are complete proteins; proteins from animal products including eggs and milk are complete because they supply amino acids the body cannot make itself. Plant proteins are incomplete because they do not contain all required amino acids, but they still play an important part in a healthy diet.

cards.text: Protein ensures the growth and development of {{c1::muscles, bones, hair, and skin}} and contributes to the formation of {{c2::antibodies and hormones}}.
A gram of protein yields {{c1::4 kilocalories}} of energy, and proteins comprise {{c2::10 to 35%}} of the daily calorie for optimal nutrition.
Foods such as {{c1::red meat, eggs, dairy products and fish}} contain protein, while beans, legumes, soy, nuts and some grains are also good sources.
Proteins are made up of organic compounds called {{c1::amino acids}}.
Proteins that contain all of the {{c1::20 amino acids}} required by the body are called complete proteins.
Proteins from animal products, including {{c1::eggs and milk}}, are complete, whereas proteins from plant foods are {{c2::incomplete}}.

cards.question: What roles do vitamins play in the body?
cards.answer: Vitamins can boost the immune system, strengthen teeth and bones, aid calcium absorption, help maintain healthy skin, help metabolize proteins and carbohydrates, and aid the brain and nervous system to function well.

cards.question: How do nutritionists divide vitamins, and which vitamins belong to each group?
cards.answer: Nutritionists divide vitamins into fat soluble and water soluble groups. The fat soluble vitamins are vitamin A, vitamin D, vitamin E and vitamin K. The water soluble vitamins are vitamin B and vitamin C.

cards.question: Why do fat-soluble and water-soluble vitamins differ in how often they must be eaten?
cards.answer: Fat-soluble vitamins can be stored in the body, so they do not need to be eaten every day; water-soluble vitamins are not stored, so they need to be eaten more frequently.

cards.question: What are the food sources of vitamins and who may need supplements?
cards.answer: Vegetables, fruits and meat are rich sources of all the vitamins. People with a restricted diet may need to take a vitamin supplement to avoid deficiency.

cards.question: Which vitamin deficiency is identified in the text as causing night blindness?
cards.answer: Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness.

cards.text: Vitamins can boost the {{c1::immune system}}, strengthen teeth and bones and aid {{c2::calcium absorption}}.
Vitamins help in maintaining healthy skin and in metabolizing {{c1::proteins and carbohydrates}}, and aid the brain and nervous system to function well.
The fat soluble vitamins are vitamin {{c1::A, vitamin D, vitamin E and vitamin K}}.
Water soluble vitamins are vitamin {{c1::B and vitamin C}}.
{{c1::Fat-soluble vitamins}} can be stored in the body so do not need to be eaten every day, while water-soluble vitamins are not stored.
Vegetables, fruits and {{c1::meat}} are rich source of all the vitamins, and people with a restricted diet may need a {{c2::vitamin supplement}}.
Deficiency of {{c1::vitamin A}} leads to night blindness.

cards.question: What are the two groups of minerals?
cards.answer: Minerals, the second type of micronutrients, are divided into major (macro-minerals) and trace minerals. The body needs a balance of minerals from both groups for optimal health.

cards.question: Define major or macro-minerals, give examples and state their functions.
cards.answer: Major or macro-minerals are elements with a Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) greater than 150 mg/day; examples are magnesium, calcium, phosphorus and potassium. They help the body balance water levels, maintain healthy skin, hair and nails, and improve bone health.

cards.question: Define trace minerals, give examples and state their functions.
cards.answer: Trace minerals are elements required in smaller amounts (microgram quantities), with RDA less than 150 mg/day; they usually play a catalytic role in enzymes. Examples are iron, selenium, zinc and manganese. They help strengthen bones, prevent tooth decay, reduce blood clotting, carry oxygen and support the immune system.

cards.question: List the food sources of minerals given in the textbook.
cards.answer: Sources of minerals include iodized table salt, nuts and seeds, vegetables, leafy greens, fruits, poultry, egg yolks, whole grains, and fortified bread and cereals.

cards.question: Which mineral is supplied by iodized table salt, and what deficiency is associated with it?
cards.answer: Iodine is supplied by iodized salt; iodine deficiency causes goiter.

cards.question: What is the role of iron and what disease results from iron deficiency?
cards.answer: Iron is a trace mineral that helps carry oxygen and support the immune system; iron deficiency causes anemia.

cards.question: What is the role of calcium and what problem results from calcium deficiency?
cards.answer: Calcium is a major mineral important for bone health; calcium deficiency results in weak bone.

cards.question: What is the role of zinc and what problem results from zinc deficiency?
cards.answer: Zinc is a trace mineral with a catalytic role in enzymes; zinc deficiency results in poor growth.

cards.question: Which micronutrient supplement is given to adolescent and pregnant women according to the review exercise?
cards.answer: Iron folic acid.

cards.text: Major or macro-minerals are elements with Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) greater than {{c1::150 mg/day}}.
Trace minerals are elements required in smaller amounts ({{c1::microgram quantities}}) with RDA less than {{c2::150 mg/day}}.
Examples of major minerals are {{c1::magnesium, calcium, phosphorus and potassium}}.
Examples of trace minerals are {{c1::iron, selenium, zinc and manganese}}.
Major minerals help the body to balance {{c1::water levels}}, maintain healthy skin, hair, and nails and to improve {{c2::bone health}}.
Trace minerals play a {{c1::catalytic role in enzymes}} and help in strengthening bones, preventing tooth decay and reducing blood clotting.
Sources of minerals include {{c1::iodized table salt}}, nuts and seeds, vegetables, leafy greens, fruits, poultry, egg yolks, whole grains, and fortified bread and cereals.
Iron deficiency causes {{c1::anemia}}.
Iodine deficiency causes {{c1::goiter}}.
Calcium deficiency causes {{c1::weak bone}} and zinc deficiency causes {{c2::poor growth}}.

cards.question: Why is water essential for survival?
cards.answer: A person can only survive a few days without water. The human body is made up of mostly water, and every cell requires water to function.

cards.question: What effects can slight dehydration cause?
cards.answer: Slight dehydration can cause headaches and impaired physical and mental functioning.

cards.question: What functions does water help with, and what is the best kind of water to drink?
cards.answer: Water helps flush toxins out, absorb shock, transport nutrients, prevent constipation, lubricate and rehydrate the body. The best choice is natural, unsweetened water from the tap or bottled sources.

cards.text: A person can only survive {{c1::a few days}} without water, and the human body is made up of mostly {{c2::water}}.
Slight dehydration can cause {{c1::headaches}} and impaired {{c2::physical and mental functioning}}.
Water helps flushing toxins out, absorbing shock, transporting nutrients, preventing constipation, lubricating and {{c1::rehydrating}} the body.
The best thing is to drink natural, unsweetened water from the {{c1::tap or bottled sources}}.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 15::15.3 Food groups and their sources

cards.question: What is a food group and how are foods commonly classified into groups?
cards.answer: A food group is a collection of foods that shares similar nutritional properties or biological classifications. Foods are often grouped according to the nutrient they contain in abundance and are typically divided into six groups based on the major nutrients they contain: vegetables, fruits, legumes and nuts, animal foods, fats and oils, and staples.

cards.question: Why is consumption of diversified foods important?
cards.answer: Different food groups provide different benefits, while most people, particularly the poor, consume only one or two types of staple foods. Consumption of diversified foods is important for the health of adults and for proper growth and development of children.

cards.question: What nutrients and benefits do vegetables provide, and what examples are given?
cards.answer: Vegetable food groups provide mostly vitamins, minerals and water. They also contain fiber, which is necessary for proper digestion and helps prevent constipation. Examples include tomato and cabbage.

cards.question: What nutrients do fruits provide, and what examples are given?
cards.answer: Fruits mostly provide carbohydrates, vitamins, minerals and water. Examples include oranges and apples.

cards.question: What does the legumes and nuts group provide, and what example is given?
cards.answer: This group provides mainly protein and is important for growth, repair and body building. It also contains a lot of fat and carbohydrates in addition to protein. Soybean is a representative example.

cards.question: What do animal foods provide and what examples are given?
cards.answer: Animal foods provide protein, fats, vitamins and minerals and contribute to growth and the development of strong bones. Examples are meat, egg and milk.

cards.question: What foods belong to the fats and oils group, and what does it provide?
cards.answer: Foods in this group include oil seeds such as soybeans, sesame seeds, linseeds and groundnuts, plus cooking oil and margarine. They provide additional energy (fat), essential fatty acids and fat-soluble vitamins.

cards.question: What foods are staples, and what do they provide?
cards.answer: Staple foods include cereal grains such as sorghum, maize, barley and oats, as well as wheat, teff, rice, starchy roots such as sweet potato, cassava and false banana, and starchy fruits like banana. They are good sources of energy, proteins, vitamins and minerals depending on how they are processed.

cards.question: From how many food groups should a healthy diet be achieved?
cards.answer: A healthy diet can be achieved by consuming food from at least four food groups.

cards.question: What is the energy share recommended for carbohydrates, fats and proteins for a healthy life?
cards.answer: For a healthy life, the recommended energy share is 55% carbohydrates, 30% fats and 15% proteins.

cards.question: Which food group mainly provides carbohydrates?
cards.answer: Staple foods, such as cereal grains, starchy roots and starchy fruits.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 15::15.3 Food groups and their sources

cards.text: A food group is a collection of foods that shares similar {{c1::nutritional properties or biological classifications}}.
Foods are typically divided into {{c1::six}} groups based on the major nutrients they contain.
Vegetable food groups provide mostly {{c1::vitamins, minerals, and water}} and fiber necessary for proper digestion and helping to prevent constipation.
Fruits mostly provide {{c1::carbohydrates, vitamins, minerals and water}}; representative examples are oranges and apples.
Legumes and nuts provide mainly {{c1::protein}} and are important for growth, repair and body building, but also contain fat and carbohydrates.
Animal foods provide {{c1::protein, fats, vitamins, and minerals}} and contribute to growth and the development of strong bones.
Foods of the fats and oils group include oil seeds such as soybeans, sesame seeds, linseeds and {{c1::groundnuts}}, as well as cooking oil and margarine.
Fats and oils provide additional energy, {{c1::essential fatty acids}} and fat-soluble vitamins.
Staple foods include cereal grains such as sorghum, maize, barley, oats, wheat, teff and {{c1::rice}}, starchy roots and starchy fruits like banana.
Staple foods are good sources of energy, proteins, vitamins and minerals depending on {{c1::how they are processed}}.
A healthy diet can be achieved by consuming food from at least {{c1::four food groups}}.
For a healthy life, the energy share of carbohydrates, fats and proteins is recommended to be {{c1::55%}}, {{c2::30%}} and {{c3::15%}}, respectively.

cards.question: State the United Nations Committee on World Food Security definition of food security.
cards.answer: Food security exists when all people, at all times, have physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food that meets their dietary needs and food preferences for an active and healthy life.

cards.question: How does a basic definition of food security differ from nutrition security?
cards.answer: A more basic definition of food security includes only access to a sufficient quantity of food, while nutrition security relates to having sufficiently nutritious food.

cards.question: Define nutrition security.
cards.answer: Nutrition security is a situation whereby individuals have access to sufficient, safe and nutritious foods, safe water and adequate sanitation, the ability to access health care services, and knowledge of sound household and community practices in childcare, food storage and preparation, and hygiene. It also includes the knowledge needed to care for and ensure a healthy and active life for all household members.

cards.question: What are the four pillars of food and nutrition security?
cards.answer: The four pillars are food availability, access, utilization (consumption) and stability.

cards.question: What is food and nutrition insecurity, and what do people experiencing it often consume?
cards.answer: Food and nutrition insecurity is a situation in which people do not have access to the basic elements of good nutrition. People experiencing food insecurity often consume a nutrient-poor diet.

cards.question: List the drivers of food insecurity given in the textbook.
cards.answer: People experience food insecurity due to lack of resources (financial and other resource types), lack of access to nutritious food at affordable prices, lack of access to food due to geographical isolation, lack of motivation or knowledge about a nutritious diet, lack of access to clean drinking water, lack of environmental hygiene, and lack of good health infrastructure.

cards.question: Which pillar of food security is the state of having adequate dietary intake and the ability to absorb and use nutrients in the body?
cards.answer: Utilization (consumption).

cards.question: What does nutrition security demand according to the unit summary?
cards.answer: The intake of a variety of foods that provide the six essential nutrients.

cards.text: Food security exists when all people, at all times, have {{c1::physical and economic access}} to sufficient, safe and nutritious food.
Food must meet dietary needs and food preferences for an {{c1::active and healthy life}}.
A more basic definition of food security includes only access to sufficient {{c1::quantity}} of food, while nutrition security relates to having sufficiently {{c2::nutritious}} food.

Nutrition security requires access to sufficient, safe and nutritious foods, safe water, adequate sanitation, health care services and knowledge of sound practices in {{c1::childcare, food storage and preparation and hygiene}}.
The four pillars of food/nutrition security are food availability, access, utilization and {{c1::stability}}.
Availability is about having sufficient quantities of appropriate food and refers to the {{c1::physical existence of food}}.
Access refers to having adequate {{c1::income or other resources}} to access food in sufficient quantity, quality and diversity, and depends mainly on household resources and {{c2::prices}}.
Utilization/consumption is having adequate dietary intake and the ability to {{c1::absorb and use nutrients in the body}}.
Stability is having access to adequate food {{c1::at all times}}, with household supply constant during the year and in the long-term.

People experience food insecurity due to lack of resources, affordable nutritious food, access caused by geographical isolation, motivation or knowledge, clean drinking water, environmental hygiene and {{c1::good health infrastructure}}.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 15::15.5 Agriculture-nutrition linkage and nutrition-sensitive agriculture

cards.question: What is the agriculture-nutrition linkage?
cards.answer: Agriculture-nutrition linkage describes the set of relationships that shows the mutual dependence of nutrition, health and agriculture. Agriculture produces the vast majority of the world's food supply and has great potential to impact the food and nutrition security of poor, rural households.

cards.question: How do agriculture and nutrition or health status affect each other?
cards.answer: Changes in the agricultural sector can have significant effects on individual health and nutritional status; conversely, changes in nutrition or health status are expected to affect agricultural production.

cards.question: What are the three pillars of good nutrition?
cards.answer: The three pillars of good nutrition are food security, good care and good health.

cards.question: Why must agriculture pay attention to nutrition, and what approach emerged in the past few decades?
cards.answer: Links between improved nutritional status and improved work capacity and productivity are clear, so to enhance agricultural productivity and food and nutrition security the agriculture sector must pay more attention to nutrition. Agricultural development is now expected to maximize opportunities to improve health and nutrition; the emergence of nutrition-sensitive agriculture in the past few decades is one such developmental approach.

cards.question: Define nutrition-sensitive agriculture.
cards.answer: Nutrition-sensitive agriculture is a food-based approach to agricultural development that prioritizes nutritionally rich foods, dietary diversity and food fortification to overcome malnutrition. It goes beyond food production to address the underlying causes of malnutrition and micronutrient deficiencies.

cards.question: What does the nutrition-sensitive approach stress and what is its overall objective?
cards.answer: It stresses the multiple benefits derived from enjoying a variety of foods, recognizes the nutritional value of food for good nutrition, and recognizes the importance and social significance of food and agriculture for supporting livelihoods. Its overall objective is to make the global food system better equipped to produce good nutritional outcomes.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 15::15.5 Agriculture-nutrition linkage and nutrition-sensitive agriculture

cards.text: Agriculture-nutrition linkage describes the set of relationships that shows the mutual dependence of {{c1::nutrition, health and agriculture}}.
Changes in the agricultural sector can have significant effects on individual {{c1::health and nutritional status}}, and changes in nutrition or health can affect agricultural production.
Food security is one of the three pillars of good nutrition, along with {{c1::good care and good health}}.
Nutrition-sensitive agriculture is a {{c1::food-based approach}} to agricultural development.
It prioritizes {{c1::nutritionally rich foods, dietary diversity, and food fortification}} to overcome malnutrition.
Agriculture is nutrition-sensitive when it goes beyond {{c1::food production}} to address the underlying causes of malnutrition and micronutrient deficiencies.
The overall objective of nutrition-sensitive agriculture is to make the global food system better equipped to produce {{c1::good nutritional outcomes}}.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 15::15.6 Malnutrition and its causes in Ethiopia

cards.question: Define malnutrition and name its two main types.
cards.answer: Malnutrition is a condition that happens when your diet does not contain the right amount of nutrients. Its two main types are under-nutrition, a lack of healthy foods in the diet, and over-nutrition, an excessive intake of unhealthy foods.

cards.question: Define obesity (being overweight) and state its health risks.
cards.answer: Obesity (being overweight) is an indicator of excess nutrient intake relative to requirements. People are considered clinically overweight when their body weight is more than 20% greater than recommended for the relevant height. They are at risk of chronic illnesses such as diabetes, heart disease and various forms of cancer.

cards.question: Define stunting and state its causes.
cards.answer: Stunting is chronic or recurrent undernutrition resulting from poor diet, repeated infection and inadequate psychosocial stimulation. Children are defined as stunted if their height-for-age is below the average for their age, usually because of insufficient food intake or frequent infections.

cards.question: Define wasting and state its causes, measurement and consequence.
cards.answer: Wasting is an indicator of acute or short-term undernutrition that results in a child who is very thin for their height and sex. It often occurs because of lack of access to food, infection or acute illness such as diarrhea. Children are defined as wasted if their weight-for-height is less than negative two standard deviations (<-2 SD) according to the WHO child growth standard. Severe wasting often leads to child mortality.

cards.question: Define being underweight and give its measurement criteria.
cards.answer: Being underweight is an indicator of both acute and chronic undernutrition; underweight children have low weight for their age. People are considered underweight when their body mass is 15% below what is considered normal for a person's age and height. Children are underweight if their weight-for-age is below negative two standard deviations (<-2 SD) according to the WHO child growth standard.

cards.question: Define micronutrient deficiency and list the most important ones of global public health with their signs.
cards.answer: Micronutrient deficiency is a deficiency of one or more vitamins or minerals required for body function, optimal health, growth and development; it can occur when the body cannot absorb nutrients from food or when not enough food containing a specific nutrient is consumed. The most important are iron deficiency (anemia), vitamin A deficiency (night blindness), iodine deficiency (goiter), zinc deficiency (poor growth), calcium deficiency (weak bone) and folic acid deficiency (neural tube defect).

cards.question: What is Body Mass Index (BMI) and how is it calculated?
cards.answer: Body Mass Index (BMI) tells us if enough energy is being consumed adequately. It is a person's weight in kilograms divided by the square of height in meters. A high BMI can indicate high body fatness; BMI screens for weight categories that may lead to health problems but does not diagnose body fatness or health. For adults over 18 it can be used as an indicator of nutritional status, but for children and adolescents the age and sex must be considered.

cards.question: What are the adult BMI categories given in the unit summary?
cards.answer: A BMI of 18.5 - 25 is considered normal, 25 - 30 is overweight, over 30 is obese and below 18.5 is thin/underweight.

cards.question: What is the magnitude of malnutrition in Ethiopia and who is mainly affected?
cards.answer: Malnutrition is among the major public health problems in Ethiopia and affects many people, primarily children, pregnant and lactating women. Stunting among children under age 5 was 57.7% in 2000, 50.8% in 2005, 44.4% in 2011, 38.4% in 2016 and 36.8% in 2019, a very high status. Wasting was 12.2%, 12.2%, 9.7%, 9.9% and 7.0%, a medium status. Underweight was 41%, 33%, 29%, 23.3% and 21%, a high status. Overweight was 1.8%, 4.0%, 1.7%, 2.8% and 2.3%. Source: Ethiopia Demographic Health Survey (EDHS).

cards.question: How are the causes of malnutrition classified, and what does each level include?
cards.answer: Immediate causes are lack of access to sufficient quality and quantity of food and poor health status with frequent incidences of infectious diseases. Underlying causes are household food insecurity, sub-optimal feeding and caring practices and health services, and WASH (Water Access, Sanitation and Hygiene) practices. Basic causes are political, financial, social, cultural and environmental conditions, and infrastructure.

cards.question: What are the short-term and long-term impacts of malnutrition?
cards.answer: In the short term malnutrition is associated with weakness and altered immunity, making individuals more vulnerable to infections and death; one-third of child mortality worldwide is attributed to malnutrition. In the long term it can lead to impaired mental development, poor educational performance in childhood, decreased ability to work productively in adulthood, and low birth weight that tracks into adulthood and may increase the risk of chronic diseases such as diabetes and cardiovascular diseases. Failure to perform physical work decreases individual productivity and eventually leads to poor economic status for individuals, societies and the country.

cards.question: List the mechanisms for solving the malnutrition problem given in the textbook.
cards.answer: The mechanisms are: educating communities about the dangers of malnutrition; promoting improved and nutrition-sensitive agricultural practices; prioritizing infants, pregnant and lactating women for nutrition-based interventions; adopting dietary changes such as eating a variety of foods rich in essential nutrients; promoting diversified, nutrient dense and safe foods; promoting animal source foods, fruits, vegetables, bio-fortified and fortified foods including iodized salt; supporting families to manage factors affecting a child's nutritional intake; and timely treating any underlying medical conditions causing malnutrition.

cards.question: Which groups are most vulnerable to malnutrition and should receive priority?
cards.answer: Infants, pregnant and lactating women are the most vulnerable group to malnutrition, and priority needs to be given to them.

cards.question: How are children whose height is below the average for their age classified?
cards.answer: They are considered stunted.

cards.question: Which forms of malnutrition result from long-term food shortages?
cards.answer: Stunting and underweight.

cards.question: What is the 2019 status of stunting among children under age 5 in Ethiopia?
cards.answer: Very high, with a prevalence of 36.8%.

cards.question: What is the 2019 status of wasting among children under age 5 in Ethiopia?
cards.answer: Medium, with a prevalence of 7.0%.

cards.question: What percentage of Ethiopian children under age 5 were underweight in 2016?
What percentage of Ethiopian children under age 5 were overweight in 2019?
What is the source of the Ethiopia child malnutrition trend data in Table 15.2?
cards.answer: Ethiopia Demographic Health Survey (EDHS).

cards.question: Which indicator reflects both acute and chronic undernutrition?
cards.answer: Being underweight.

cards.question: Which form of malnutrition is an indicator of excess nutrient intake relative to requirements?
cards.answer: Obesity (being overweight).

cards.question: What share of child mortality worldwide is attributed to malnutrition?
cards.answer: One-third of child mortality.

cards.question: Which chronic diseases may result when low birth weight tracks into adulthood?
cards.answer: Diabetes and cardiovascular diseases.

cards.question: What does WASH stand for among the underlying causes of malnutrition?
cards.answer: Water Access, Sanitation and Hygiene.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 15::15.6 Malnutrition and its causes in Ethiopia

cards.text: Malnutrition happens when your diet does not contain the {{c1::right amount of nutrients}}; its two main types are {{c2::under-nutrition and over-nutrition}}.

People are considered clinically overweight when their body weight is more than {{c1::20%}} greater than recommended for the relevant height, putting them at risk of diabetes, heart disease and cancer.
Children are defined as stunted if their {{c1::height-for-age}} is below the average for their age, usually from insufficient food intake or frequent infections.

Wasting is an indicator of {{c1::acute or short-term undernutrition}}; children are wasted if their weight-for-height is less than {{c2::negative two standard deviations (<-2 SD)}} according to the WHO child growth standard.
People are considered underweight when their body mass is {{c1::15%}} below the normal range for age and height, or when weight-for-age is below <-2 SD.

The most important micronutrient deficiencies of global public health are iron deficiency ({{c1::anemia}}), vitamin A deficiency (night blindness), iodine deficiency (goiter), zinc (poor growth), calcium (weak bone) and folic acid (neural tube defect).
BMI is a person's weight in {{c1::kilograms}} divided by the square of height in {{c2::meters}}.
A normal BMI is {{c1::18.5 - 25}}, overweight is {{c2::25 - 30}}, obese is over {{c3::30}} and thin/underweight is below {{c4::18.5}}.
In Ethiopia, stunting among children under age 5 declined from {{c1::57.7%}} in 2000 to {{c2::36.8%}} in 2019, but its status is still very high.
In Ethiopia, wasting among children under age 5 was {{c1::12.2%}} in 2000 and {{c2::7.0%}} in 2019 (medium status), while underweight fell from 41% to {{c3::21%}} (high status).
Immediate causes of malnutrition are lack of access to sufficient quality and quantity of food and {{c1::poor health status and frequent incidences of infectious diseases}}.
Underlying causes of malnutrition include household food insecurity, sub-optimal feeding and caring practices and health services, and {{c1::WASH (Water Access, Sanitation and Hygiene) practices}}.
Basic causes of malnutrition are {{c1::political, financial, social, cultural, and environmental conditions, and infrastructure}}.
In the short term malnutrition is associated with weakness and altered immunity, and {{c1::one-third of child mortality}} worldwide is attributed to malnutrition.

In the long term malnutrition can lead to impaired mental development, poor educational performance, decreased ability to work productively and increased risk of chronic diseases such as {{c1::diabetes and cardiovascular diseases}}.

Mechanisms for solving malnutrition include educating communities, nutrition-sensitive agricultural practices, dietary changes, diversified nutrient dense safe foods, and prioritizing {{c1::infants, pregnant and lactating women}}.
Interventions promote animal source foods, fruits, vegetables, bio-fortified and fortified foods including {{c1::Iodized salt}}, and timely treatment of underlying medical conditions.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 16::16.1 Importance of diversified food production

cards.question: What is agricultural food diversification?
cards.answer: Agricultural food diversification is the act of introducing or producing a variety of food from agricultural activities.

cards.question: Why is it important to produce and consume different types of food?
cards.answer: Different food types provide different nutrients that people need to be healthy; because different foods and food groups are good sources of various macro and micronutrients, a diverse diet is the best way of ensuring people have all the nutrients they need.

cards.question: How does food variety benefit adults and women who are pregnant or breastfeeding?
cards.answer: Adults need a variety of food to have energy and be productive. Women who are pregnant or breastfeeding need different foods for the baby and for themselves to be healthy and strong.

cards.question: Define an integrated farming system as given in the key term box.
cards.answer: An integrated farming system is a sustainable agricultural system that integrates livestock, crop production, fish, poultry, tree crops, plantation crops and other systems that benefit each other. It is based on the concept that 'there is no waste'.

cards.question: What subsystems are involved in agricultural diversification or integrated farming systems, and why are their interactions important for nutrition?
cards.answer: They involve several subsystems including crops, animals and fish. These synergistic interactions have a greater total effect on nutrition than the sum of the individual effects.

cards.question: How can improved nutritional and health status affect household production and income?
cards.answer: Improved nutritional and health status can increase individual productivity, which leads to improved household production and income.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 16::16.1 Importance of diversified food production

cards.text: Agriculture is an indispensable sector for {{c1::food and nutrition security}}.
Children need a variety of food to {{c1::grow well and develop properly}}.
It is recommended that an individual consume at least {{c1::four food groups}} in each meal.
An integrated farming system is based on the concept that '{{c1::there is no waste}}'.
A diverse diet most likely meets both {{c1::known}} and, as yet, {{c2::unknown}} needs for human health.
Diversification of foods grown by a household can improve {{c1::dietary diversity and nutrition outcomes}}.

cards.question: Define dietary diversity.
cards.answer: Dietary diversity is defined as the number of different individual food items or food groups consumed over a given period of time.

cards.question: Which food groups are often lacking in the Ethiopian diet described in the text?
cards.answer: The diet often lacks animal source foods (meat, fish, eggs and dairy products) and fruits and vegetables.

cards.question: What is the purpose of food and dietary diversification strategies at the community and household levels?
cards.answer: Such strategies can maximize the availability of adequate amounts and a greater variety of nutritious foods.

cards.question: List the dietary diversification activities that involve cropping and farming systems and the introduction of new crops.
cards.answer: They include promotion of mixed cropping and integrated farming systems, and introduction of new crops with high nutritional/health importance such as soybean.

cards.question: What does encouraging the use of underexploited traditional foods and home gardens involve?
cards.answer: It involves encouraging people to use traditional foods that are underexploited and to establish or use home gardens so that a greater variety of nutritious foods is available.

cards.question: Which crops does the text recommend for urban farming, and why?
cards.answer: It recommends fostering urban farming of crops with high nutritional value, that is, deep colored fruits and green leafy vegetables.

cards.question: Which animal-related activities are encouraged as dietary diversification strategies?
cards.answer: Keeping small animals (goats, sheep and poultry) and fish farming are encouraged.

cards.question: How does improved preservation and storage of fruits and vegetables support dietary diversification?
cards.answer: It reduces wastage, post-harvest losses and the effects of seasonality, making nutritious foods available for longer periods.

cards.question: Name two diversification strategies related to processing and income.
cards.answer: Strengthening small-scale agro-processing and food industries, and encouraging income generation at individual or household level.

cards.question: What is complementary feeding, and what other nutrition education topics are promoted?
cards.answer: Complementary feeding is food in addition to breast milk for children between 6 and 23 months of age. Other nutrition education topics include food quality and safety, hygiene and sanitation issues.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT a dietary diversification strategy: sheep farming, soybean production, mono-cropping, or complementary feeding?
cards.answer: Mono-cropping is not a dietary diversification strategy; the others are listed as diversification activities.

cards.text: Low dietary diversity is a particular problem in Ethiopia where the diet is frequently based on starchy staples such as {{c1::teff, maize, sorghum, enset, and wheat}}.
Consumption of diversified foods is important for the {{c1::health of adults}} and the {{c2::proper growth and development of children}}.
Community and household strategies maximize the availability of {{c1::adequate amounts}} and {{c2::greater variety of nutritious foods}}.
Introducing new crops with high nutritional/health importance includes crops such as {{c1::soybean}}.
Promotion of mixed cropping and {{c1::integrated farming systems}} is a dietary diversification strategy.
Urban farming of crops with high nutritional value focuses on {{c1::deep colored fruits and green leafy vegetables}}.
Encouraging the keeping of small animals includes {{c1::goats, sheep and poultry}}, together with fish farming.
Improved preservation and storage of fruits and vegetables reduces wastage, {{c1::post-harvest losses}} and effects of {{c2::seasonality}}.
Strengthening {{c1::small-scale agro-processing and food industries}} is a food and dietary diversification strategy.
Complementary feeding means food in addition to breast milk for children between {{c1::6 and 23 months}} of age.
Nutrition education promoted as a diversification strategy includes food quality and safety, hygiene and {{c1::sanitation}} issues.

cards.question: What are dietary modifications?
cards.answer: Dietary modifications are changes made to increase the bioavailability of micronutrients in food at the commercial or household level.

cards.question: At what levels and stages can dietary modifications occur?
cards.answer: They can occur at the commercial or household level, during food preparation, processing, and consumption.

cards.question: What is the main aim of most dietary modifications, and give one example?
cards.answer: Most modifications aim to reduce micronutrient deficiencies. One example is the simultaneous consumption of iron-rich foods with ascorbic acid (vitamin C).

cards.question: Define bioavailability as stated in the key term box.
cards.answer: Bioavailability is the ability of a substance to be absorbed and used by the body.

cards.question: List all six reasons why the normal diet may be modified.
cards.answer: To provide a change in the constituents of the diet; to maintain, restore or correct nutritional status; to include all nutrients in the diet; to increase or decrease the energy value of the diet; to provide foods bland in flavor; and to modify the intervals of feeding.

cards.question: Which reasons for diet modification concern energy value, flavor and feeding intervals?
cards.answer: The diet may be modified to increase or decrease the energy value of the diet, to provide foods bland in flavor, and to modify the intervals of feeding.

cards.question: Name the four techniques of nutrient enrichment described in this unit.
cards.answer: The four techniques are fortification, germination, fermentation and roasting.

cards.question: What is the goal of dietary modifications in terms of the population, according to the unit summary?
cards.answer: The goal is to reduce the number of people in the population who suffer from micronutrient deficiencies, and to increase the nutritive value of food.

cards.text: Dietary modifications are changes made to increase the {{c1::bioavailability}} of micronutrients in food.
Dietary modifications may occur during food {{c1::preparation, processing, and consumption}}.
One example of dietary modification is the simultaneous consumption of iron-rich foods with {{c1::ascorbic acid (vitamin C)}}.
{{c1::Bioavailability}} is the ability of a substance to be absorbed and used by the body.
The normal diet may be modified to maintain, restore or correct {{c1::nutritional status}}.
The normal diet may be modified to include {{c1::all nutrients}} in the diet.
The four techniques of nutrient enrichment are {{c1::fortification, germination, fermentation and roasting}}.
Dietary modifications can be done at the {{c1::commercial or household}} level.

cards.question: Define food fortification.
cards.answer: Food fortification is the practice of deliberately increasing the content of an essential micronutrient, that is, vitamins, minerals and trace elements, in a food.

cards.question: What does food fortification aim to achieve?
cards.answer: It aims to improve the nutritional quality of the food supply and provide a public health benefit with minimal risk to health.

cards.question: Why is adding micronutrients to staples and condiments important?
cards.answer: Diets that lack variety can be deficient in certain nutrients, and staple foods of a region can lack particular nutrients; adding micronutrients to staples and condiments can prevent large-scale deficiencies.

cards.question: Why is food fortification considered a sound public health strategy?
cards.answer: It is cost effective and can reach large segments of at-risk populations through existing food delivery systems without requiring major changes in existing consumption patterns.

cards.text: Food fortification deliberately increases the content of {{c1::an essential micronutrient}} in a food.
Food fortification reduces the number of people with {{c1::dietary deficiencies}} within a population.
According to the FAO, the most common fortified foods are cereals and cereal-based products, milk/milk products, {{c1::fats and oils}}, tea and other beverages, and infant formulas.
Fortification reaches at-risk populations through {{c1::existing food delivery systems}} without requiring major changes in consumption patterns.

cards.question: What is germination as a food processing method, and for whom is it traditionally used?
cards.answer: Germination of pulses and cereals is a traditional method of food processing, extensively used in preparing foods for weaning babies and for elderly people. It is a process in which a pulse or cereal sprouts small shoots when kept with a small amount of water.

cards.question: How should grains and pulses be soaked before sprouting, and what mistake causes nutrient loss?
cards.answer: They need to be soaked in just enough water so that all of it is absorbed. If the extra water in which they are soaked is thrown away, a lot of nutrients are lost.

cards.question: Name grains that can be sprouted and describe what is done after sprouting.
cards.answer: Grains like wheat, barley and sorghum can be sprouted. They can then be dried in shade and roasted lightly, then ground and used in many dishes. Pulses are sprouted first and then steamed and consumed.

cards.question: What happens to vitamin content when sprouting is followed by fermentation?
cards.answer: When sprouting is followed by fermentation, the vitamin content becomes much more improved.

cards.question: How does germination increase the digestibility of foods?
cards.answer: Some carbohydrates and proteins are broken down into smaller and easily digestible forms; grains and pulses become soft after sprouting, so they take less time for cooking and are easy to digest.

cards.question: What effect does germination have on nutritive value, cost and vitamins/minerals?
cards.answer: Germination increases the nutritive value of food with no additional cost. Some vitamins and minerals also increase: vitamin B becomes almost double in quantity while vitamin C increases almost 10 times.

cards.question: Which nutrient enrichment technique is described as costing nothing extra and is the low-cost option in the review exercise?
cards.answer: Germination: it increases the nutritive value of food with no additional cost, making it the low-cost technique compared with fortification, fermentation and roasting.

cards.text: Germination is a process in which a pulse or cereal will sprout small shoots when kept with {{c1::a small amount of water}}.
Normally, {{c1::8 to 16 hours}} are needed for soaking and {{c2::12 to 24 hours}} for sprouting.
The cloth in which the soaked grain or pulse is tied should be kept {{c1::moist all the time}}.
When sprouting is followed by fermentation, the {{c1::vitamin content}} becomes much more improved.
Germination increases the digestibility of foods because some {{c1::carbohydrates and proteins}} are broken down into smaller, easily digestible forms.
During germination, vitamin B becomes almost {{c1::double}} in quantity while vitamin C increases almost {{c2::10 times}}.
Grains and pulses become {{c1::soft}} after sprouting, so they take less time for cooking and are easy to digest.

cards.question: Define fermentation as described in the unit.
cards.answer: Fermentation is a process in which some micro-organisms are added to the food; it is the chemical breakdown of a substance by bacteria, yeasts or other microorganisms, typically involving effervescence and the giving off of heat.

cards.question: How do micro-organisms change nutrients during fermentation?
cards.answer: They change nutrients already present in foods into simpler and more easily digested forms and also make other new nutrients. In dough they use up some nutrients and change them into better quality nutrients, and make some new nutrients.

cards.question: What visible change does fermentation cause in dough?
cards.answer: Fermentation is what makes dough rise and become almost double in quantity.

cards.question: Give three examples of fermented foods in Ethiopia.
cards.answer: Milk curd, bread and Injera are examples of fermented foods in Ethiopia. Kita is not listed as an example.

cards.question: Which minerals are improved by fermentation, and what is the nutritional result?
cards.answer: During fermentation of cereals and foods such as peas, chickpeas and beans, calcium, phosphorus and iron are changed into better quality forms that are then easily absorbed by the body.

cards.question: How does fermentation improve digestibility and acceptability of foods?
cards.answer: Micro-organisms break proteins and carbohydrates into smaller parts that are easier to digest; fermented foods become spongy and soft and are liked by children and adults.

cards.text: Different micro-organisms are used in fermentation: {{c1::yeast}} for bread and {{c2::bacteria}} for yoghurt.
Fermentation typically involves {{c1::effervescence}} and the giving off of {{c2::heat}}.
Fermentation makes dough rise and become almost {{c1::double in quantity}}.
Milk curd, bread and {{c1::Injera}} are examples of fermented foods in Ethiopia.
During fermentation of cereals and pulses, {{c1::calcium, phosphorus, and iron}} are changed into better quality and are easily absorbed by the body.
Fermented foods become {{c1::spongy and soft}} and are liked by children and adults.

cards.question: Define roasting as a cooking method.
cards.answer: Roasting is a cooking method that uses dry heat where hot air envelops the food. It uses indirect, diffused heat as in an oven and can enhance the flavor of food.

cards.question: For which foods and cooking situations is roasting suitable?
cards.answer: Roasting uses indirect, diffused heat as in an oven, so it is suitable for slower cooking of meat in a larger, whole piece. Meats and most root and bulb vegetables can be roasted; it is mainly used for fleshy food like fish, meat or chicken.

cards.question: Explain how roasting keeps food juicy.
cards.answer: The heat seals the outside part of the food, and the juice inside the food cooks it. When heat is applied to the outer covering it seals it up, thereby trapping all the juices inside the food.

cards.text: Roasting is a cooking method that uses {{c1::dry heat}} where hot air envelops the food.
Roasting uses {{c1::indirect, diffused heat as in an oven}}, which is suitable for slower cooking of meat in a larger, whole piece.
In roasting, the heat seals the outside part of the food and the {{c1::juice inside the food}} cooks the food.
Roasting is mainly used when cooking fleshy food like {{c1::fish, meat or chicken}}.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 16::16.4 Indigenous knowledge in nutrition sensitive agriculture

cards.question: Describe the farming systems and production practices of Ethiopian farmers in the nutrition-sensitive agriculture section.
cards.answer: Ethiopian farmers are engaged in mixed crop/livestock farming systems. They produce both plant- and animal-based foods for household consumption and for market, and organic vegetable and fruit production is becoming a common practice in most parts of the country.

cards.question: What is Chuko, where is it common, and why is it valued?
cards.answer: Chuko is a common food in most parts of Oromia regional state. It is made from barley flour mixed with concentrated butter and is a very rich source of essential nutrients.

cards.question: How is enset used as a traditional food, and where?
cards.answer: Enset is utilized in its many forms, for example Kocho, mainly in the southern part of Ethiopia.

cards.question: How are nutrient-rich traditional foods such as Chuko and Kocho typically used?
cards.answer: They are luxurious and are often used to complement staple foods or during ceremonies.

cards.question: Name three wild plants with potential for diversified food consumption and state what they contain.
cards.answer: Wild plants such as shoot of bamboo (Oxytenanthera abyssinica L.), stinging nettle (Urtica simensis L.) and some wild mushroom species have been found to be rich in valuable minerals.

cards.question: In which parts of Ethiopia are these mineral-rich wild plants dominantly found, and how are they used?
cards.answer: They are dominantly found in north-western Ethiopia, the central highlands and south-western Ethiopia, and are consumed as food by local communities in the areas where they are found.

cards.question: How can edible wild plants contribute to nutritional security according to the text?
cards.answer: Domestication of these edible wild plants in appropriate agroecologies and their promotion for consumption can contribute towards improving food diversification of diet and nutritional security.

decks.name: Grade 11::Unit 16::16.4 Indigenous knowledge in nutrition sensitive agriculture

cards.text: In Ethiopia, farmers are engaged in {{c1::mixed crop/livestock farming systems}} and produce both plant- and animal-based foods.
Chuko, common in most parts of Oromia regional state, is made from {{c1::barley flour mixed with concentrated butter}}.
Enset is utilized in its many forms, for example {{c1::Kocho}}, mainly in the southern part of Ethiopia.
Nutrient-rich traditional foods are luxurious and often used to {{c1::complement staple foods}} or during ceremonies.
Wild plants rich in valuable minerals include shoot of bamboo ({{c1::Oxytenanthera abyssinica L.}}), stinging nettle (Urtica simensis L.) and some wild mushroom species.
These wild plants are dominantly found in {{c1::north-western Ethiopia, central highlands and south-western Ethiopia}}.
They are consumed as food by {{c1::local communities}} in the areas where they are found.
Domestication of edible wild plants in {{c1::appropriate agroecologies}} and promotion for consumption improve food diversification of diet and nutritional security.
